# Flourish Forever — visual and interaction design

**Creator / creative direction:** Babuni.dev.  
**Source:** current 0.3.1-beta UI Lua. The initial audit found no artwork; creator-supplied portfolio artwork was added on October 27, 2026.

## A stage manager for a character's gestures

The player isn't authoring a new combat effect. They're deciding **how their character reacts to moments already happening in game**. That implies a configuration tool which stays out of combat most of the time.

Flourish Forever uses a Blizzard-style inset window rather than floating new action buttons over the battlefield. The approximately **620×520-pixel** panel can be dragged and closed; its content is plainly divided between the spell that triggers a flourish and the actions the character might perform afterward.

The player opens it with **/flourish**, while `/flourish config`, `ui`, `/flourishforever`, and `/rit` are other entry points. Because the UI is built lazily, nothing has to stay onscreen during a fight.

## Progressive choices inside the panel

At the top, one **Enable ability emotes** checkbox acts as the character's master switch. This doesn't erase the spell configurations and is initially enabled but silent when no abilities are added.

Immediately below, **Add ability** opens a dropdown populated from the character's spellbook, excluding known passive spells. The configured abilities occupy a scrollable list on the left. Choosing an item reveals its controls in the editor on the right; removing it removes both its saved settings and session cooldown entry.

The right editor answers three approachable questions:
- **How often?** Chance from 0% to 100%, in 1% increments.
- **How soon again?** Cooldown from 0 to 120 seconds, in whole seconds.
- **What can happen?** A scrollable list of native WoW emote tokens with independent checkboxes. One enabled token gets picked at random.

No random emote plays when the player leaves the pool empty. A spell added for the first time starts at 100% chance, 6-second cooldown and ROAR checked; those are starter values, not an immutable character identity.

## Visual vocabulary

The addon uses the existing game UI templates: `BasicFrameTemplateWithInset`, `UICheckButtonTemplate`, `OptionsSliderTemplate`, `UIDropDownMenuTemplate`, `UIPanelButtonTemplate`, native scroll frames and standard fonts. There are **no runtime sprites, custom fonts, emote previews or animation assets**. Promotional artwork lives separately in `assets/portfolio/`. The actual flourish comes from `DoEmote` and the client/race's built-in result.

This restraint makes the addon an expressive tool rather than an art asset mod. In-game character personality is created by **selection and timing**, not new textures.

## Interaction details worth testing

The ability selector sorts spellbook results alphabetically, with ID ordering for equal names. Its *stored* key is a lowercase name, however, so rank variants may share settings; the UI could show multiple entries that edit one configuration. The scrollable emote list can be long and inherits the client's token availability.

There is currently **no built-in preview button**, no separate custom text authoring, no emote-scene editor and no UI control for keeping cooldowns through logout. These are potential future decisions, not overlooked documentation of existing functionality.

Possible accessibility/UX questions include slider readability at small scales, a visible warning that actual emotes may appear in normal chat, filtering unavailable tokens, and avoiding too many repeated noises in group content. None has been verified through an in-game test in this documentation audit.

The code and commit messages do not prove the full initial brainstorming, all alternatives or which tool generated each earlier code line.

## Source-level tradeoffs

**Cast success versus damage hit:** The original introductory text said “when that ability lands.” The actual implementation observes **UNIT_SPELLCAST_SUCCEEDED**. That avoids parsing combat damage/target effects but may emit a flourish even when a cast later misses, is resisted or has no meaningful target hit. No new trigger is approved.

**Name-key versus ID-key:** The event carries a spell ID and the UI lists spellbook IDs, but saved configurations are keyed by **normalized spell name**. This can make multiple ranks share one expressive identity, while risking same-name collisions and localization-induced mismatches.

**Independent cooldowns versus global social volume:** Every configured ability has its own timestamp; there is no overall emote budget. That respects distinctive spell personalities but two different abilities can emote close together. Any future global throttling is a creator decision.

**Cooldown only on a fired emote:** A failed chance check or empty emote pool doesn't consume it. Chance therefore determines frequency independently from the *last actual emote*, though the zero default timestamp may suppress a very early first attempt.

**Transient runtime state versus persisted preferences:** Ability choices persist by GUID; timers reset on UI reload/relog. This is simpler but won't provide a durable anti-spam cooldown if a player logs in and out quickly.

**Game-native emotes versus custom writing:** Native token discovery gives many options and localized game behavior, but does not let the player write unique roleplay lines or choose custom sounds. That keeps scope small.

**Legacy compatibility versus fully automatic migration:** Current source can adopt `ROARitFOREVERStorage` only when already loaded. It doesn't read an arbitrary old disk file. Name-realm legacy keys are not evidence of separate game realms on Forever.

**Packaging vs release assets:** The repository has CurseForge packager metadata and two GitHub release entries with no attached assets. No installer, ZIP checksum or distribution success should be invented.

## Unapproved questions for later discussion

Should the first-cast `GetTime()` behavior be corrected? Should cooldowns survive reload? Should live hits (when knowable) be used rather than cast success? Should duplicated spell names be distinct configurations? Should a global emote frequency ceiling coexist with per-ability cooldowns? Should there be a preview button? Should the addon publish explicit license terms? Record an actual Babuni.dev choice before treating any as accepted.

# Flourish Forever — emote vocabulary, character settings and assets

**Creator:** Babuni.dev · **Platform:** WoW: Forever interface 16001.  
**Evidence:** `FlourishForever_ActionEmotes.lua`, storage module, TOC and release records.

## What is configurable content?

This addon has **no custom prose library** and no manually authored class dialogue lines. It binds two kinds of game-provided content:

| Content | Source | Persistence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ability display names, IDs | Client `C_SpellBook`/legacy spellbook APIs | Config records last selected spellID and name |
| Spell cast event | `UNIT_SPELLCAST_SUCCEEDED` from client | Not stored as a log |
| Emote tokens | `EMOTE%d+_TOKEN` globals + ROAR fallback | Each configured spell has enabled token set |
| Native emote animation/chat | `DoEmote(token)` | Determined by game, not stored in addon |
| Chance and cooldown settings | Slider input | Saved by character profile |
| Last emote-fire timestamp | `GetTime()` table | **Session-only**; resets on reload/relog |

Emotes are **discoverable from the installed client** rather than hardcoded as a fixed number of choices. A client update may change how many tokens appear, which ones have a slash command, or how specific gestures display on an individual character.

The result is a single native game emote each time a configured ability's chance and cooldown conditions are met. The source calls `DoEmote(token)`; it does not generate sentences, modify spell tooltips, attach sound files or alter game combat mechanics.

## Defaults and saved profiles

The TOC has **`SavedVariables: FlourishForeverStorage`**. Its root includes a `profiles` table indexed by **player character GUID**. That choice matches the realmless Forever client identity model rather than relying on identical first names or any supposed separate-realm collision behavior.

Each profile stores:
- `actionEmotesEnabled`, default **true**.
- `instances` map keyed by a trimmed lowercase **spell name**, initially empty.
- Per instance: `name`, `spellID`, `chance` (default **100**), `cooldown` (default **6**), `emotes` enabled-token map (default **ROAR=true**).

The `instances` field name is a historical code key; it does **not** imply instance or dungeon-specific settings. Configuration is by character and ability-name, not by WoW dungeon, raid, zone or server realm.

Older `ROARitFOREVERStorage` may be adopted if already loaded. Legacy character profiles may also have been stored under plain name or name-realm keys; current code moves a matching old table to the character's GUID key when needed. Do not assume a removed addon automatically loads its old variables for migration.

**Not saved:** last emote timestamp, every cast event, a chat transcript, cooldown between logout/reloads, party-member identity, target information or cross-player communications.

## Commands and UI text

- `/flourish`, `/flourishforever`, `/rit` with `config`, `ui`, and `status`.
- Window title **Flourish Forever**.
- Labels **Enable ability emotes**, **Add ability**, **Configured abilities**, **Emotes (one is chosen at random)**, **Chance**, **Cooldown**, **Remove**.
- Status prints master enabled state, configured ability count, and a **GUID-bearing** profile reference.

The source relies on English UI strings and fallback emote labels, with game-global tokens/spell names potentially localized. There is no dedicated localization table, translated settings copy, or runtime icon bundle. Portfolio artwork is stored separately under `assets/portfolio/`.

# Gather Map

**A self-learning resource map overlay for World of Warcraft 1.12**

**Creator:** Babuni.dev  
**Addon version:** 0.4.3 · **Interface:** 11200 · **SavedVariables:** `GatherMapDB`  
**Implementation:** [`GatherMap.lua`](GatherMap.lua), [`GatherMap.toc`](GatherMap.toc)  
**Documentation audit:** 2026-10-26 — verified against source and Git history; **no new in-game tests performed**.

Gather Map remembers **where you successfully gathered resources** and shows those discoveries on both the minimap and zone world map. It started as a herbalism tool and grew into a broader record of herbs, minerals, custom Survival trees, skinned loot, lockpicking chests and ordinary treasure chests. The map learns as you play: **it does not import an authoritative catalog of currently available spawns**.

Instead of opaque dots, the overlay uses **four small difficulty-colored corner markers**. The world map also shows the associated resource icon. Markers re-evaluate against the *current character's* skill or level, while discoveries remain available across the account.

![Saved herbs on the Tanaris world map](Screenshots/world-map-tanaris.png)

## What is recorded

| Resource kind | How it is learned | How color is determined | When it is visible |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Herbs** | Gather completion or recognized loot after Interact | Herbalism requirement | Current character has Herbalism |
| **Minerals** | Mining success, with some loot-to-node fallback | Mining requirement | Current character has Mining |
| **Survival trees** | Successful Woodcutting/recognized tree loot | Survival requirement | Current character has Survival |
| **Skinning** | Looted hide/leather/scale/item after skinning; saved as an approximate hunting spot | Requirement inferred from creature level | Current character has Skinning |
| **Lockpicking chests** | Recognized locked chest interaction | Lockpicking requirement | Current character has Lockpicking |
| **Ordinary chests** | Recognized world chest interaction | Known chest tier compared with character level | All characters |

The code associates a resource with a zone, subzone, map position, type, requirement where known, icon where available, and occurrence count. The main database is **account-wide**, but profession filtering and colors adapt to each character. **Skinning markers indicate places where a creature was skinned, not guaranteed stationary spawns.**

Custom resource tooltips can supply requirements; unknown requirements produce **purple** corners instead of an invented difficulty. A few known loot-to-node mappings are deliberately cautious: Thorium Ore alone cannot reveal a small versus rich Thorium vein.

## Two map presentations


### Minimap — subtle four-corner markers

Saved locations currently in range appear as four colored corners, with a hover label. The minimap visualization uses coordinates, zoom state, estimated scaling and custom-zone dimensions to position markers.

![Minimap marker and tooltip](Screenshots/minimap-tooltip.png)

### World map — resource icons plus corners

When you open a specific **zone** on the world map, saved locations appear with their matching resource icon and corner dots. The **Gather Map** checkbox near the upper-left of the map toggles this overlay separately from the minimap. It remembers that setting.

![Merged resource markers](Screenshots/world-map-merged-markers.png)

Nearby markers for the **same resource kind and name** merge if their marker bounds overlap. Their four corner dots expand to the outside of the combined rectangle. Different resources do **not** merge. The rendering code caps each map at **300 displayed marker groups**; this is a display cap, **not a cap on saved discoveries**.

### Difficulty colors

| Color | Profession requirement compared with current skill |
| --- | --- |
| Red | Skill below the requirement |
| Orange | Skill meets the requirement, up to 24 points above |
| Yellow | 25–49 above |
| Green | 50–99 above |
| Gray | 100+ above |
| Purple | Requirement unknown |

For ordinary treasure, the algorithm compares the **chest tier to player level**, not profession skill: red at 6+ levels above; orange 3–5 above; yellow from 2 below through 2 above; green 3–9 below; gray 10+ below; unknown purple. Gray has **85% opacity**, the other categories 100%.

## Commands

| Command | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `/gathermap`, `/gathermap count`, `/gathermap status` | Show saved counts by type, profession skills and current zone support |
| `/gmap` | Alias for the same slash command family |
| `/gathermap on` or `show` | Show **minimap** markers |
| `/gathermap off` or `hide` | Hide **minimap** markers but continue recording discoveries |
| World-map **Gather Map** checkbox | Independently show/hide the **world-map** overlay |

The two visibility choices live in `GatherMapDB.enabled` and `GatherMapDB.worldMapEnabled`. Turning off minimap pins does **not** stop gathering or necessarily hide world-map pins.

## Install

1. Copy the project folder to `World of Warcraft/Interface/AddOns/GatherMap/`. Place `GatherMap.lua`, `GatherMap.toc` and `Icons/` inside that folder together.
2. Restart WoW, enable **Gather Map**, and use **Load out of date AddOns** if your particular 1.12-compatible client requires it.
3. Gather a recognized resource successfully, then run `/gmap count` and check the minimap/world map for the learned point.
4. Optionally install [Interact](https://github.com/lookino/Interact) for its hotkey behavior; Gather Map does **not require** it.

**Compatibility:** The TOC declares interface **11200**. The source includes additional outdoor/event map sizes for named custom zones; that is not proof every third-party 1.12 client has been verified. Several event strings, profession names, resource names and tooltip patterns are in English; **full localized-client support has not been demonstrated**.

## Supported custom maps

The current `customZoneSize` table contains **15** names: Hyjal, Scarlet Enclave, Lapidis Isle, Gillijim's Isle, Tel'Abim, Alah'Thalas, Gilneas, Icepoint Rock, Blackstone Island, Thalassian Highlands, Winter Veil Vale, Grim Reaches, Balor, Northwind and Moonwhisper Coast. ## Upgrade if you used the old name

This project was originally named **Octo Gather**. Renaming the folder and saved-variable name does **not automatically migrate** old `OctoGatherDB` data into `GatherMapDB`.

With WoW **fully closed**, install `GatherMap` beside the old addon, open PowerShell in the new addon folder, and run the supplied migration helper with paths you supply:

```powershell
.\Upgrade-SavedData.ps1 -ClientPath "C:\Games\World of Warcraft" -PreviousAddonName "OctoGather"
```

The helper reads the old/new TOC declarations, scans saved-variable files, backs up sources in `AddonUpgradeBackups`, copies converted files to the new name, refuses existing destination files, and **does not execute saved Lua**. It leaves the original files in place. Disable the old addon, check the migrated data and retain the backups. The helper's contents were reviewed, but **it was not executed in this session**.

For non-Windows setups the older README includes a manual migration approach: back up your WTF SavedVariables first; copy old named SavedVariables files to the new name and change **only the top-level declaration** from the old TOC variable to `GatherMapDB`. Do not do this with WoW running.

For ordinary updates **without a folder/name change**, standard WoW SavedVariables persistence applies.

## How reliable is the data?

This is a **personal discovery record**, not a live-world sensing system. WoW's existing tracking dots may show a resource is currently spawned; Gather Map records places previously encountered. A failed cast should not create a node, but correctness depends on game event text, loot timing, tooltip availability and position APIs. The source contains debouncing and pending-state handling to reduce duplicates; these need client-level verification.

The current code polls map updates at approximately **0.10 seconds**, merges markers, and uses an upper display limit of 300 groups per map. Large saved databases, many custom zones, localized clients and interaction-hook load orders merit performance and compatibility tests.

The repo includes two regression-test scripts, **not an all-encompassing automated test suite**:
- `tests/test_interact_hook.py`: tests recursive Interact-hook behavior with **lupa / Lua 5.1** fixture code, not a live Vanilla client.
- `tests/test_upgrade.ps1`: tests migration from a synthetic previous addon name using temporary fixture directories.

Neither was executed during the 2026-10-26 documentation pass.

# GatherMap — concept and original creative direction

**Creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Public project:** Gather Map, formerly Octo Gather  
**Target:** Vanilla WoW 1.12-compatible addons, with additional named custom maps.

## Learn the world by exploring it

Rather than filling the map with an imported atlas from the start, Gather Map learns **from what the player actually gathers**. A successful action creates a local discovery that the player can recognize on a subsequent journey. It turns ordinary gathering into a gradual act of mapping.

That makes two forms of knowledge coexist: the world may contain a resource *now*, and the player may remember *where one previously appeared*. The addon deals in the second kind of knowledge. It does not know whether a mining vein or herb currently exists at a stored position. Skinning locations are even looser: they are memories of moving creatures yielding items, not static spawn-point promises.

The basic experience is personal and unobtrusive. It rewards curiosity and revisiting familiar routes without taking over navigation or gathering actions.

## A visible language of four corners

The visual system is intentionally different from a map full of solid opaque pins. **Four small corner dots** surround a location on the minimap; the world map adds the recognizable resource artwork inside those corners. The corner colors describe how hard the resource would be for the **character currently playing**. Red is too difficult, orange is just reachable, yellow and green become easier, gray is old territory, and purple communicates uncertainty.

A single account-wide memory can therefore look different for an experienced herbalist and a character who has yet to learn the profession. The data belongs to the player; the presentation is contextual.

When same-resource markers overlap, the dots are pushed to the outside of the merged group instead of stacking a blur of duplicate frames. Distinct resource types remain independent.

## From herbs to a broader ecology

The first September 5 version documented herbs. The September 6 commits expanded the world that could be remembered: minerals, chests, skinning, woodcutting trees and profession-aware hiding. This growth is a meaningful creative turn—not merely a bigger database. Each resource asks a different question of the interface:
- A herb or ore deposit has a fixed node, often a known gathering requirement.
- A chest may have a skill lock or only a tier relative to the character's level.
- A skinned creature leaves behind a hunting memory, not a node.
- A custom Survival tree belongs to a profession absent from standard Vanilla 1.12.
- Unknown custom resources may reveal their own requirements through a tooltip, or remain honestly purple.

The current implementation accommodates those distinctions while keeping one consistent visual vocabulary.

## The engineering context is part of the work

Additional client maps do not necessarily preserve numeric zone indices from classic Gatherer. The implementation uses zone names, aliases and specific scaling dimensions; it also handles an optional Interact hotkey API. The September 7 fix for recursion after other addons wrap `Interact` demonstrates how an apparently simple quality-of-life project has to cope with shared, mutable game-client functions.

In September the project moved from **Octo Gather** to the more provider-neutral **Gather Map** identity. The rename was both technical and documentary because SavedVariables, icon paths and installation names had to match—and old saved data needed a careful migration.

## Creative authorship, not an invented origin story

These principles are grounded in the original README, feature history and current source. The available commits do **not** reproduce all of Babuni.dev's original thinking or show who drafted every function. The creator's core ideas and direction remain credited to Babuni.dev. The AI documentation assistant's later analysis and wording are a separate contribution.

Do not replace this living exploration record with a generic imported-mining database, excessive map clutter or a conventional web-map dashboard without the creator's decision.

# GatherMap — narrative development journal

**Original creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Retrospective written:** October 26, 2026 from GitHub commits, repository README, Lua, migration utility, tests and screenshots. No missing original chat transcript has been fabricated.

## The first idea: let the map learn the player's routes

Gather Map began as **Octo Gather**, a Vanilla 1.12 map addon that learned a location *after* the player successfully picked a herb. It wasn't meant to supply a permanent imported atlas that magically knew every resource spawn. The player discovers something, and the client remembers it for later.

That distinction is the heart of the creative contribution. It is modest in terms of interface but meaningful in terms of experience: the world becomes legible through play. The record is **account-wide**, yet the markers can change their colors when another character views the same place with a different profession skill.

The initial substantive commit, **`0cd8e97` on September 5, 2026**, arrived as “Initial Octo Gather release.” It included a nearly finished herbalism prototype, `OctoGather.lua`, a 1.12 TOC at version **0.2.6**, 29 herb art files, and four documentation screenshots. That first version displayed saved herbs on both the minimap and selected zone world map with difficulty-colored rectangular outlines. It read current Herbalism skill and compared it against requirements, initially drawing a maximum of 100 pins.

The source already credited [Gatherer](https://github.com/jsb/Gatherer) for original zone scaling and herb artwork and [MetaHunt](https://github.com/DuvelCorp/MetaHunt) for the Grim Reaches map dimensions. Those aren't incidental footnotes: using verified existing map geometry and recognizable game artwork made the creator's own recording and UI logic usable in an older game client. The portfolio must distinguish **Babuni.dev's creative/system design** from those upstream resources.

The original repository history does not contain a separate recorded ideation conversation. This journal interprets the intent through the README and code, rather than claiming to quote an unavailable design discussion.

## September 6: the herb notebook becomes a resource atlas

The next day's changes were unusually concentrated. Commit **`7d4d029`** expanded the program to learn **mining, skinning, locked chests and ordinary treasure**. The data format needed a `kind` field because one location could no longer mean only “herb.” The addon started handling more tooltip, cast, loot and skill information to make those categories recognizable; the maximum rendered group count increased to 300.

That expansion revealed that not all “resource locations” mean the same thing. An herb sits at a ground node. Mining loot may identify its likely ore source, though it may not uniquely identify a vein. A skinned hide is produced by a **moving creature**, so a saved point is a useful hunting memory rather than a reliable stationary node. Locked chests use **Lockpicking** difficulty, while ordinary chests lack profession requirements and instead use a tier relative to the player's level.

Two later September 6 commits show small, deliberate improvements to accuracy: **`4eabd57`** corrected the difficulty formula for low-level skinnable creatures, and **`bd98a2d`** mapped known skin materials to better inventory icons. The current internal DB migration later clears older unreliable skin requirements while keeping saved locations—evidence that the design values preserving player discoveries more than preserving every early formula result.

The same day, **`8f890b2`** hid nodes when the current character lacked their profession, without deleting them from account-wide storage. This change protected readability. A new character shouldn't be confronted with every previous herbalism memory unless it has a reason to use it.

Then **`bec4f92`** added **Survival Woodcutting** and six specific tree types: Simple, Bright, Shade, Tropical, Dead and Star Wood. This mattered because the custom-client ecosystem supported a profession that standard Vanilla didn't. The project was becoming a flexible place-memory system rather than a fixed table of old Blizzard herbs.

## September 7: a visual language becomes distinct

The project originally used full colored rectangular outlines. Commit **`dc6f4ba`**, “Replace marker outlines with corner dots,” transformed that into **four small colored corner dots** on the minimap and a resource icon nested within four dots on the world map.

The system continues to group overlapping markers for the **same resource** into one larger rectangle; but the rectangle is now expressed only by its outer corners, leaving the underlying native map more visible. When a line of same-resource marker bounds overlaps transitively, the merge algorithm repeatedly checks the growing group. Other resources are kept independent, preventing a confusing combined cluster that means no particular thing.

Later that day **`9572119`** increased gray marker opacity to **85%** and refreshed screenshots. That is a concrete usability iteration, not merely a CSS-style cosmetic tweak. A marker representing an easy or low-value node still needs to remain visible enough to be useful.

The user-facing map has two independent display toggles. One is the chat command controlling minimap markers; another is the world-map checkbox. Hiding pins doesn't erase previously learned data, which fits the project's original premise of accumulating exploration memory.

## September 7: learning to coexist with other addons

The commit **`1cb631f`**, “Prevent recursive Interact hook chains,” tackles a technical problem that is especially interesting in a portfolio narrative. Gather Map supports the optional [Interact](https://github.com/lookino/Interact) hotkey. It needs to notice when that API is used because a subsequent loot event may identify a resource even when the game never exposed an ordinary object tooltip.

But WoW addons can replace global Lua functions. If Gather Map's wrapper always consults **one shared variable** holding a previous `Interact` function, another addon can wrap Gather Map, which then rewraps that addon, causing the supposedly old function reference to point into the new chain. The result can be recursive calls rather than one clean delegation.

The revised `InstallInteractHook` closes over a **different predecessor for each installed wrapper**, so an older wrapper continues pointing to the function it was created to wrap. It also checks for repeated installs and is invoked during later update checks to notice replacement.

That fix came with **`tests/test_interact_hook.py`**, a narrow regression fixture that uses Lua 5.1 through Python lupa to demonstrate the old chain's recursion and validate the new approach under synthetic conditions. The test is part of the project history; this documentation pass **did not execute it** and it cannot replace an actual WoW 1.12 integration test.

This is an example of why development process deserves a place in the finished portfolio: the visible result remains four harmless map corners, but it relies on subtle cooperation between independently authored addons.

## September 18: the project finds a more general identity

The September 18 commit **`0a01737`**, “Use provider-neutral names and client compatibility descriptions,” renamed **Octo Gather** to **Gather Map** throughout the addon title, Lua script, TOC, SavedVariables identifier, icon path and README. The manifest became version **0.4.3**.

The user-facing identity was broader, but the rename came with a technical cost. A player's old discoveries were in files named for the previous addon and a top-level variable **`OctoGatherDB`**. Simply changing the folder and enabling the new code would not automatically restore that data.

So the repository added **`Upgrade-SavedData.ps1`**: a migration helper that reads the TOC variables, copies relevant saved files, preserves originals, creates backups, refuses to overwrite an existing destination and rewrites top-level variable assignments without evaluating saved Lua. It also added **`tests/test_upgrade.ps1`** with synthetic account/character SavedVariables, Unicode text, backup checks and overwrite/path-name refusal checks.

This is a distinct iteration beyond maps and gathering. The project needed to respect the player's accumulated personal history precisely because the idea was to remember exploration. A migration that silently lost nodes would defeat the original concept.

No execution log for the PowerShell fixture was inspected in this audit. The source is a safeguard design, not proof that a user's actual files were successfully migrated.

## October 26: from code archive to portfolio record

The next visible commits on **October 26** updated the TOC/README author attribution to **Babuni.dev** and added a first set of short documentation files and links. The current documentation review expands those into a technical architecture, interaction-design record, content/provenance inventory, roadmap, decisions register and this narrative journal.

A complete public account must preserve several boundaries. The saved map is a **memory of observed points**, not a live spawn oracle. Skinning is a hunting approximation. Marker color derives from current skill, not a frozen reward label. Custom-client zones have configured dimensions rather than universal compatibility guarantees. The original visual and technical work belongs to the creator, while upstream artwork/data belong with the credited projects.

## The next creative and technical questions

What does the player experience on a crowded minimap with hundreds of saved locations? How does the marker system feel for a Skinner who is chasing moving creatures rather than revisiting static resource nodes? How should custom map aliases be tested across game clients? When should the system prefer an unknown purple marker over a guessed requirement? These are productive next questions, not approvals to replace the existing system.

The most revealing part of this project may be its pattern of iteration: **learn a herb, learn more kinds of world object, refine the marks, fix compatibility, preserve the player's memories through a rename**. # GatherMap — technical architecture

**Source audited:** `GatherMap.lua` (1,237 lines), `GatherMap.toc`, saved-data helper and tests, October 26, 2026. **Static code review, not client execution.**

## Lifecycle, events and state

```text
ADDON_LOADED (GatherMap / optional Interact)
    -> InitializeDatabase()
    -> InstallInteractHook()

PLAYER_ENTERING_WORLD
    -> InitializeDatabase(), UpdatePins(), UpdateWorldMapPins()

SPELLCAST_START / CHAT_MSG_SPELL_SELF_BUFF / SPELLCAST_STOP
    -> BeginResourceAction() / recorded successful resource text
    -> RecordNodeOnce() if valid
SPELLCAST_FAILED / SPELLCAST_INTERRUPTED
    -> ClearPending()
CHAT_MSG_LOOT
    -> classify item and capture mining/herb/wood or skinning loot
SKILL_LINES_CHANGED / MINIMAP_UPDATE_ZOOM / ZONE_CHANGED_NEW_AREA
    -> refresh minimap and world-map markers
WORLD_MAP_UPDATE
    -> refresh world-map markers

OnUpdate approximately every 0.10 seconds
    -> expire pending loot
    -> InstallInteractHook() if global changed
    -> refresh pins, world pins and hovered labels
```

The source uses Vanilla 1.12's implicit `event`, `arg1`, `this` callback conventions and Lua 5.0 compatible syntax. The TOC loads one Lua file, optional-depends on `Interact`, and initializes account-wide `GatherMapDB`.

## Categories and gathering state machine

The current `actionKinds` table maps:
- `Herb Gathering` → herb
- `Mining` → mineral
- `Skinning` → skin
- `Woodcutting` → wood
- `Opening` → treasure
- `Pick Lock` → lock

`BeginResourceAction` reads the object tooltip or target context, storing **pendingNode**, **pendingRequirement**, **pendingKind**, **pendingTexture**, pending flag, and a time window for loot arriving after an interaction. A successful self-buff/action phrase such as `You perform ... on ...` may directly name a resource; `SPELLCAST_STOP` can commit a pending node if identified. Failures clear state. Skinning awaits loot so the record can name the **actual item** received.

`InstallInteractHook` watches the optional global `Interact`, records a last-interact timestamp, and delegates to the function that existed when the wrapper was created. On later replacement it can wrap again with a **new locally captured predecessor**; a shared predecessor previously produced recursive chains. The dedicated Python/Lua fixture tries to reproduce the old recursion and exercise the current wrapper. Interact itself is not bundled.

The **Interact loot fallback** can infer herbs, ore deposits or wood through recognized looted item names. Some names are inherently ambiguous (e.g. Thorium Ore can come from different vein types), so the source uses a generic node/unknown requirement instead of falsely choosing a specific deposit.

**Locale caution:** Several action names, English chat patterns, profession strings, chest keywords and resource names are literal English. This limits assertions of universal localization support.

## Data model and deduplication

```text
GatherMapDB
├── version = 3
├── enabled = true/false         # minimap overlay only
├── worldMapEnabled = true/false # independent world map
└── nodes
    └── "<continent>:<zone>" = [
          {
            name, kind, x, y, required?,
            texture?, count, zoneName, areaName
          }, ...
       ]
```

A resource's position is read from the player's current zone map, stored as normalized map coordinates. `RecordNode` rejects absent names/positions, finds same-type+name nodes within **0.004** in both X and Y, then updates their **weighted average position and count**. Otherwise it appends a new entry. `RecordNodeOnce` also suppresses same-kind+name events within **2 seconds**. These two mechanisms differ: the first groups repeated visits spatially, the second filters repeated event emissions temporally.

The key `"<continent>:<zone>"` uses the map indices in the **currently loaded client**. Added custom maps can change indices and zone mapping; migrating SavedVariables across clients with different zone indices needs special testing. `zoneName` and `areaName` are saved alongside positions, but the current primary lookup is still the numeric key.

On init, **old database version 1** entries missing `kind` become `herb`; old **version 2** skin points retain their location but have stale `required` cleared due to earlier low-level formula error. The current version is **3**.

## Current-skill presentation

The source reads skill lines named Herbalism, Mining, Skinning, Lockpicking and Survival. `ShouldShowNode` hides profession-based markers if the current character lacks the respective skill (rank 0); treasure always shows.

Profession colors compare requirement to current rank:
- unknown → purple;
- skill below required → red;
- skill required to required+24 → orange;
- +25..+49 → yellow;
- +50..+99 → green;
- +100 and above → gray.

Treasure uses player level instead of profession: required tier minus player level ≥6 red, ≥3 orange, ≥-2 yellow, ≥-9 green, otherwise gray.

Skinning requirement inversely calculates Vanilla's level/skill rule: creature level up to 10 yields 1; levels 11–20 use `(level - 10)*10`; above 20 use `level*5`. Saved skinning points name the **looted item**, not necessarily the creature name.

## Coordinate conversion and custom maps

`GetPosition` finds the current main map zone by normalized **zone name** (`GetRealZoneText` checked against `GetMapZones`), then uses `GetPlayerMapPosition`. It may call `SetMapZoom` to resolve (0,0) position when map not visible.

`zoneScale` maps normal zone names to classic Gatherer-derived factors; `continentScale` and `minimapZoomYards` convert zoom into minimap offsets. **15** `customZoneSize` width/height pairs enable extra event/custom maps. `zoneAliases` handles spelling variants such as Mount Hyjal → Hyjal. A custom map's configured dimensions are **not automatically a live-tested compatibility guarantee**.

## Rendering and interaction

- `UpdatePins` computes minimap offsets relative to player, applies visibility and a circular minimap radius. The minimap shows **four 3px colored corner dots** per grouped hit area, with hover labels.
- `UpdateWorldMapPins` requires an open specifically selected zone, not a continent overview. It converts normalized X/Y to the `WorldMapButton` dimensions, adds game/bundled resource icon textures and four corner dots.
- `AddMarkerGroup` merges overlapping rectangles **only for identical kind + name**, and rechecks after expansion for transitive overlap. The **highest difficulty priority** wins within a merged group; different resources can overlap without merging.
- A reusable pool of frames cuts repeated creation, and `MAX_PINS=300` limits groups **rendered** on each map, not database size.
- A separate custom cursor tooltip avoids dependence on fragile old tooltip templates while the game tooltip is used for gathering recognition.
- `GatherMapDB.enabled` controls minimap only; the world-map checkbox saves `worldMapEnabled` independently. Recording continues when markers are hidden.
- Gray groups have 85% alpha; other groups full alpha. The refresh loop triggers around **10 times per second**, which may be expensive on dense maps.

## Dependencies and migration helper

`GatherMap.toc` declares `OptionalDeps: Interact`; `Interact` is not required. Bundled `Icons/Herb*.tga` (29 files) are credited to [Gatherer](https://github.com/jsb/Gatherer) alongside minimap scaling. Grim Reaches map data is credited to [MetaHunt](https://github.com/DuvelCorp/MetaHunt).

`Upgrade-SavedData.ps1` supports renaming SavedVariables after the transition from **OctoGatherDB** to **GatherMapDB**. It checks that WoW is closed, limits addon-name input, reads old/new TOCs, backs up discovered SavedVariables, refuses overwrites and rewrites only top-level assignments in the copied text without executing Lua. This is separate from in-addon schema migration.

Two fixture tests are committed. `tests/test_interact_hook.py` requires **lupa/Lua 5.1**; `tests/test_upgrade.ps1` runs on PowerShell. Neither is evidence of client correctness absent execution logs.

**No actual game testing or helper execution occurred in this documentation-only review.**

# GatherMap — visual, navigation and interaction design

**Creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev.

## A map that remembers, not a map that reveals everything

Gather Map begins with a subtle design decision: it learns **after discovery**. The overlay is a personal memory of gathering and exploring, so it should remain recognizable as an annotation layer on the game's own maps rather than pretending to know live spawns.

The work is not an alternative full-screen navigation app. It attaches to the native **minimap** and **world map**, retaining their familiar spatial context.

## Four corners, space in the middle

A small resource is marked by **four 3-pixel colored corner dots**, leaving its center mostly clear on the minimap. When the world map is open, a resource icon sits inside matching colored corners. The design moved here from early full rectangular outlines, with a visible September 7 commit documenting that choice.

Hovering uses a separate compact label frame so the map can display the resource name without competing with the native GameTooltip used during gathering. This is especially appropriate in a 1.12 UI, where tooltip behavior and mouse layers vary.

![Minimap tooltip](../Screenshots/minimap-tooltip.png)

## Dynamic difficulty as a personal reading of the world

Red, orange, yellow, green, gray and purple are not static property labels printed on resources. They are interpretations relative to the **current character's skill or level**. Something once red can become gray as the player grows; an old account-wide discovery can become red again for a new character.

Purple is meaningful uncertainty: the addon cannot derive a requirement from its known table or an object tooltip. It avoids guessing. Gray uses **85% opacity**, a September adjustment from less legible variants.

Profession resources are hidden if the character doesn't know the corresponding skill. That keeps a low-level/new-profession minimap from becoming an irrelevant collection of everything the account has ever found. Ordinary treasure is the exception and can remain visible to any class.

## Grouping without erasing identity

Same-type and same-name markers merge when their drawn rectangles overlap. The group's four corners expand to the new overall bounds. If multiple nearby nodes have different requirements, the group's strongest difficulty priority is used. Resources with different names/types remain separate even when they overlap.

This prevents the visual clutter of duplicate marks without collapsing distinct types into meaningless giant boxes.

![Grouped world map markers](../Screenshots/world-map-merged-markers.png)

## Controls and affordances

The minimap overlay is governed by `/gmap on` / `off`, while a **Gather Map** checkbox on the world map controls the world overlay. Both are stored. No control removes learned locations or turns off discovery merely to hide markers.

The status command prints total saved points, type counts, skill ranks and whether the current zone has known scaling. This makes the system slightly diagnosable without introducing another settings window.

## Areas requiring genuine user testing

- Dense nodes vs. 300-group drawing cap.
- Different minimap sizes, UI scaling and indoor/outdoor zoom.
- Readability of colored 3px corner dots and 85%-opacity gray in varying environments.
- Hover zones and mouse-layer conflicts with other minimap addons.

# Group Buff Toggle

**Creator:** Babuni.dev · **Version:** 1.2.0 · **Game:** World of Warcraft Vanilla 1.12 · **Interface:** 11200 · **License:** [MIT](LICENSE)

**Group Buff Toggle** is a lightweight, Blizzard-style addon that places **up to 16 beneficial aura icons beside each of four default party-member frames** and, independently, **up to 16 beside the default target frame**. Two familiar **Buffs** checkboxes make those overlays easy to switch on or off. The checkboxes can also be independently hidden via slash commands.

**Both buff displays begin switched off**, so installing the addon does not immediately put new buff icons on the screen. Both checkbox-visibility preferences begin on, but a checkbox appears only while its corresponding party or target unit frame is available. The four switches are saved **account-wide**.

The addon *displays buffs only*. It does **not** apply, remove, prioritize, cast, dispel, track remaining durations, show debuffs as a separate list, or automatically choose a target.

## Install and enable

Copy the project folder so that the source and manifest are here:

```text
World of Warcraft/
└── Interface/
    └── AddOns/
        └── GroupBuffToggle/
            ├── GroupBuffToggle.toc
            └── GroupBuffToggle.lua
```

Restart WoW or run `/reload`. Enable **Group Buff Toggle** at character selection. The [published v1.2.0 release](https://github.com/babunidev/GroupBuffToggle/releases/tag/v1.2.0) provides [GroupBuffToggle.zip](https://github.com/babunidev/GroupBuffToggle/releases/download/v1.2.0/GroupBuffToggle.zip) and a SHA256SUMS text file. The release exists; its files were **not downloaded and checksum-verified in this documentation audit**.

The addon has no required external library and no configuration window. It is specifically built for **default Blizzard PartyMemberFrame1–4 and TargetFrame anchors**, not for substitute party/target frames from other UI addons.

## How to use it

With a party, tick **Buffs** below the lowest currently visible party frame to show member buffs in two eight-icon rows beside each displayed party member. Untick it to hide them. Select a target, then tick its separate **Buffs** checkbox to display that unit's buffs. Hover a buff icon for the native **GameTooltip**.

The checkboxes themselves appear only in context: the party control requires a visible, populated party frame; the target control requires a visible target frame with a target. A missing checkbox when solo or without a target does **not** mean the account setting has been lost.

### Four independent controls

| Saved key in `GroupBuffsDB` | Default | Command | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | **false** | `/groupbuffs group on\|off\|toggle` | Show/hide **party buff icons** |
| `groupCheckbox` | **true** | `/groupbuffs groupbox on\|off\|toggle` | Show/hide the **party Buffs checkbox** |
| `targetEnabled` | **false** | `/groupbuffs target on\|off\|toggle` | Show/hide **target buff icons** |
| `targetCheckbox` | **true** | `/groupbuffs targetbox on\|off\|toggle` | Show/hide the **target Buffs checkbox** |

Type `/groupbuffs` alone to see help and the status of all four controls. For example, `/groupbuffs group on` turns on party buffs, while `/groupbuffs groupbox off` hides only their checkbox. **Hiding a checkbox does not disable its buff icons**; slash controls still work.

Aliases accepted by the source: `party` for `group`; `groupcheckbox` or `partybox` for `groupbox`; `targetcheckbox` for `targetbox`. All take `on`, `off`, or `toggle` as a separate second argument. The addon does not register a separate `/targetbuffs` command.

The README previously said “stores only two settings,” but that described the initial display toggles; **current v1.2.0 code actually persists all four settings**. This source-based correction is part of the present documentation review.

## Buff layout and refresh

Each of four party rows and the target row is a **16-icon, two-row (8+8)** grid. Each icon is **20×20 px**, with **2 px** spacing. The party grid sits to the right of its corresponding frame, and the target grid also sits beside the normal target frame. The addon reads `UnitBuff("party1" .. "party4", index)` and `UnitBuff("target", index)` for **indices 1–16**, shows the texture when present, and hides an absent buff button.

It refreshes on `VARIABLES_LOADED`, `PLAYER_ENTERING_WORLD`, `PARTY_MEMBERS_CHANGED`, and `UNIT_AURA`, as well as a simple **0.5-second** periodic refresh. Tooltips use `GameTooltip:SetUnitBuff` with the unit and buff index. The code doesn't store item IDs, party/target names or a permanent buff history.

**Limits:** this is party-plus-target, **not raid-frame integration**; it shows buff textures, **not durations or charge overlays**. Stacks returned by `UnitBuff` are not rendered. A buff can appear or disappear with up to approximately a half-second timer delay in cases not covered by immediate events. Client and addon interoperability weren't independently tested in this audit.

## Upgrade from the old name: Octo Group Buff Toggle

The addon originally used folder/TOC **OctoGroupBuffToggle**, saved variable **OctoGroupBuffsDB** and title **Octo Group Buff Toggle**. The September 18 rename changed the folder/script and root variable. **Simply replacing files is not enough to recover an old SavedVariables file under its former name.**

1. Exit WoW completely and **back up your WTF SavedVariables folders**.
2. Install the new **GroupBuffToggle** folder beside the original **OctoGroupBuffToggle** directory.
3. On Windows/PowerShell, open the new addon folder and run:

```powershell
.\Upgrade-SavedData.ps1 -ClientPath "C:\Games\World of Warcraft" -PreviousAddonName "OctoGroupBuffToggle"
```

The helper reads the actual TOC declarations, finds saved files, copies backups to `AddonUpgradeBackups`, writes renamed copies without replacing any existing target file, and changes **only top-level** variable assignments from the old to new names. It does **not execute saved Lua** and leaves old files intact. Verify the copied settings, then disable the old addon. Do not run this while WoW is open.

On Linux, back up and manually copy the old `WTF/Account/.../SavedVariables/OctoGroupBuffToggle.lua` to the corresponding **GroupBuffToggle.lua**, and change the top-level assignment to **GroupBuffsDB**. Don't alter values inside the table; preserve the original until you verify the settings.

The [migration fixture](tests/test_upgrade.ps1) is present in the repository and simulates saved-data moves, backups, Unicode text and overwrite refusal. It **was not executed in this audit**.

# GroupBuffToggle — concept and creative direction

**Creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev. **Project:** Group Buff Toggle for WoW Vanilla 1.12.

## Put helpful information beside the people it describes

Buff icons usually live inside or around the game's unit-frame information hierarchy. When fighting alongside a party or watching a target, a player may want to know **which positive effects are active** without cramming more status information on top of the name, health and mana bars.

The project's concrete answer is a **small supplementary buff strip beside** each normal party frame and the selected target frame. Up to sixteen aura icons fit in two rows of eight, leaving the original frame readable. Hovering a symbol uses the familiar built-in game tooltip rather than introducing a separate interpretation layer.

This is deliberately not a complex raid frame, aura-warning assistant or combat automation system. No casts, prioritization, suggestions or warnings are authored; it simply makes current buffs easier to inspect when the player chooses to.

## Respect the existing UI until invited

An unusually valuable design constraint is present from the initial version: **both displays default to off**. Installing Group Buff Toggle should not dramatically change the player's screen by surprise. The controls are familiar native **Buffs** checkboxes, positioned only when a matching unit frame is present.

The September 10 second commit pushed user control further: **checkbox visibility itself** became independent from **the buff display**. A user could leave party buffs showing and hide the small toggle control for a cleaner layout—or turn everything off without leaving a permanently unused widget. That is a meaningful design refinement: the checkbox is an optional affordance, not the owner's source of truth.

The four switches persist account-wide. “Off by default” applies to **buff icons**, not to checkbox availability. That distinction is part of the authored user experience and shouldn't be blurred.

## Lightweight means bounded and local

The addon uses client `UnitBuff` data for a maximum of **four party members plus one target**, capped at **16 icons each**. It attaches to Blizzard's already-present `PartyMemberFrame1` through `4` and `TargetFrame`. It does not rebuild the frames, ask for an addon framework or create an external service.

The cost of that approach is limited compatibility with wholesale unit-frame replacements and a deliberately modest information set: aura **icons with hover details**, not timers, stack badges, or comprehensive raid support. These are limits of the current code, not promised future features.

## Identity and creative provenance

The repository started on September 10 as **Octo Group Buff Toggle**, aimed at an older Vanilla-compatible environment. The September 18 version changed to a provider-neutral title, `GroupBuffToggle`, and renamed its SavedVariables while retaining the small original interaction concept.

The MIT License makes reuse terms explicit, and its existing 2026 copyright notice now credits **Babuni.dev**. Git proves the dated code changes but does not reproduce the creator's original conversations or necessarily the author of every line. The original purpose and creative decisions belong to Babuni.dev; later AI source interpretation is separately credited in the collaboration record.

# GroupBuffToggle — narrative development journal

**Project creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Retrospective prepared:** October 27, 2026. Sources inspected: current 303-line Lua, manifest, MIT LICENSE, README, saved-data migration helper and fixture, September Git patches and GitHub v1.2.0 release metadata. This is **not** a recovered transcript of original planning conversations.

## The question is not whether buffs exist, but whether the player wants to see them

Group Buff Toggle is a good example of an addon whose small scale is the point. It does not build a new combat system, automate group maintenance or turn every spell effect into an alert. It makes a narrow visual request: let me inspect the **beneficial effects on my party and my target** without covering the existing unit frames.

The creator's solution is spatial rather than statistical. Four normal `PartyMemberFrame` units and the normal `TargetFrame` stay in place. If the player opts in, compact grids of aura icons appear to their right—no separate window, no hovering status meter elsewhere on the screen and no requirement to keep tracking an entire raid.

Each grid is two rows of eight icon buttons. At 20 pixels each with a 2-pixel gap, it is small enough to fit beside familiar unit frames but wide enough to present a substantial buff list. A hover surfaces the game's native `GameTooltip:SetUnitBuff` information, so the icon itself doesn't have to explain what the spell does.

This intent is attributed to **Babuni.dev** as creator, not to the AI documenting the work later. The available repository doesn't contain the first brainstorm or direct statements of every reason behind the layout. We can faithfully describe what the source and original README say without inventing a design meeting.

## September 10, 2026 — the first committed Octo Group Buff Toggle

The repository's first visible commit, **`31411b3c252b`** (“Initial release”), is dated **September 10**. It introduced the name **Octo Group Buff Toggle**, `OctoGroupBuffToggle.lua`, a version **1.1.0** TOC, a README and an explicit MIT license with the creator's earlier pseudonym.

The initial implementation already had both party and target buff displays and their respective native-looking checkboxes. It relied on `UnitBuff` rather than duplicating a spell database. That saved a large amount of maintainable content and let the game supply icons directly. The code worked with the four default party frames and the target frame, not modern raid APIs or re-skinning every unit.

One decision makes the addon polite: **both buff overlays default off**. On a first installation, a small checkbox becomes available in context but the player has to enable the extra aura information. The source doesn't presume the screen needs more icons simply because the addon is installed.

The original `/groupbuffs` was a straightforward single toggle for party buffs. This was not yet a full preference interface. The initial README described only two saved display settings, matching that earlier design. Its later continued use of the phrase “stores only two settings” became outdated.

The first version was already usable-shaped. Still, an upload and version number alone do not prove a particular game-client playtest or a series of rejected visual sketches.

## Later September 10 — moving from two switches to four

Just minutes after the initial commit, **`c20bc1805b1f`**, “Add independent slash controls,” introduced a small but conceptually important extension. The code gained **`groupCheckbox`** and **`targetCheckbox`** SavedVariables, on top of the original party and target overlay flags.

This separated **the state of the information** from **the state of its control**. Perhaps a player likes seeing buffs but doesn't want the checkbox to remain visible. Perhaps they want the toggle there but prefer the icons off until a particular encounter. The implementation now supports both with explicit `/groupbuffs group / groupbox / target / targetbox on|off|toggle` commands.

Importantly, hiding the checkbox was not implemented as another way of disabling buffs. The two pieces are independent: the button can disappear while its corresponding aura strip keeps showing, and the slash commands remain available. This makes the addon more flexible without adding another settings panel.

The command parser also added aliases for party vs group and checkbox names, status reporting on blank/unknown input, and updates to the displayed check state when settings are changed from chat. Version advanced from **1.1.0** to **1.2.0** in the manifest.

The actual commit proves the code change. It doesn't contain the conversation that prompted it, whether an AI suggested the extra controls, or whether a specific party member complained about clutter. This journal deliberately does not claim any of that.

## The small engineering decisions supporting the gesture

The 303-line current Lua file demonstrates how much detail is needed to make a small visual addition feel as though it belongs to the game. For each party member the addon creates sixteen hoverable icon buttons and anchors their container just beyond the right edge of the default party frame. The target gets its own matching grid at an offset that fits beside Blizzard's target artwork.

The party checkbox doesn't float at a fixed world-screen coordinate. The source scans the party members from fourth down to first, finds the last visible populated frame and puts the checkbox just below that member. As the group grows, it moves with the list. The target checkbox follows the target frame and hides when there is no target.

The source refreshes on world entry, group changes and aura updates. A half-second periodic pass also rechecks frame visibility and position. This is a straightforward legacy-client solution: older addons have limited layout change signals, so polling ensures the display can recover from missed updates. It also creates repeated work even when nothing changed; performance should be assessed in a real client instead of assumed good or bad.

The icon-border texture uses a file named `UI-Debuff-Overlays`, which could mislead someone reading the name alone. The code's data path is `UnitBuff`: it shows **buffs**, not a separate debuff list. There are no aura duration numbers, charge overlays, timers, dispel hints, group-message logs or raid-unit panels. These absences are part of an honest source inventory, not evidence that features were intentionally rejected in an unavailable discussion.

# GroupBuffToggle — code architecture and runtime dataflow

**Audited:** `GroupBuffToggle.lua` (303 lines), `GroupBuffToggle.toc`, Git commits and migration scripts. October 27, 2026; **static review only**.

## Single-module package

```text
GroupBuffToggle.toc
  Interface: 11200 | Version: 1.2.0
  SavedVariables: GroupBuffsDB  (account-wide)
  GroupBuffToggle.lua
     ├─ default party and target frame references
     ├─ 4 party grids of 16 icon buttons
     ├─ 1 target grid of 16 icon buttons
     ├─ group + target Blizzard UICheckButtonTemplate controls
     ├─ event handling / 0.5-second polling
     └─ /groupbuffs command dispatch
```

There is no dependency/library, network synchronization, hidden targeting routine or alternative unit-frame abstraction. The source calls the built-in game's `UnitBuff` and `GameTooltip:SetUnitBuff` APIs.

## Default state and persistence

```text
GroupBuffsDB = {
  enabled = false,          -- party buff icons
  targetEnabled = false,    -- target buff icons
  groupCheckbox = true,     -- party checkbox affordance
  targetCheckbox = true     -- target checkbox affordance
}
```

On `VARIABLES_LOADED`, each key is populated **only if nil**, preserving saved user choices. The source doesn't restore default values on every login. This is an **account-wide** table declared as `SavedVariables`, not per-character. The previous README claimed only two settings, but the post-September-10 source has four.

`BuffsEnabled` and `TargetBuffsEnabled` require strict true; the checkbox-visibility functions require only **not false**, so missing checkbox keys behave as enabled even before initialization.

## Frame creation and placement

**Party:** for members 1–4, `CreateMemberBuffs` finds `PartyMemberFrameN`, then creates one container under `UIParent` anchored `TOPLEFT` to the party frame's `TOPRIGHT` with offset **(8,-4)**. Each container has 16 buttons, `MAX_BUFFS=16`; `ICONS_PER_ROW=8`, `ICON_SIZE=20`, `ICON_GAP=2`. Position of button i is computed using `math.mod(i-1,8)` for the column and `math.floor((i-1)/8)` for the row.

**Target:** one container anchored to `TargetFrame` `TOPRIGHT` at offset **(38,-18)**, also 16 icons in two rows. The target checkbox is positioned beside `TargetFrame` at offset **(4,-38)**. The party checkbox sits below the **highest-index visible, existing** party frame, found scanning member 4 down to 1, offset **(4,-6)** from its bottom-left.

The icons use native textures from `UnitBuff`, cropped via tex coords (0.07..0.93) and a subtle border texture from the game's `UI-Debuff-Overlays` sheet. That **border texture** does not make the displayed auras debuffs: the source only calls **UnitBuff**, not **UnitDebuff**.

## Refresh path and visibility

```text
VARIABLES_LOADED  -> initialize defaults, create checkboxes, UpdateAll
PLAYER_ENTERING_WORLD
PARTY_MEMBERS_CHANGED  ---> UpdateAll()
UNIT_AURA
OnUpdate every 0.5s ----> UpdateAll()

UpdateAll:
  for member in 1..4: UpdateMember(member)
  UpdateCheckboxPosition()
  UpdateTargetBuffs()
```

`UpdateMember` reparents position relative to the live party frame, then hides its container if party overlay disabled, unit doesn't exist, or the frame isn't shown. Otherwise each of the 16 slots calls `UnitBuff("partyN", index)`, sets the icon texture and visible state, and remembers the unit and buff index for hover.

`UpdateTargetBuffs` similarly hides its grid when target buff display disabled, target absent or `TargetFrame` hidden; its checkbox is visible only if `targetCheckbox` and target/frame visibility conditions all hold. It queries `UnitBuff("target", i)` only when enabled with a target.

**Important:** a visible checkbox flag isn't the same thing as enabled overlay. Hiding the checkbox leaves the overlay's independent saved flag unchanged.

If all four party and one target grid are visible, each full refresh can query up to **80 aura slots** (4×16 + 16) in addition to frame/checkbox work. Combined with a twice-per-second poll this is **up to about 160 periodic UnitBuff queries per second**, excluding event-triggered updates. This is a theoretical source-level maximum, **not** a measured performance result.

## Hover and update semantics

Party buttons set `button.unit="partyN"` and `buffIndex=i` when a buff is found; target buttons set their unit/index at frame creation. On hover, `GameTooltip:SetUnitBuff(this.unit,this.buffIndex)` displays the native buff tooltip; on leave it hides the tooltip.

The addon currently displays **only icons**, not remaining duration, stacks, source player, dispellability or buffs beyond the 16th. It has no persistent aura log or personal data collection mechanism.

On each periodic refresh the source adjusts positions and current buff icon visibility, but it doesn't replace default party/target frame internals. Custom unit-frame addons that remove those named frames won't be supported by this code without adaptation.

## Commands

The sole registered slash command is `/groupbuffs`. After trimming/lowercasing, its parser expects two tokens: **control** and **on/off/toggle**.

| Control aliases | Saved key |
| --- | --- |
| `group`, `party` | `enabled` |
| `groupbox`, `groupcheckbox`, `partybox` | `groupCheckbox` |
| `target` | `targetEnabled` |
| `targetbox`, `targetcheckbox` | `targetCheckbox` |

Invalid or empty messages print syntax and current state. Valid commands modify one key, print new state, update visible checkbox checks and call `UpdateAll`.

## Migration, licensing and test limits

September 18 changed old **OctoGroupBuffToggle** identity and root variable **OctoGroupBuffsDB** to **GroupBuffToggle / GroupBuffsDB**. `Upgrade-SavedData.ps1` maps old/new TOC variable names, copies source to backups, rewrites only root assignments in newly created files and refuses overwrites. A separate `tests/test_upgrade.ps1` fixture builds synthetic temporary SavedVariables trees to check Unicode, backups, original retention and refusal behavior.

The repository includes **MIT LICENSE** with Babuni.dev copyright and [v1.2.0 release](https://github.com/babunidev/GroupBuffToggle/releases/tag/v1.2.0) with ZIP/checksum files. Historic release notes **report** syntax/migration verification. Neither game-client validation nor execution of scripts was performed in this review.

# GroupBuffToggle — interface and interaction design

**Creative director:** Babuni.dev. **Evidence:** original README, current code and the two September 10 commits.

## A native UI affordance, not another configuration window

The addon uses Blizzard's familiar **UICheckButtonTemplate** and a small **Buffs** label placed where players are already looking: below their visible party frame stack and beside their current target. No new floating options panel, media bundle or unfamiliar controls are required.

The content sits **to the right** of existing unit frames, so health and resource bars aren't covered. Four possible party grids and one target grid each have two rows of eight small icons (16 total per unit). Buff buttons can be hovered for familiar native tooltips. This uses the game visual language rather than inventing a new type of aura graphic.

## Opt-in by default

A central design decision is that **buff overlays default off**. The user must tick a checkbox or enable a slash setting to alter the information density of the game UI. The checkboxes can be offered when units exist, even if the overlay itself is currently off.

This small restraint is significant. Unit frames are already visually busy; adding 16 icons for each member without invitation might create a disruptive change. The creator's solution keeps the new information available but doesn't insist on showing it.

## The September 10 interaction refinement

The first version had only two persistent visibility flags for party and target buffs. The same-day **“Add independent slash controls”** revision introduced two additional settings controlling **the visibility of the checkboxes**. The player can choose to show buffs while removing the toggle itself, or keep the control present but leave the icons hidden.

That creates four independent states rather than two, with clear direct `/groupbuffs` commands to access each. It is an example of making a small interface less intrusive through a second design pass rather than making it larger.

## Context matters for placement

The party checkbox follows the **last visible party-member frame** in the normal vertical stack; there is no party checkbox when no appropriate unit frame exists. The target checkbox follows the target frame and is shown only when a target exists. These rules keep controls from floating around the screen unattached to any subject.

The icon grids also hide when their corresponding units or Blizzard frames aren't shown. Each refresh reanchors positions to the currently available frames, supporting changing roster layouts within the default UI.

## Visual details and limits

Each buff icon is **20 px**, with a small **2 px** gap, cropped to remove empty texture edges and shown with a quiet gray border. The code uses a native texture sheet named `UI-Debuff-Overlays` as a *decorative frame*, but does not query debuffs. No durations, stacks, counters, expiration effects, sorting or aura type labels are currently drawn.

The amount and placement of information is intentionally fixed; an expanded raid layout would be a separate approved feature, not a small styling tweak.

## Future tests, not design claims

The icon-only layout should be examined at low resolutions, large UI scales, for color-vision accessibility, and with other buffs already present around unit frames. Check whether the target grid overlaps default status elements and whether tooltip hit areas remain easy to use. No screenshot or game-client usability test is in the current repo, and none was conducted during this audit.

## Tradeoffs visible in current design

**Checkbox vs icon-overlay independence.** Hiding the control does not hide the data. This supports minimalist UI arrangements but can be confusing unless documented. The README is corrected accordingly.

**Defaults.** The two buff displays default off, so install doesn't unexpectedly fill the screen. Checkbox visibility defaults on only when unit-frame context exists.

**Fixed native anchors.** Placing content near Blizzard party/target frames is simple and natural but creates a compatibility boundary with custom unit-frame replacements.

**Fixed 16-icon cap.** Two rows of eight produce predictable geometry. Additional buffs, stacks and expiry information are not shown.

**Event + 0.5s poll.** Occasional polling protects against events/visibility changes that don't arrive as expected in old clients, but means regular periodic work even when content is unchanged.

**Account-wide settings.** Same four preferences apply to every character; separate character profiles aren't part of today's design.

**Open source under MIT.** Unlike repositories missing licenses, this addon intentionally includes MIT terms. Current notice credits Babuni.dev; its legal terms are not to be silently altered by an AI collaborator.

Download the published [v0.2.2 LootFeed.zip](https://github.com/babunidev/LootFeed/releases/download/v0.2.2/LootFeed.zip), extract the `LootFeed` folder into `Interface\AddOns`, and restart WoW. Enable **Loot Feed** at character select.

## Upgrade from a previous add-on name

If you used this add-on under a previous folder name, migrate your saved data
before playing with the new installation. A normal file replacement is not
enough when the folder and saved-variable names change.

1. Fully close the game. Keep the previous add-on installed for this step.
2. Install the new `LootFeed` folder beside the previous folder.
3. Open PowerShell in `LootFeed` and run the following, replacing both example values:

   ```powershell
   .\Upgrade-SavedData.ps1 -ClientPath "C:\Games\World of Warcraft" -PreviousAddonName "PreviousAddonFolder"
   ```

The helper reads the previous TOC, copies account-wide and per-character saved
data to the new names, and saves backups under `AddonUpgradeBackups` in the
game folder. It keeps the original files intact and refuses to overwrite
existing saved data for the new add-on. It does not execute saved Lua code.

4. Disable the previous add-on and enable **LootFeed** before entering the world.
5. Check your settings and saved data. Keep the backups until you have verified them.

Further updates using the same add-on name keep your saved data normally.
On other operating systems, back up the files, then copy the previous add-on's
`.lua` file in each `WTF/Account/**/SavedVariables` directory to `LootFeed.lua`.
Change only the top-level variable name declared in the old TOC to the matching
name in the new TOC; leave its table contents unchanged. Do this with the game closed.

## Commands

- `/lfeed unlock` — drag into position; `/lfeed lock` to finish.
- `/lfeed test` — preview the feed.
- `/lfeed testroll` — preview a group roll; hover the dice as it progresses.
- `/lfeed scale 1` — adjust size.
- `/lfeed duration 6` — seconds before fading.
- `/lfeed direction up` or `down` — change stack direction.
- `/lfeed chat off` — hide personal item loot in chat; `chat on` restores it.
- `/lfeed reset` — restore defaults.

Settings are saved account-wide. Quest labels follow the item's tooltip; ordinary materials needed for quests are not marked.

Group rolls use the normal game's Need/Greed/Pass buttons. Active rolls add rows
as needed and stay until resolved; results remain for 15 seconds, paused while
hovering. The winner appears beside the dice. Detailed loot messages
(`showLootSpam`) are enabled to receive everyone's choices and rolls. Players
whose choice has not been received are shown as waiting/eligibility unknown.
If identical items are rolled simultaneously, Vanilla's chat cannot distinguish
the copies; the tooltip reports that limitation instead of guessing. Missing
results time out explicitly without inventing a winner. Rolls in progress before
the add-on loads cannot be reconstructed.

## What the source actually does

The installed addon folder is **LootFeed**, with **LootFeed.toc**, **Rolls.lua** and **LootFeed.lua**. The TOC declares interface **11200**, version **0.2.2** and account-wide SavedVariables **LootFeedDB**. The interface registers **/lfeed** and **/lootfeed** as equivalent aliases.

**Ordinary loot:** the five-row limit applies to *normal* item and money notifications. Incoming identical item links can be coalesced while still in the queue, but items already visible are not merged away. Entries animate in, slide to their new stack position, then fade after the selected delay (default **6 seconds**, adjustable from **2–20 seconds**). New rows are inserted no more frequently than about **0.32 seconds**. When ordinary rows are full, the oldest is expired rather than allowing an unlimited stack.

**Group rolls:** roll rows are **extra** and may exceed those five normal rows. They remain displayed while unresolved and can show **Need / Greed / Pass**, reported numbers and eventual winner. On completion, the row remains for around **15 seconds** before fading; hover pauses the visible feed timer. This is session-only roll tracking, **not a permanent saved history of group decisions**. The roll tracker itself retains completed records internally for up to **300 seconds** to handle delayed messages.

The dice are drawn by the addon as a tiny five-pip symbol rather than requiring an external image. Hover the dice for the participant breakdown. The normal Blizzard Need/Greed/Pass window remains in control of the player's actual roll.

**Important interaction side effect:** when the client setting `showLootSpam` is `0`, `Rolls.lua` sets it to `1` so detailed choice and number messages become available. The addon does **not** restore the previous value when switched off/unloaded. Likewise, `/lfeed chat off` wraps the legacy global `ChatFrame_OnEvent` handler to hide recognized **personal item** messages in chat. It does not suppress money messages or group-roll tracking. Review compatibility with other chat-handler addons if both are installed.

**Limits:** the self-loot parser uses the client's `LOOT_ITEM_*` string formats; the roll parser uses `LOOT_ROLL_*` templates with positional placeholder support. Full localized/custom-server behavior is not independently proven. Quest Item detection checks for the binding text on the actual item tooltip; **quest-needed materials** lacking that text are not labeled. A loot item may arrive before `GetItemInfo` finishes caching, so the display retries an item refresh.
