# LootFeed — creative concept

**Original creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev.  
**Game-client target:** original World of Warcraft 1.12 (TOC 11200).  
**Historical identity:** Octo Loot → Loot Feed.

## Giving rewards a moment on screen

LootFeed is a small interface experiment about **the feeling of getting something**. The ordinary game chat tells a player what was looted, but that information is easy to lose while traveling, fighting and talking. This addon makes those moments briefly visible in a **compact stack of softly animated notifications**. Rarity colors, item art, quantities, money denominations and genuine quest-item labels are placed close together without taking over the game.

The default design has **five short rows for regular loot**, set against a dark translucent backing, with a small entrance pop, smooth vertical movement and a fade-out. The player can move the anchor, choose direction and adjust scale and duration. **Hovering pauses** the stack so an item can be inspected. It is a deliberately temporary visual memory, not an inventory manager or an item database.

The initial September 8 release already carried this visual identity. The exact original brainstorming conversations are not present in the inspected Git history; Babuni.dev retains authorship of the creative direction. This document describes the result rather than inventing an origin scene.

## From receiving loot to understanding group decisions

On September 11 the addon expanded beyond **personal** loot. A group Need/Greed/Pass roll is a shared decision whose details often disappear into the combat or chat stream. LootFeed added **extra, longer-lived roll rows** with a small drawn die. Hovering the die reveals names, choices and roll numbers; once the outcome arrives, the winner is shown directly on the row.

This is an important change in scope. Five short personal notifications are a stream. Roll decisions need **state over time** and sometimes more than five visible rows. Rather than replacing Blizzard's buttons or triggering a roll for the player, LootFeed observes the game's roll events and messages, preserving the player's agency.

## Make uncertainty visible

Vanilla loot chat contains an item link but not a unique roll identifier for every identical concurrent drop. The implementation does not pretend to match a player's response to one indistinguishable copy. It marks those cases as **ambiguous** in the tooltip.

Similarly, a missing winner does not justify inventing one. The row can say **“Ended (result unavailable)”** when the original deadline is exceeded. If a late genuine result arrives, that status is **provisional** and may be updated. When a local roll prompt closes, that is not automatically evidence that the group has completed the roll.

The small interface thus carries a broader creative principle: **give the player useful feedback without claiming knowledge the client does not provide**.

## The project's boundaries

LootFeed doesn't auto-roll, compare another player's fairness, rank loot recipients, redistribute items, or save an archival database of group behavior. It uses old-client Lua UI primitives and optional local chat hiding, with all remaining item/roll decisions made through normal game UI.

Potential improvements—reduced motion, more localization or different roll privacy—remain options for Babuni.dev rather than approved changes. The portfolio should show this as a compact interaction-design work, not expand it into a conventional loot-management dashboard without permission.

# LootFeed — the creative and technical development journal

**Original creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Retrospective prepared:** October 26, 2026. Evidence: current README, TOC, both Lua source files, PowerShell migration utility and test, screenshots, dated Git diffs and v0.2.2 release metadata. This is **not a transcript of every earlier conversation**; unknown motives are labeled rather than invented.

## Beginning with a small reward moment

The idea embodied in LootFeed is that picking up an item should be a pleasant, legible moment rather than another easy-to-miss chat message. The game's inventory system already knows what a player owns; this addon was designed to show the **event of receiving** something, briefly and clearly, while the player continues adventuring.

Its initial identity was **Octo Loot**. The first substantive Git commit, **`dde82cb8130f`** on September 8, 2026, was already described as a **0.1.5 release**. It came with one Lua source file, a 1.12 TOC, a concise README and three screenshots. That is the earliest preserved committed state, not proof that the entire idea and all of its design trials were completed in one sitting. Earlier creator dialogue or local test sessions were not recovered in the repository review.

The interface at that point was intentionally compact. There were **five small rows**, each able to display an item texture, colored name and stack count; money had a coin icon, and genuine Quest Items could receive a gold secondary label. These rows appeared with a modest scale/pop and moved into a stack before fading after a short duration. Hovering both paused the messages and surfaced the native item tooltip.

The original design offered player-controlled location, scale, lifetime and whether the stack builds up or down. A tiny green drag handle became visible only when unlocked. The appeal is in *reducing friction*: a player can keep playing, and each useful pickup remains momentarily intelligible.

Several small technical details express that direction. An item icon may not be cached when the item chat event arrives, so the UI retries `GetItemInfo` later rather than permanently displaying a question mark. Identical item links are combined **while waiting in the queue**, but an already displayed row retains its own short history. A Quest Item is detected by reading its tooltip's binding text, not by guessing whether a material is used by some quest.

Even the money icon tells a story about working within old client resources. Source comments say the developer visually inspected the Vanilla interface MPQ coin icons and selected different item textures for copper, silver and gold. This is historical technical evidence, not an independent repeat of that inspection in October.

## September 11 — a quick personal feed becomes group-aware

A few days later, commit **`fbbd50fac74d`**, “Add persistent group-roll entries with live dice tooltips,” expanded the addon from brief *personal loot* into a window on a **shared decision**.

A group Need/Greed/Pass roll cannot be represented well by one fading item notification. The roll remains in progress while several players make choices, sometimes while numerical results arrive later. A new **Rolls.lua** module appeared, handling roll start/cancel events, item-link keyed chat messages, participants, choices, numbers, winners and the possibility that results simply never appear.

The UI gained **additional roll rows** beyond its five ordinary rows. Each had a die drawn directly through Lua, with a small tooltip enumerating the players. The design left Blizzard's actual rolling buttons intact. LootFeed watched and explained a collective activity; it did not decide Need or Greed on the player's behalf.

This feature introduced an important technical dependency of a different kind: the addon needs detailed loot-roll chat. Its `Rolls.Init` enables the game CVar `showLootSpam` when disabled. There is no bundled library requirement, but there **is** a user-setting side effect. The current source does not save/restore the previous setting. This is a review item the portfolio should preserve rather than assuming it was consciously approved in all circumstances.

The source parses the game's own `LOOT_ROLL_*` localized templates, including numbered positional placeholders. Yet those messages still identify a player and item link without a stable ID for **which instance of an identical item** is being rolled. When two identical drops are up simultaneously, the addon declines to invent assignments and marks the outcome ambiguous. Unknown participant choices remain “Waiting / eligibility unknown.”

The developer created a **/oloot testroll** preview (now **/lfeed testroll**) that simulates ExampleMage and ExampleRogue choices. It is clearly labeled as a preview, offering a lightweight way to inspect the die/tooltips without asking a group of real players to run a test.

## Later September 11 — a bug in what “finished” meant

The second September 11 commit, **`86036564974e`**, is an especially revealing piece of development history. Its message was “Keep tracking group rolls after the local prompt closes.”

The initial roll handling had treated closing the *local* UI prompt as evidence of approaching group completion, with a short cancellation grace period. That assumption was too broad. The game's prompt can close for one player while choices and results are still traveling through the group.

The new code records `promptClosed` without making the roll done. It waits for **a genuine winner message, everyone passing, or the original deadline**. If the deadline arrives without proof, the record enters **Ended (result unavailable)** rather than assigning a fictional winner.

Even that status isn't necessarily the final word. A late authentic result can correct an earlier provisional timeout, while delayed numeric rolls may still arrive after a winner. The source retains completed records for a bounded time and refreshes the visual row when the status changes.

This is a concrete correction of an earlier implementation hypothesis. The commit demonstrates the code change; it doesn't reveal an entire debugging dialogue, a particular user's complaint, or a successful in-game reenactment. Keeping the distinction protects the project's true history while still explaining why the present solution exists.

## September 18 — changing names without losing the player's settings

Commit **`6126df1f90d7`**, “Use provider-neutral names and client compatibility descriptions,” renamed **Octo Loot** to **Loot Feed**, the project to `LootFeed`, the Lua globals, frame/TOC identifiers and account-wide saved variable from **OctoLootDB** to **LootFeedDB**. So the repository gained **`Upgrade-SavedData.ps1`** and **`tests/test_upgrade.ps1`**. # LootFeed — architecture and roll-state guarantees

**Source inspected:** `LootFeed.lua` (316 lines), `Rolls.lua` (190 lines), manifest, migration helper and fixture, October 26, 2026. **Static review only**; no game or PowerShell test executed.

## Installed package

```text
LootFeed.toc   Interface 11200, Version 0.2.2
               SavedVariables: LootFeedDB (account-wide)
               Rolls.lua -> LootFeed.lua
Rolls.lua      LootFeedRolls global; roll records, message parser, timeouts
LootFeed.lua   feed rows, queue, icons, tooltip, animation, chat hook, commands
```

The TOC actually lists **Rolls.lua** first, then **LootFeed.lua**. The game uses the Vanilla-style globals `event`, `arg1` and `this`; no modern loot-history API, external library or server endpoint is required.

## Normal loot and money pipeline

```text
ADDON_LOADED ("LootFeed")
  -> LootFeedDB defaults and scale/duration clamps
  -> compile client LOOT_ITEM_* personal loot patterns
  -> make 5 normal UI row frames
  -> LootFeedRolls.Init(callback)
  -> Place() + lock anchor
  -> wrap original ChatFrame_OnEvent if available

CHAT_MSG_LOOT
  -> also pass into LootFeedRolls.Event for roll parsing
  -> if personal LOOT_ITEM_* match, extract item link / quantity
  -> Enqueue(item)

CHAT_MSG_MONEY
  -> parse localized denominations, select coin icon
  -> Enqueue(money text)

OnUpdate (every frame)
  -> LootFeedRolls.Tick()
  -> inject demos at ~0.7s spacing if active
  -> if hovering, pause visible stack and insertion
  -> expire and animate rows
  -> insert queue at >=0.32s spacing
  -> place/fade current rows
```

`Enqueue` coalesces **identical item links only among queued entries** by summing their quantity; items already active retain their separate display history. The standard `LIMIT=5` covers **non-roll** rows. When full, the oldest normal row is pushed into expiration, preserving the finite on-screen flow. Roll rows are not counted against the ordinary limit; they can create additional frames.

Rows use **270×40** logical dimensions, **5px** gap and a `0.9` compact scale layered onto the user scale. `LootFeedDB.duration` defaults **6s** and is clamped to **2–20s**; scale defaults 1 and is clamped **0.6–1.8**. Entrance pop runs around **0.32s**, fade around **0.7s**, while ordinary insertion is spaced by **0.32s**. Stack position eases toward the target. Up/down direction inverts the offsets.

`GetItemInfo` may be temporarily uncached. The renderer falls back to link text/known icons and retries refresh about every **0.5 seconds** until the texture resolves.

## Item and quest recognition

The source compiles six original `LOOT_ITEM_*` client string constants for self-loot and extracts `|Hitem:...|h` links. This compiler recognizes `%s` and `%d` substitutions but **does not** implement the positional-template mapping present in Rolls.lua, so language/provider support is not uniformly guaranteed.

Quest Item status is determined by scanning an actual `GameTooltip` and matching a line exactly to `ITEM_BIND_QUEST` (or the English fallback). That does **not** mean an ordinary item needed for a quest gets labeled.

Money text is normalized into copper, then picks a coin icon: total >= **10000** → gold, >= **100** → silver, otherwise copper. The note in source says the specific old-client coin icon paths were visually inspected from a client MPQ; this historical code comment does **not** count as new independent validation today.

## Group rolls as stateful records

```text
LootFeedRolls.records[id] = {
  id, link, item key, texture, amount,
  players[name] = { name, choice?, number? },
  order = [participant names],
  status, deadline, done?, winner?, finished?,
  promptClosed?, ambiguous?
}
LootFeedRolls.pending[id] = { duration, untilTime } # if link missing initially
```

The tracker receives `START_LOOT_ROLL`, `CANCEL_LOOT_ROLL` and `CHAT_MSG_LOOT`. On start, it asks `GetLootRollItemLink` and `GetLootRollItemInfo`, then takes an initial participant list from party or raid unit names. A roll with no item link is retried for **three seconds**; once resolved, the deadline is its supplied duration in milliseconds converted to seconds plus **15 seconds**.

`Rolls.Init` compiles client `LOOT_ROLL_*` format strings, including positional `%s`/`%d` placeholders. It also sets `showLootSpam=1` when the value is 0 so choices/numeric rolls are available in chat. The code does not revert that setting later.

For each matched message, the tracker searches for a **single unresolved matching item link**. Vanilla chat does not attach a unique roll ID to every chat choice. If multiple roll records share the link, it marks them ambiguous instead of attaching the message to one arbitrarily.

`CANCEL_LOOT_ROLL` sets **promptClosed** but **does not** declare a result. The group may still be rolling. A “winner” or “everyone passed” message completes the roll; otherwise the original deadline produces **Ended (result unavailable)**, with no invented winner. A genuine later result can update that provisional completion; delayed numeric outcomes may also arrive after a winner. Completed roll records are purged after **300 seconds**.

The UI callback `RollChanged` allocates an extra row if needed, draws a five-pip die, and refreshes a hover tooltip with participant status, numbers, winner or explicit ambiguity. While unresolved, row.age is held near the entrance value; once complete, the roll row displays around **15 seconds**, then fades. Hover pauses the **visible feed**, but `LootFeedRolls.Tick` still processes external roll events before the hover pause.

`/lfeed testroll` creates a **clearly labeled demo roll** with fictional ExampleMage/ExampleRogue members, not a real network action.

## Chat handler integration and risk

Vanilla lacks modern `ChatFrame_AddMessageEventFilter`. `LootFeed.lua` stores the current `ChatFrame_OnEvent` global and replaces it with a delegate that suppresses **recognized personal item CHAT_MSG_LOOT** only when `LootFeedDB.mute` is true. Other chat messages delegate to the prior function. Other addons may also wrap that global; load order, handler replacement and lifecycle need real client compatibility tests. Hiding loot in chat does **not** stop the feed recording it or stop group roll data.

Settings persisted: **x, y, scale, duration, direction, mute** in account-wide `LootFeedDB`. **Roll history is session-memory only.**

# LootFeed — interface and interaction design

**Creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev.

## A small celebration that doesn't become a second inventory

The feed is meant to be **noticed briefly**, not always visible. Standard entries are dark, compact rows that show a recognisable item icon, rarity-colored title and stack count. Coin drops use simple denominations; real Quest Items get a discreet golden label. Items pass through a smooth pop, slide and fade rather than suddenly appearing as chat-line text.

The initial September 8 version deliberately allowed only **five ordinary rows**. This constraint preserves screen space and keeps a busy looting moment from turning into a permanent inventory summary.

![Standard loot feed](../Screenshots/loot-feed.png)

## Positioning and timing

The green anchor handle becomes interactable with **/lfeed unlock**. The player drags it to a preferred side of the interface and locks it afterward. Scale ranges **0.6–1.8**; duration ranges **2–20 seconds**; the stack can build **upward or downward**. These settings are account-wide, not per-character.

Hovering an item reveals the game's tooltip while pausing the entire visual stack. That turns a fast notification into inspectable information without a separate details panel. An item whose client cache is still loading falls back to textual/icon placeholders and refreshes when more data arrives.

![Hover item tooltip](../Screenshots/item-tooltip.png)

The gold **Quest Item** label relies on the actual game's tooltip binding text, not on guessing which items a current quest needs.

![Quest item indicator](../Screenshots/quest-item.png)

## Roll details should remain inspectable

Group rolls don't fit in the five-row constraint. They can last longer than a standard loot notification and need room for people and numbers to arrive in stages. The design therefore creates **additional roll rows** that remain while unresolved, show a drawn five-pip die, and keep the winner near that die when known.

Hovering over the dice opens a compact detailed list of Need/Greed/Pass choices and numeric rolls, including waiting/unknown states. The built-in game Need/Greed/Pass dialog remains the place where the player makes a choice; LootFeed is observational only.

Two important UI messages resist false precision:
- Simultaneous identical item drops can be **ambiguous** because item-link chat messages don't identify the unique roll.
- A deadline without a received winner becomes **result unavailable**, which may later update if a real message arrives.

## Behavioral surprises requiring usability review

The source automatically turns on the game's detailed **showLootSpam** option when it was off so the roll details can be received. That has an effect beyond LootFeed's own tiny interface. The optional **/lfeed chat off** also wraps a global chat handler to hide personal loot lines, which may affect interaction with other addons using the same handler.

These are implemented choices, not silently approved future changes. Decide whether a clear opt-in/explanation for the game CVar would better support the creator's direction after an actual in-game test.

## Accessibility tests still outstanding

Test small-scale text contrast, accessible alternatives to color-only rarity distinctions, animation sensitivity, hover-to-pause discoverability, 24px dice-hit targets and busy simultaneous roll displays. No such test was run in this documentation session and no redesigned interface was implemented.

The code tells us what changed; it cannot prove the full design debate or who typed each implementation line in September.

## Tradeoffs embodied in code

**Ordinary notification limit vs roll expansion:** five regular rows preserve space, but group decisions may need extra simultaneous entries. Both behaviors coexist, rather than truncating important roll status to enforce a universal cap.

**Observed data vs invented certainty:** a chat link identifies an item but not one unique simultaneous roll for identical drops. Ambiguity is displayed explicitly. A timeout lacks a winner and is provisional, so it can be revised by a late authentic message.

**Local prompt vs shared state:** closing the local popup isn't the same as resolving the group. The September 11 correction records this semantic distinction directly in code.

**Chat filtering vs interop:** Vanilla has no modern ChatFrame_AddMessageEventFilter; LootFeed wraps `ChatFrame_OnEvent` to hide only personal item messages. It has a real global-function compatibility surface.

**Data completeness vs control of preferences:** richer roll tooltips require detailed loot spam; the addon sets `showLootSpam=1` if initially off and doesn't restore it. That is a source-visible side effect worth testing and asking the creator about, not something to conceal in a user guide.

**Account-wide preferences, transient events:** display choices carry between characters, while loot and group roll records do not survive reloads. Keeping privacy/lifetime bounded is an observed design outcome, not proof of a specific retention-policy meeting.

**Rename vs continuity:** the general LootFeed name requires migrating old `OctoLootDB`. The helper backs up originals and refuses existing destinations.

## Visual message types

| UI content | Source data | How it is represented |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Personal item drop | Recognized `CHAT_MSG_LOOT` self-item formats | Item link, item name, cached texture, rarity tint, amount |
| Money | `CHAT_MSG_MONEY` and localized denomination words | Text plus gold/silver/copper icon determined from copper-equivalent amount |
| Quest Item | Actual item binding line of a scanned tooltip | Gold **Quest Item** secondary label |
| Group roll | `START_LOOT_ROLL` + parsed roll chat | Item and dice with players, choices, numbers, status, winner if known |
| Group roll uncertainty | Missing winner or duplicate item-link messages | **Ended (result unavailable)** or explicit ambiguity |
| Preview item feed | `/lfeed test` | Synthetic Linen Cloth, Shadowgem, Peacebloom, Night Watch Shortsword and other examples |
| Preview group roll | `/lfeed testroll` | Synthetic ExampleMage / ExampleRogue; tooltip explicitly calls it a preview |

The addon references the game client's **item/icon textures**, not bundled custom artwork. The dice icon is composed in Lua from a square and five little pips, avoiding a dependency on client-specific dice textures. Rarity coloring comes from the item link's color code.

## Saved data and non-saved state

The manifest declares **SavedVariables: LootFeedDB**. Its current settings are:
- `x, y`: anchor offsets from a defined UIParent anchor.
- `scale`: clamped 0.6–1.8, default 1.
- `duration`: seconds, clamped 2–20, default 6.
- `direction`: up/down, default down.
- `mute`: suppress recognized personal item chat messages via wrapped ChatFrame handler, default false.

**Not saved:** past loot feed messages, queue contents, per-roll participant records, winners, temporary hover/demo state. The phrase “persistent group rolls” historically means visible through the group decision, not stored account-wide.

## Localization and origin of values

Normal self-item templates are drawn from global `LOOT_ITEM_*` strings; rolls are matched using `LOOT_ROLL_*` strings with support for numbered positional placeholders. The quest item binding text references `ITEM_BIND_QUEST`; denominations refer to `GOLD`, `SILVER`, `COPPER`. Text-matching limitations still exist, particularly unusual server formats or positional self-loot strings.

# Melee Start Attack

**A minimal auto-attack companion for Vanilla World of Warcraft**

**Project creator:** Babuni.dev  
**Version:** 1.3.1  
**Client declared in manifest:** World of Warcraft 1.12 / interface 11200 (the project describes 1.12.1)  
**Source:** [MeleeStartAttack.lua](MeleeStartAttack.lua) · [MeleeStartAttack.toc](MeleeStartAttack.toc)  
**Verification:** source and dated Git history reviewed October 26, 2026. No in-game tests performed here.

Melee Start Attack connects **the player's intention to fight** to the game's ordinary auto-attacks. If you press a configured ability as a **Paladin, Warrior or Shaman** against a living, attackable target, the addon can start your basic melee swing **before** the original ability executes—even when a spell is on cooldown or you don't have enough mana or rage. It does not cast abilities for you, select targets, analyze combat performance, or replace the original game action.

Unlike the earlier [WarriorStartAttack](https://github.com/babunidev/WarriorStartAttack), this version has class-specific built-in ability lists, runtime controls and a **learn-the-next-ability** feature that saves additional start/stop behaviors by class.

## Install

Copy both committed files into the AddOns directory with this folder name:

    Interface/AddOns/MeleeStartAttack/
      MeleeStartAttack.toc
      MeleeStartAttack.lua

Restart or reload the game, enable **Melee Start Attack**, and look for the chat message *Melee Start Attack loaded.* A printed load message verifies Lua execution, **not** successful interception of every action API.

The TOC defines SavedVariables **MeleeStartAttackDB**; learned abilities survive reloads/logins, but the simple on/off toggle is **reset to enabled at every load**.

### Recommended attack-state setup

Put WoW's ordinary **Attack** action (from the General spellbook tab) on **any action bar**. The addon scans slots 1–120, remembers an Attack action slot and uses **IsCurrentAction** to check whether basic swings are on. If there is no Attack action present, it uses an in-memory flag updated through combat events and its own calls.

This fallback is less precise: being *in combat* isn't necessarily identical to actively auto-attacking. Repeated presses are **designed** to avoid toggling attacks off, but that behavior has not been verified on an actual client during this audit.

## Supported default ability families

| Class | Built-in start-attack actions |
| --- | --- |
| Paladin — **7 icons** | Seal of Righteousness, Seal of the Crusader, Seal of Light, Seal of Wisdom, Seal of Justice, Seal of Command, Judgement |
| Warrior — **20 icons** | Bloodthirst, Cleave, Demoralizing Shout, Disarm, Execute, Hamstring, Heroic Strike, Intercept, Mortal Strike, Mocking Blow, Overpower, Pummel, Rend, Revenge, Shield Bash, Slam, Sunder Armor, Taunt, Thunder Clap, Whirlwind |
| Shaman — **5 icons** | Earth Shock, Flame Shock, Frost Shock, Stormstrike, **Lightning Strike (custom-ability mapping)** |

The implementation uses **32 class-scoped icon mappings**, not unique spell identifiers. Some ability names are historical source/README labels; the game client must supply matching internal icon textures. Vanilla/custom-client icon collisions or changed textures can produce unexpected matches or omissions.

**Built-in stop-attack exception:** **Warrior Intimidating Shout**. Additional stop actions can be learned for the current class.

## Commands

The primary command aliases are **/meleeattack** and **/msa**:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `/msa` or `/msa toggle` | Toggle automatic start/stop behavior |
| `/msa on` / `/msa off` | Enable or disable automatic triggering **for this session** |
| `/msa status` | Report whether enabled and which auto-attack detection mode is active |
| `/msa learn` or `/msa learn start` | Learn the next recognized ability for **starting** auto-attack |
| `/msa learn stop` | Learn the next recognized ability for **stopping** auto-attack |
| `/msa list` | List learned abilities for your current class |
| `/msa unlearn <spell name>` | Remove the first matching learned **localized spell name** for your class |
| `/msa reset` | Remove all **learned** entries for your current class; built-in icons remain |
| `/start_auto_attack` | Manually start swings if a living hostile/attackable target exists and attack seems off |
| `/stop_auto_attack` | Manually stop swings if attack seems active |

For example, type **/msa learn stop** and press a spell the addon can identify by an internal icon and spellbook name. It will save a **class-specific** entry with `icon`, localized `spellName` and action `stop`. The learned entry follows the ability's **icon** if you move it between action-bar slots. The same press that completes learning also passes through regular start/stop matching; it is not a read-only capture event.

The manual `/start_auto_attack` and `/stop_auto_attack` commands are independent of the automatic enable toggle. The current code also permits learning entries for a class beyond the three with default lists, because learned entries are keyed by whatever class token the client returns; **three classes** is the declared built-in coverage, not a hard runtime restriction for custom learning.

## How ability recognition works

1. Action bar: wrap **UseAction** and query **GetActionTexture**.
2. Spellbook: wrap **CastSpell** and query **GetSpellTexture**.
3. Macros and other addon commands: wrap **CastSpellByName**, find the locally named ability in the spellbook, then compare its **icon**.

These wrappers call the original function after checking the icon. The effect occurs **before** the client can reject a spell for low resources or cooldown. They do not guarantee that a spell succeeded; they do not deliberately auto-cast, queue an ability or change the target.

An icon can be whitelisted and learned at the same time. In the current source **stop takes precedence** over start when a texture is recognized in both lists; learning an opposite behavior does not consistently erase a built-in mapping.

## Persistence and version migrations

MeleeStartAttackDB stores **customAbilities** by **class**, not separate profiles for individual characters. Different characters of the same class using one account SavedVariables table may share learned entries, even if localized names or abilities differ. Earlier version **1.1.2** stored **customStartIcons**; the current code migrates these to records with action **start** and placeholder name **(legacy learned icon)**, then clears the legacy table. To give an old entry a usable name, use learning again on its ability.

No other preferences are saved in the source (in particular, enabled/disabled state and cached Attack-action slot are session-only).

## Known limitations and next checks

- The in-combat fallback does not prove that actual white swings are active, so toggling **AttackTarget()** can be wrong if state drifts.
- Learning is **by icon**, not unique spell ID. Shared icon artwork and same-class custom spells are ambiguous.
- Learning needs a recognizable spellbook name; some macro/custom buttons cannot be identified and may leave learning armed for the next press.
- `/msa off` does not disable the two **manual** start/stop commands.
- Stop/start logic is separate from spell success, mana, rage, GCD and cooldown rules.
- Global function wrappers can conflict with other addons wrapping the same functions, including the related WarriorStartAttack addon.
- True multilingual compatibility was not independently tested; it is the **icon-based design goal**.
- This repo has **no LICENSE file**. Do not assume an open-source license or add one without Babuni.dev's decision.

The [roadmap](ROADMAP.md) gives a reproducible target-client test matrix. Everything above describes current code, **not proven gameplay performance**.

# MeleeStartAttack — concept

**Creative author:** Babuni.dev  
**Implementation target:** Vanilla WoW 1.12.1 / Lua 5.0.  
**Status:** A source-grounded creative reconstruction, not the missing original planning dialogue.

## When the player chooses to fight

The practical problem is small but persistent: selecting an offensive ability and beginning an ordinary melee attack can be two separate steps in old WoW. In low-rage and low-mana moments, or with a spell unavailable on cooldown, the player still intends to engage. **MeleeStartAttack** treats the player's chosen action as the signal to begin normal swings when a living hostile target is present.

The addon doesn't automate decisions about which attack to cast. It reacts to what the user already pressed, then delegates to the game's original ability invocation. Keeping ordinary player intent intact is central to the concept.

This expands the separate WarriorStartAttack idea to **Paladin, Warrior and Shaman**. Its key creative difference is not simply more predefined abilities, but letting the player declare new start or stop actions *from within the game*.

## Making an old-client limitation into an interaction

Vanilla lacks the later spell-identity APIs common to modern addons. The implementation compares internal spell **icon paths**, which are largely independent of the client's translated spell names. This avoids maintaining a multi-language textual whitelist and can work for new custom abilities with familiar game icons.

Runtime learning turns that technical method into an approachable workflow: issue `/msa learn start` or `/msa learn stop`, then press the intended ability. The addon finds an icon and spellbook name, stores the behavior under the character's **class token**, and remembers it after reload. It follows a moved action-bar button because the icon, not the original slot number, is the identity.

The downside is that **icons are not unique spell IDs**; two unrelated spells can use the same art. Real correctness requires careful client tests, especially on custom server builds.

## The right rhythm for a toggling attack API

The API function `AttackTarget()` toggles attack state. Calling it blindly on every offensive press can stop the player's swings. The project therefore seeks the normal Attack action on an action bar and uses its current-state flag. If no Attack action is present, it falls back to a combat-event-driven local guess.

August development progressively focused on that problem: moving from repeated scanning/flag checks to caching a genuine Attack action location. The idea was to **keep the addon invisible** while preventing an invisible mistake from interrupting combat.

## A start-and-stop language

The built-in lists cover 7 Paladin, 20 Warrior and 5 Shaman actions. Warrior's **Intimidating Shout** is a built-in stop exception. Learning extends both sides: players can mark abilities as **start** or **stop** without editing Lua. The macro commands offer a direct manual option.

This is an embodied usability idea, not a damage rotation. There are no efficiency metrics, recommendations, graphics panels or target-selecting AI.

## What remains unknown

The August and September Git commits document the progression of code and readmes. They do not reveal all reasoning, debugging sessions or original human–AI conversations. The creator's authorship is primary; source inspection by an AI assistant later cannot retroactively assign individual concept decisions to itself.

The future portfolio should show the evolution from a single-class intervention to an extensible three-class toy for improving feel, with implementation tradeoffs and actual client-test results kept distinct.

# MeleeStartAttack — narrative development journal

**Project creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Retrospective compiled:** October 26, 2026 from current Lua/TOC/README and dated Git diffs. This is **not** a verbatim restoration of earlier chats; motivations without direct evidence are identified as interpretations.

## A small Warrior idea becomes a family of interactions

The goal behind MeleeStartAttack is a simple form of respect for player intention. Someone clicks an attack-oriented ability to engage an enemy. In Vanilla WoW that ability may not succeed: the character may lack rage or mana, or the cooldown may not have completed. Those failures shouldn't necessarily keep the character from making ordinary melee swings. An addon can fill that tiny gap without attempting to make the player's decisions for them.

The creator had already explored the problem in the separate **WarriorStartAttack** project, uploaded earlier in August 2026. **MeleeStartAttack** broadens the approach beyond a Warrior-only whitelist: Paladin Seals and Judgement, a Warrior suite of actions, and Shaman Shocks and Stormstrike all gain the same kind of possible start trigger. The sources establish this close conceptual kinship; they don't prove a particular explicit port or original private conversation between the two repos.

The emotional benefit is not a new interface panel or a spectacular feature. It is the feeling that ordinary game controls do what the player expects them to do: if you engage a hostile target, your character begins attacking; if you are already swinging, repeated ability presses shouldn't turn that off.

## August 22, 2026 — first committed multi-class version

The repository's creation and first implementation commit **`ef0acb0`** are dated **August 22, 2026**. The initial file was roughly 150 lines and declared addon version **1.1.0** for interface **11200**, targeting Vanilla 1.12.1 / Lua 5.0.

This first implementation was intentionally small. It defined per-class icon tables for **Paladin, Warrior and Shaman**, a Warrior stop exception for Intimidating Shout, and a single interception point—**UseAction**—for action-bar presses. It checked a living attackable target and attempted to avoid blindly toggling `AttackTarget()`, a function that can both start *and stop* normal swings.

There was also an on/off/status slash-command system. The enabled state was deliberately (or at least as-coded) reset to true on each reload rather than stored. At that point, there was **no runtime learning system**, no macro-cast wrappers, no account-wide saved custom ability list, and no caching of the Attack action location.

The README described multi-class support and action-on-attempt behavior; it did not demonstrate a real game-client success. The exact original brainstorming and who authored particular lines were not available in this review, so the concept remains credited to **Babuni.dev**, and the implementation is described by what Git actually contains.

## August 29 — listening beyond action buttons and teaching the addon

The commit **`2eafab6`**, dated **August 29**, carried the title *“Refine melee start attack triggers.”* It expanded the Shaman table with a **Lightning Strike** icon, initially annotated as a special ability on a named custom provider. Later wording would remove that provider name, but the **custom-client origin of this mapping** is worth preserving rather than presenting it as a guaranteed base Vanilla ability.

The more substantial change was in how the addon understood an action. The original code deliberately wrapped only `UseAction` to avoid interfering with other spell-cast APIs. The revision added wrappers for **CastSpell** and **CastSpellByName**, making the behavior available when an addon, macro or spellbook invoked those APIs directly. That widened compatibility ambitions, but also widened potential interactions with other addons that hook global functions.

That week also introduced **`/msa learn`**: the next recognized icon could become a new start-attack rule for the player's class, stored in **MeleeStartAttackDB.customStartIcons**. No longer did every new or custom class ability require a Lua edit. The player could teach the system from inside the game. It was still start-only learning and it saved raw icon keys rather than named records.

The source marks these mechanisms as features present in code. No in-game test log was recovered to prove which macros, localized spell names, or custom providers they worked with.

## August 30 — the problem with AttackTarget being a toggle

On **August 30**, commit **`02515ea`** made the state model more deliberate and versioned the TOC to **1.2.1**. The core challenge is that WoW's `AttackTarget()` isn't a one-way StartAttack function. It toggles. If the addon calls it on every eligible button press, the player can accidentally cancel swings.

Earlier code scanned action-bar slots looking for an active Attack action, then fell back to a boolean based on combat enter/leave events. The new version looked for the **normal Attack action**, cached a found slot, and queried the game's `IsCurrentAction` state directly when that slot remained valid. If no Attack action could be found, it retained the old combat-event boolean as a compromise for players who hadn't placed Attack on a bar.

This revision also introduced explicit **/start_auto_attack** and **/stop_auto_attack** macro commands. Together, these changes made state detection more visible and gave players controlled direct commands in addition to automatic action-trigger interception.

The compromise remained imperfect in theory: entering combat and auto-swinging are not synonymous. The addon might infer an attack from combat events when no white swings are running. That is an architectural risk, **not a confirmed regression**. The development record can explain it without inventing a debugging incident.

## August 31 — personalizing behavior by class

The next day's commit **`83f9b37`** advanced the addon to **version 1.3.1**, adding more refined **per-class learning**. Instead of storing only a set of icons that should start attacks, each learned record contained the icon path, the localized spellbook name and an action of **start** or **stop**. Players could type **/msa learn stop** and select an ability that should stop auto-attacking, inspect the list with **/msa list**, remove entries by localized name or reset that class's learned rules.

Importantly, this update **migrated** older 1.1.2 saved icon collections into named-entry data while retaining their original start behavior. The migrated names were marked as **(legacy learned icon)** and could be refreshed by relearning. That is a visible concern for continuity, even if we don't have a discussion showing who originally requested backward compatibility.

This revision also contains a subtle constraint: an icon is still the central identity, and the runtime checks **stop before start**. If a built-in start icon is also learned as stop, both match; the stop wins. Conversely, learning start on the built-in Intimidating Shout stop icon won't remove its stop behavior. The system is therefore a combination of static class decisions and user learning, not an unrestricted override model.

The new learning records are shared across characters **of the same class** within the account-wide SavedVariables table, not saved per character. That choice may be convenient or surprising depending on the creator's intended use; it should be tested and discussed rather than retroactively justified.

# MeleeStartAttack — source architecture (v1.3.1)

**Sources:** `MeleeStartAttack.lua` (435 lines), `MeleeStartAttack.toc`, 2026-10-26. **Static code inspection**; no client runtime test.

## Flow through the three intercepted functions

```text
UseAction(actionSlot, checkCursor, onSelf)
    -> GetActionTexture(actionSlot)
CastSpell(spellSlot, bookType)
    -> GetSpellTexture(spellSlot, bookType)
CastSpellByName(spellName, onSelf)
    -> find matching localized spellbook name
    -> GetSpellTexture(matching spellSlot)
           |
           v
     if automation enabled:
        if learning mode armed:
           learn icon + spellbook name for current class
        if IsStopAttackIcon(icon): StopAutoAttack()
        else if IsStartAttackIcon(icon): StartAutoAttack()
           |
           v
     invoke original WoW function with original arguments
```

These are direct wrappers of **global game functions**, not secure post-hooks. Other addons can hook the same globals; behavior and original delegation depend on load order. The current code recognizes source changes **at attempt time**, before checks for rage, mana, cooldown, range or cast success.

## Recognized class data

The hard-coded `startAttackIcons` has **7 PALADIN**, **20 WARRIOR**, **5 SHAMAN** entries. The five Shaman entries include a client-specific **Lightning Strike** assumption, labeled *custom ability* in the source. The `stopAttackIcons` table maps Warrior **Intimidating Shout** only.

Lookup uses `PlayerClass()` (the English class token returned by `UnitClass`), and checks that class's texture table, so default entries aren't global. **GetLearnedAbility(texture)** checks the current class's SavedVariables first. Both `IsStartAttackIcon` and `IsStopAttackIcon` return true if either the built-in table or matching learned action says yes; the wrapped call gives **stop first** priority.

**Conflict caution:** learning `stop` on a built-in start icon may cause both predicates to be true and stop wins. Learning `start` on a built-in stop icon similarly cannot override the stop. A learned record updates by **matching icon**, not by unique spell name.

## Hybrid auto-attack state

```text
GetAttackActionSlot():
   cached slot still IsAttackAction? -> reuse
   else scan action slots 1..120 for first IsAttackAction
   cache slot or nil

IsAutoAttacking():
   attack slot present? -> IsCurrentAction(slot)
   otherwise         -> attackActive in-memory flag

StartAutoAttack():
   UnitExists(target)
   AND not UnitIsDead(target)
   AND UnitCanAttack(player, target)
   AND not IsAutoAttacking()
      -> AttackTarget() [TOGGLE], attackActive = true

StopAutoAttack():
   if IsAutoAttacking(): AttackTarget() [TOGGLE]
   attackActive = false
```

On **PLAYER_ENTER_COMBAT**, `attackActive=true`; on **PLAYER_LEAVE_COMBAT**, `attackActive=false`. There is **no server-confirmed swing state** in fallback mode. Combat membership and active white attacks are different concepts, so the fallback requires game testing, especially when the Attack button is missing and another addon interacts with the toggle.

The source describes the cached Attack action as the more reliable mode. Unlike the August 22 version, later code does **not repeatedly scan all slots when its remembered Attack slot is still valid**, though moving/removing the Attack action triggers a rescan.

## SavedVariables and learning

```text
MeleeStartAttackDB (TOC SavedVariables; account-wide)
└── customAbilities
    ├── PALADIN = [{ icon, spellName, action="start"|"stop" }, ...]
    ├── WARRIOR = [...]
    ├── SHAMAN = [...]
    └── other class token if user explicitly learns one
```

On load the Lua initializes missing tables, and if `customStartIcons` exists, iterates it and inserts **start-only** records with `spellName="(legacy learned icon)"`, then clears the old field. That is explicit migration from the version-1.1.2 schema. **No per-character profile** exists; storage is by class across the account SavedVariables file.

`learnAction` is session-local (nil, `start` or `stop`). Learning an icon requires either a supplied `GetSpellName` from spellbook/cast or a successful `FindSpellNameByIcon` scan. A macro action without a resolvable spellbook name may fail to learn and leave the capture active. The **capturing input also passes through normal start/stop matching**; learned behavior can take effect on that same press.

Unlearning locates the first case-insensitive match by **localized spellName**, not icon, so migrated placeholder-name records are awkward to remove individually until relearned. `reset` clears current-class learned entries only; it does not change built-in lists.

## Runtime commands and enabled state

`SLASH_MELEESTARTATTACK1` and `2` register **/meleeattack** and **/msa**. They handle on/off/toggle/status/learn/learn start/learn stop/list/unlearn/reset. The code additionally registers standalone **/start_auto_attack** and **/stop_auto_attack**.

`enabled` is initialized `true` every Lua execution, with **no persisted enabled key**. The manual start/stop slash commands call their functions directly even when disabled; disabling only bypasses the wrapped input logic, not the commands themselves. Automatic lookup is class-scoped; manual start can work on any class with a valid hostile target.

## Compatibility and package shape

The TOC declares **Interface 11200**, **Version 1.3.1**, **Author Babuni.dev**, **SavedVariables MeleeStartAttackDB**, loading just **MeleeStartAttack.lua**. No custom GUI, media, network communication or external service was found. The source uses Vanilla-style **global event** in a simple registered event frame and Lua 5.0 syntax.

No automated tests, client logs or LICENSE were found in the inspected tree. This document describes source rules, **not experimentally verified game behavior**.

# MeleeStartAttack — interaction design

**Creative author:** Babuni.dev.

## A tiny intervention at the moment of intent

The user already pressed Heroic Strike, Judgement or Shock to engage a hostile target. The addon should not demand a separate auto-attack activation before normal melee begins. Its interface is therefore deliberately almost invisible: it adds a **conditional action-state change** to the player's ordinary interaction with the game.

The most visible UI is chat feedback from **/msa**. There is no options window, performance graph, combat overlay or automated target selection. Built-in icon tables are complemented by a short in-game learning ritual that removes the need to modify code for each custom ability.

## Learning as a design gesture

Typing **/msa learn start** or **/msa learn stop** sets a one-use capture mode. The next eligible ability press resolves an icon and a local spellbook name, and writes a class-scoped rule. The same rule stays with the ability when moved to another action slot, because the icon remains the key.

A failed capture (e.g. an unrecognizable macro icon) may leave learning active. The input used to learn is also processed as a gameplay input rather than suppressed, so the user should experiment on a safe target. A future confirmation/replay preview might help, but none is implemented or approved here.

## Attack-action mode versus fallback

The README encourages placing the ordinary **Attack** action on any bar. The addon can display which mode is used through **/msa status**. It will prefer the real game action's active-state flag over its own estimate, making normal button presses more predictable. When absent, it falls back to an event-based flag that can be wrong about active swings.

This is a useful two-tier compromise between reliable control and no extra setup. Making that tradeoff transparent in the user guide helps someone diagnose a toggle problem without a hidden interface.

## A meaningful stop gesture

Warrior Intimidating Shout has an explicit stop behavior, and any class can learn custom stops. This expresses that **not every action signals fighting more intensely**; some represent disengagement or control. Stop behavior takes precedence when a texture belongs to both start and stop lists.

## Per-class, not per-character personalization

One account-wide SavedVariables table holds the learned entries grouped by class. That shares rules across same-class characters; it does not represent individual character preferences. The automatic enable toggle is intentionally (or at least currently) ephemeral and resets on reload.

The creator has not yet specified whether a per-character opt-in system or separate GUI is desired. These remain options, not decisions.

## Testable ergonomic concerns

- Does the tooltip/status make it clear that normal Attack-action mode is preferred?
- Is the name-based unlearn command predictable in a localized client?
- Should custom stop rules override built-in start behavior in a visible way?
- Are alerts adequate when learning remains armed after an unsupported spell?
- Is a session-only on/off toggle surprising after reload?

Only direct in-game tests with representative users can answer these. This documentation pass changed no UI or behavior.

## Specific tradeoffs and ambiguities

The goal of avoiding **AttackTarget** toggle-off motivates a state check. The installed Attack action is a more direct clue than **PLAYER_ENTER_COMBAT**, but requires the user to place Attack on a bar. The event fallback lowers setup requirements but cannot guarantee actual swing state.

The original Aug 22 version only wrapped **UseAction**, expressly avoiding the other global cast functions. The Aug 29 implementation **added CastSpell and CastSpellByName** so macros or spellbook casts could trigger. This is an observable direction change, not proof of any particular discussion over compatibility.

Learning by icon allows easy handling of custom spells whose numeric IDs aren't available to Lua 5.0. It also makes different spells sharing artwork indistinguishable, and uses the *first* spellbook matching name/icon when learning. A learned opposite direction is not always an override: if the icon is both start and stop, **stop gets priority**.

The initial learning format saved icon booleans per class. Aug 31 changed the schema to records including action and localized name, while migrating older icons with a **legacy placeholder**. That migration itself is evidence of supporting existing user settings, but no user acceptance/performance result is recorded.

# Resist Forever

**Creator:** Babuni.dev · **Current version:** 1.0.2 · **Target:** World of Warcraft: Forever 1.60.1 · **TOC interface:** 16001 · **License:** [MIT](LICENSE)

**Resist Forever** explains how a character's or pet's magical resistance might affect **direct spell damage**. Hover **Fire, Nature, Frost, Shadow or Arcane resistance** in the character/pet panel to see the chance of each **10% damage-resisted outcome**, together with **base spell miss** against an attacker of a given level.

It extends the existing Blizzard tooltip instead of replacing it, so the game's original resistance information stays visible.

## Install

Place the files in a folder named `ResistForever` under your client's `Interface/AddOns` directory:

```text
Interface/
└── AddOns/
    └── ResistForever/
        ├── ResistForever.toc
        └── ResistForever.lua
```

Enable **Resist Forever** in the game's addon list and open your character sheet. Hover a resistance row, or open the **pet character panel** and hover its corresponding resistance row. No slash commands or settings screen are defined by the current source; the addon does not write SavedVariables.

The [v1.0.2 GitHub release](https://github.com/babunidev/ResistForever/releases/tag/v1.0.2) was published **October 20, 2026**, but GitHub's release metadata lists **no attached downloadable asset**. Use the repository source rather than assuming a release ZIP exists. This build targets the specific Forever UI conventions used by `CharacterStatFrameScrollBoxIconElementMixin`, `PaperDollStatTooltip` and the 16001 interface—not ordinary Vanilla 1.12 or modern retail WoW by default.

## How to read the tooltip

The addon appends a **Resist Forever** section below Blizzard's native tooltip. It can show two contexts:

- **Against level N**: the hypothetical attacker's level equals the displayed **player/pet's level**.
- **Current target · Level N**, or the **target's name · Level N**: the **selected target's level** is used as the hypothetical attacker's level when it differs from the defender's level. The target's *resistance* is **never** substituted for yours.

For each context it lists only non-negligible, non-zero **10%, 20%, ... 100% damage resisted** probabilities. The **0% damage resisted** outcome exists internally but is intentionally hidden in the tooltip. Percentages are rounded to one decimal; suppressed/rounded-zero rows mean the visible rows do **not** necessarily sum to 100%.

The final **Base spell miss** row is a level-difference estimate **before any enemy spell-hit bonuses**. It is separate from resistance-based partial damage reduction: a missed spell is not the same as a landed spell suffering a partial resist.

A simple *model illustration*, **not an observed client combat test**: 90 resistance against a level-10 attacker has an average resisted fraction of `90 / (90 + 9 × 10) = 0.5`. Under the middle-range triangular distribution, its visible nonzero outcomes are **40% damage resisted: 25% chance; 50%: 50%; 60%: 25%**. At equal attacker/defender level, modeled base spell miss is **4%**. Actual gameplay differs with spell-specific mechanics and unobserved enemy stats.

## Current Forever beta formulas

The source intentionally uses the October 20 **v1.0.2** formulas, not the earlier Classic model:

| Quantity | Current behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Average fraction of *direct spell* damage resisted | `a = R / (R + 9L)`, for positive readable defender resistance `R` and attacker level `L` |
| Partial outcomes | **0%, 10%, 20%, ... 100%** resisted; 0% is calculated but not shown |
| Middle of distribution | `P(x) = max(0, 0.5 - 2.5 × abs(x - a))`, for discrete steps `x` |
| Near the 0% / 100% edges | Separate closed-form three-bucket distributions prevent edge loss |
| Base spell miss, defender minus attacker level **d ≥ 3** | **17%**, under this current Forever model |
| Base spell miss, **d < 3** | `max(0, 4% + d × 1%)` |
| Minimum unavoidable miss chance | **None assumed**: a calculated 0% is allowed and omitted from visible rows |

These formulas reflect the **Forever beta model documented in the current code and v1.0.2 changelog**. They aren't an independently verified guarantee for every server state, spell or future patch. In particular:

- This is for **direct magical spell damage**, not binary resist checks, non-channeled periodic ticks, channel damage, or a spell-specific damage model. Source comments note those behave differently.
- Enemy **spell penetration** and **spell-hit bonuses** are unknown, so displayed resistance/miss odds are baseline estimates, not exact personalized probabilities.
- A nonpositive/unknown resistance does not cause invented partial-resist probabilities; base spell miss may still appear.
- Some special/unknown target levels may return no valid `UnitLevel`; the addon omits that target comparison instead of guessing a boss's level.

## Player, pet, live values and safe fallbacks

The source recognizes resistance rows by their **Fire/Nature/Frost/Shadow/Arcane atlases** and classifies them under the **player** or **pet** statistics scroll box. For resistance it prefers the frame's already-readable `numericValue`; otherwise it reads `UnitResistance` (effective value first, then real). It separately obtains the defender's level.

Forever's UI can present **secret/protected values**. The addon checks value accessibility before calculating and maintains a small session-only cache of previously readable player/pet levels and resistance. If a valid last-known value is used, the tooltip marks it with **“Using last available resistance value”**. No persistent data or private combat logs are stored.

Changes in target, auras, pet state, equipment, resistance or level trigger attempts to refresh the cache/open tooltip. Hooks are installed through `hooksecurefunc` rather than wholesale replacement of Blizzard's original tooltip routine. There may be updates delayed by the client or missing when data is inaccessible; stale results are identified instead of silently treated as fresh.

## History and limitations

**September 28 — 1.0.0:** First implementation, initially using Classic-style resist outcome buckets. **October 12 — 1.0.1:** Pet support and an updated Classic PvP/PvE split for level-based misses. **October 20 — 1.0.2:** Replaced those estimates with the present Forever beta **10%-step resist and base spell miss** models. Those are genuine modeling revisions, not three simultaneous calculation modes.

The repo contains only one runtime Lua file and a TOC, with a [.pkgmeta](.pkgmeta) pointer to the manual changelog. **No automated test script** was found in this repository during the October 27 documentation audit. No game-client test, combat-log statistical validation or runtime code change was performed here. The [MIT license](LICENSE) is preserved.

# ResistForever — concept and creative direction

**Human creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Environment:** World of Warcraft: Forever 1.60.1 / UI interface 16001.

## Numbers the character sheet hints at, but does not explain

Resistance is one of those statistics players can invest in without easily reading what it means in a fight. A Fire resistance number on the character sheet is not intuitively equal to a chance to resist a spell, nor does it say how much damage a successful spell might lose. And the question grows more complicated when the enemy is several levels above or below the defender.

The creative purpose of Resist Forever is to make this **existing character-sheet information** understandable exactly where the player already looks. Instead of opening a calculator, external guide or unrelated addon window, hovering a resistance row extends the same tooltip with a breakdown: **what amount of direct spell damage could be resisted, and how likely is each amount?**

The feature is intentionally small. Its ambition is not to build a DPS meter, automatic gearing adviser or comprehensive boss-spell simulator. It gives a player a readable interpretation of their own—or their pet's—defensive statistic and allows them to decide what it means for their equipment and encounters.

## Protect the game interface's continuity

The extension **doesn't replace Blizzard's tooltip**. It appends a clearly titled **Resist Forever** section under the native resistance explanation, using the game's own font color system and left/right rows. The same five resistance schools—Fire, Nature, Frost, Shadow and Arcane—are recognizable from their existing atlas icons.

A new context appears if the player has selected a target at a different level. The target supplies the **hypothetical attacker level**, not a source of resistance values. This lets the user see how the same armor/resistance statistic reads against a more or less powerful caster while retaining the character/pet as the defender.

In October 2026, pet resistances were included too. This extended the idea from the player's own character sheet to companions without inventing a second visual language.

## Honor uncertainty rather than sell false precision

This particular client builds some values as **secret/protected UI numbers**, so the addon checks whether it can safely read and calculate with them. If only the last-known valid resistance or level is available, the tooltip says so. If no reliable value exists, the extension omits the calculation.

The same restraint applies to mechanics. Spell hit and penetration of an unseen enemy aren't known from the resistance row. Binary spells, periodic ticks and channels are not modeled by the direct-damage distribution. A target with an unknown/skull level isn't silently guessed as “+3.”

This is part of the authored interaction idea: **context-rich estimates, explicitly labeled as estimates**, make resistance easier to learn without turning the addon into an oracle.

## The actual creative iteration

The current program is shaped by a visible calculation evolution. The initial late-September release used historical Classic-style partial outcomes. Version 1.0.1 refined different miss curves for players and pets and added the pet sheet. On **October 20, 2026**, version **1.0.2** adopted a documented Forever beta model with **10% partial-resist steps**, average `R/(R+9L)` and a single base spell-miss function rather than the earlier Classic PvP/PvE split.

That last change is not merely a formatting update: it changed what the numbers *mean*. The source and changelog establish the revision; they don't expose every discussion or prove the underlying combat model against a live test in this review.

## The question behind a resistance number

A number like 90 Fire resistance occupies a very small piece of the World of Warcraft character sheet. But that number prompts more questions than it answers: Does it make the player less likely to be hit by a Fire spell? Does it reduce the damage when a spell lands? If it reduces damage, how much? Does the opponent's level make the investment stronger or weaker?

**Resist Forever** reflects Babuni.dev's interest in making mechanics visible through the game's own interface. Rather than replacing the character pane or inventing a separate calculator that a player has to remember to open, the addon adds a small explanatory table when the player hovers Fire, Nature, Frost, Shadow or Arcane resistance. The same existing tooltip remains in place, and the custom detail follows it.

That restrained design is part of the creative work. The goal is to help the player *interpret the character*, not to perform a combat rotation or turn statistics into a recommendation engine. The tool is particularly appropriate to **World of Warcraft: Forever**, where the resistance rules were changing during the beta period and old Classic assumptions could give confidently incorrect probabilities.

## October 12 — a companion's defense and a level-curve correction

Commit **`c64797aa276b`**, “Fix player spell-miss curve and show pet resistance tooltips,” was released as **v1.0.1** on October 12. This change had two distinct threads.

One was an interaction expansion: the **pet character pane** received the same hover behavior as the player's resistance panel. The source learned to classify rows as player or pet through their frame ancestry and kept separate cached levels/resistances for those units. This is an elegant extension of the original design. A player examining their pet's survivability should be able to ask the same resistance questions without opening a new addon window.

The other change corrected how the addon treated casters at different levels. At that stage it distinguished **Classic-derived PvP and PvE miss curves**: player defenders used a 13%-at-+3 rule with +7% continuation; pets and non-player defenders used 17%-at-+3 with +11% continuation. The changelog specifically illustrated why a level-10 caster attacking a level-22 player should not be shown as an automatic 100% miss under that then-current model.

That was an actual mathematical revision, not merely a label or new tooltip style. Importantly, it would later be **superseded**. A publishable project history should keep the reasoning and correction visible without confusing a visitor about which curve is currently used.

## October 20 — leaving the Classic model behind for Forever

Commit **`8a9f09612d32`**, “Update Forever beta resist and base spell-miss models,” produced **version 1.0.2** on October 20. This is the most consequential visible pivot in the repository's short history.

The project moved from calculating in classic 25% partial reduction outcomes to representing **0, 10, 20, ..., 100%** damage resisted for direct magical spell hits. The source describes the new average as **`R/(R+9×attackerLevel)`**, derived from the then-current Forever beta/wowsims combat-log model rather than trusting the earlier **ExpectedSpellResistance** interface helper. The result is turned into a discrete probability distribution: a triangular band around the mean in the middle and special formulas near the 0% and 100% edges.

Only the meaningful positive reduction rows are drawn. The **0% reduction** case is still computed internally but never displayed; tiny rounded-zero chances also disappear. That keeps a potentially long tooltip from filling with statistically negligible numbers, although it also means the visible probabilities may not sum to a complete 100%.

At the same time, the addon abandoned the Classic-derived player-versus-pet miss split. Its new **Forever model** calculates baseline spell miss from defender minus attacker level: **17%** if the defender is three or more levels above the caster, otherwise `max(0, 4% + 1% per level difference)`. Unlike an older assumption, a **1% minimum is not unavoidable**. Equally importantly, the row is now labeled **Base spell miss**, not simply spell miss, because the enemy may have spell-hit bonuses the addon cannot see.

This revision expresses a broader lesson in game-mechanics development: the client interface may contain a formula intended for display, a legacy formula may be well known from earlier versions, and the actual server-specific behavior may be different from both. The addon had to choose which model to communicate and be transparent about its scope and evidence.

The source explicitly limits these partial odds to **direct spell damage**. It notes that periodic non-channeled ticks, channels and binary spells can follow different mechanics. Enemy spell penetration is unknown from the paper doll. Those caveats are not an afterthought—they are the difference between a useful explanatory approximation and a promise that any specific hit will behave exactly as predicted.

## Maintaining trust in a changing user interface

The current 1.0.2 source is also careful about **where the numbers came from**. It attempts to use the exact resistance value already stamped on the hovered frame. If unavailable, it tries the effective/real returns from `UnitResistance`, then falls back to a small session-only cache. A previously readable level is reused if a new one cannot be accessed.

The cache is especially relevant to a client exposing **secret** values. The code wraps accessibility checks and arithmetic validation in guarded calls instead of assuming every number can be compared. A fallback adds the muted text **“Using last available resistance value”**. If there is no safe context, the addon simply doesn't append a speculative value.

The tooltip has two useful perspectives. One is a **same-level hypothetical attacker**, always phrased as “Against level N.” The other, shown only if a different-level target has a real readable level, uses that target as a hypothetical caster. An invalid/skull level isn't treated as +3 by fiat. And no part of the calculation changes the subject of the tooltip: when hovering the pet, it is still the **pet's resistance** being modeled, not the resistance of a selected enemy.

The code attaches through secure post-hooks to Blizzard's stat-row and tooltip functions, uses event-driven cache refreshes and guards against recursive rows. This avoids a wholly separate window and reduces the risk of trampling the original tooltip, but it depends on client-specific 1.60.1 frame structures. There is no permanent tracking database or user settings file.
