# ROARR — technical architecture, separate repository snapshot

**Basis:** current `roarr.lua` and `roarr.toc`, inspected 2026-10-26. No actual game client was run.

## Call flow

```text
Configured action-bar slot pressed
  -> global UseAction wrapper
     -> ensureLoaded() once (ROARRDB -> local state)
     -> optional WATCH_MODE print
     -> watched slot matches?
        -> doBattleEmoteNow()
           -> ENABLED?
           -> GetTime() beyond BATTLE_COOLDOWN?
           -> update LAST_BATTLE_EMOTE_TIME
           -> math.random(1,100) <= battle_chance?
              -> pick one of 5 tokens
              -> DoEmote(token) or fallback EMOTE text
     -> delegate to previously captured _Orig_UseAction
```

**Timing nuance:** last-attempt time is updated *before* the chance roll. Even a failed roll blocks further checks until cooldown expires. `LAST_BATTLE_EMOTE_TIME` starts at zero, so eligibility of the first press depends on game uptime.

## Configuration

| Symbol / key | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WATCH_SLOT` / `ROARRDB.slot` | unset | Action slot to monitor |
| `WATCH_MODE` | false | Temporary slot-number printout; not persisted |
| `battle_chance` / `ROARRDB.battle_chance` | 100 | Chance 0–100 |
| `BATTLE_COOLDOWN` / `ROARRDB.battle_cd` | 6 | Nonnegative seconds, no enforced maximum |
| `ENABLED` / `ROARRDB.enabled` | true | On/off preference |
| `LAST_BATTLE_EMOTE_TIME` | 0 | Session-local last eligible attempt |
| `EMOTE_TOKENS_BATTLE` | five tokens | Fixed source table |

`ROARRDB` is declared by the TOC as **SavedVariables** (account-wide, not character-specific). On the first action press or slash command, `ensureLoaded` initializes in-memory state. `PLAYER_LOGIN` only seeds the pseudo-random generator; `PLAYER_LOGOUT` writes current local state to the DB.

**Potential state-loss edge case:** logging in and out without any action or slash command may write initial/default values over a previously saved configuration, because login does not call `ensureLoaded`. This is a **static risk**, not a reproduced error.

## Slash commands

`/roarr` uses Lua `string.find`, `string.gsub` and `tonumber` to parse commands. It implements `slot`, `watch`, `chance`, `cd`, `on`, `off`, `info`, `reset`, `save`, and `tutorial`. The unique source change in this repo is the longer multi-line tutorial.

The slot command accepts any numeric value without checking legal bar-slot bounds or integer requirements; chance is constrained to 0–100; cooldown is constrained to be nonnegative.

## Dependencies, packaging and runtime

- Files: `roarr.lua`, `roarr.toc`; manifest interface `11200`, version `1.0`, author Babuni.dev.
- Uses standard WoW addon events `PLAYER_LOGIN` and `PLAYER_LOGOUT`; no update-loop scheduler.
- Built-in game `DoEmote` tokens are the only emote selection content.
- No custom sound/media resources, no cross-addon protocol, no sync layer or GUI.
- Global `UseAction` hook may interact with other addons; event/cast success is not checked.

# ROARR — interaction and onboarding design

**Creative author:** Babuni.dev.

## Core emotional effect

The addon attaches a playful expression to the player's existing action-bar behavior. ROAR or CHARGE can punctuate aggression; CHEER celebrates; FLEX shows swagger; BORED interrupts the battle with a comic contrast. A short pool of game-native emotes keeps the behavior simple and immediately recognizable.

The player still decides what to press. The addon does not control movement, attacks, targeting or combat priorities.

## The seven-step tutorial: this repo's distinct iteration

The previous ROARR implementation in `babunidev/roar` contains only a compact `tutorial` command summary. In this repository, commit `4fc6a68` on **2025-11-23** replaced that summary with **seven numbered messages**:

1. Toggle slot watch and press buttons.
2. Assign a watched slot.
3. Set a chance percentage.
4. Set a cooldown.
5. Switch the addon on or off.
6. Inspect current configuration.
7. Save settings.

The purpose can be reasonably read as easier **first-use guidance**, especially for someone unfamiliar with action-slot numbers. That interpretation is an editorial reading of code; the original creator discussion explaining the change is not available.

## Text-first experience

The user configures the addon through `/roarr` commands; a red `ROARR:` prefix distinguishes feedback in the chat frame. There is no graphics panel, animation editor or tutorial popup. The original source has a short sample command sequence in README, and the expanded source tutorial can be run on demand.

The `watch` toggle prints every captured action ID while enabled; turning it off keeps later play quieter. The `on`/`off` toggle allows a reversible pause without wiping the chosen slot.

## Emote cadence

Default cooldown: **6 seconds**. Default proc chance: **100%**. After a valid slot press, the enabled/cooldown checks run; the clock is updated before chance is sampled. This means `chance 40` and `cd 12` provide at most one 40% roll per 12-second cooldown opportunity, not one roll on each press.

## Limitations and accessibility checks

Many on-screen status lines make the tutorial readable but potentially noisy; test this in live chat. English command descriptions and fixed token names may depend on client locale. If the slot changes when the action bar layout changes, the player must update `/roarr slot`. Input validation currently accepts noninteger numeric slot values. Actual usability and compatibility remain to be tested.

# ROARRunlimited — turn your action bar into a war drum

**Creator / author:** Babuni.dev  
**Target:** World of Warcraft 1.12 / Lua 5.0, as declared in the addon  
**Version:** 1.1 (manifest and source)  
**Runtime status:** Not tested during this documentation review

ROARRunlimited builds on the action-triggered emote idea by letting a player associate **as many numbered configurations as needed** with action-bar slots. Each numbered instance has its own chosen action slot, trigger chance, and cooldown. Pressing a configured button can play a randomly selected native WoW battle emote while leaving the button's normal action intact.

The creator's original README captured the personality of the project in one line: **“ROARRunlimited turns your action bar into a war drum.”** This is character-flavor tooling, not a spell rotation, combat automation, or a custom audio/animation system.

## Important packaging check

**The current TOC names `roarrunlimited.lua`, but the repository's file is `ROARRunlimited.lua`.** These differ in capitalization. That may prevent loading on case-sensitive file systems or addon loaders. For a deployment where filename case matters, ensure the file reference and actual filename match. This documentation pass flags the inconsistency but **does not rename or edit runtime files**.

The intended folder layout, pending that correction or client verification, is:

```text
Interface/AddOns/ROARRunlimited/
  ROARRunlimited.toc
  ROARRunlimited.lua
```

Restart the game and enable the addon. Confirm that the game actually loads the Lua code before following the commands below.

## Quick setup

```text
/roed watch
```

Press the buttons you want to use and note their reported action-slot numbers. Type `/roed watch` again to turn off the debug messages.

```text
/roed slot1 13
/roed slot2 24
/roed chance1 40
/roed timer1 6
/roed chance2 80
/roed timer2 12
/roed info
```

This example configures instance **1** for action slot 13 (40% chance, six-second interval) and instance **2** for slot 24 (80%, twelve seconds). Instances are numbered labels; the digit after `slot`, `chance`, or `timer` identifies the **same configuration**, not the physical action-slot number.

### Commands

| Command | Source-defined behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `/roed watch` | Toggle reporting of pressed slot numbers |
| `/roed slotX <slot>` | Create/update numbered instance `X` to watch an action slot; reset that instance's last-attempt time |
| `/roed chanceX <0-100>` | Set chance for existing instance `X` |
| `/roed timerX <seconds>` | Set a nonnegative cooldown for existing instance `X` |
| `/roed info` | Show each instance's slot, chance and cooldown |
| `/roed on`, `/roed off` | Enable or disable triggering without clearing configurations |
| `/roed reset` | Clear **all** configured instances |
| `/roed` | Display a condensed command summary |

An instance must exist before its chance and timer can be changed. Defaults on creation are **100% chance** and **six seconds**. There is no GUI and no explicit maximum instance number in the parser, although large configurations would still use resources.

## What actually happens

On a regular action-bar press, the addon scans its numbered instances and checks those assigned to that slot. Each matching instance independently applies its own cooldown and probability. Its attempt timestamp is advanced **before** the probability roll—so a failed roll still consumes the configured interval.

It then selects one of **four** built-in WoW emotes: **ROAR, CHARGE, CHEER, FLEX**. The earlier version also included BORED, which was removed in a January 2026 code revision. If two instances watch the **same physical slot**, both may respond separately to the same button press. The addon forwards control to the original `UseAction`, but does not verify that the ability actually succeeded.

Configuration is stored in account-wide `ROEDDB`. The nested `slots` entries include each instance's `slot`, `chance`, `cd`, and `last` fields. The per-instance `last` timestamp also persists, which deserves special testing after restarting a client because `GetTime()` is session-relative.

## Relationship to other ROAR projects

[The earlier `roar` repository](https://github.com/babunidev/roar) and [`roarr`](https://github.com/babunidev/roarr) implement a simpler **single watched-slot** design. ROARRunlimited, created in December 2025, independently stores multiple numbered instances with separate odds and timing. A later project named RoarForever has its own history; shared naming should not silently merge their codebases or authorship.

## When one roar is not enough

Earlier ROAR/ROARR addons let the player pick one action-bar button to occasionally trigger a built-in emote. **ROARRunlimited expands that idea from one watched action into a configurable collection of independent expressive triggers.** A different button can have a different personality rhythm: frequent enthusiasm on one action, rarer celebration on another.

The source implements this through numbered configurations (“instances”), each pairing a WoW action slot with a probability and a cooldown. The numbering is a convenient reference in slash commands, not a cap of one or two predefined buttons. The player retains control of every actual action.

The original repository description says ROARRunlimited “plays battle-themed emotes from multiple watched action slots.” Its README finishes with the creator's metaphor of turning the **action bar into a war drum**. This supports the artistic goal without requiring us to invent an original design dialogue.

## Experience principles embodied in code

- **Player action drives expression:** `UseAction` presses provide timing rather than an autonomous interval event.
- **Independent patterns:** a chosen instance may have its own emote probability and cooldown.
- **One coherent voice:** the built-in token pool makes gestures recognizable in the game without custom graphics or music.
- **Simple configuration:** `/roed slotX`, `chanceX`, and `timerX` pair numbers with settings; no persistent window.
- **Reversible quiet:** `/roed off` suspends the effect without clearing the configuration.
- **Lightweight flavor:** no targeting choices, damage, cast automation or PvP advantage.

## A meaningful evolution across the committed code

The first December 2025 source indexed entries directly by watched action-slot ID. A subsequent revision indexed entries by **instance number**, allowing slot assignments to be changed while chance/cooldown values remain associated with a named configuration. In January 2026 a further source revision normalized old saved entries and reduced the pool to four native emotes, removing BORED. These changes are supported by actual diffs; they are **not proof of a recorded author vote, a specific design disagreement, or a tested release process**.

## What still needs author input

The code allows more than one instance to watch the same physical action slot, potentially producing multiple emotes on one press. Whether this is creative flexibility or an edge case to prevent is for Babuni.dev to decide. The current documentation does not implicitly approve restricting it.

This repo should be preserved as a distinct step in the broader ROAR addon family, but direct migration or inheritance beyond demonstrated similarities requires evidence.

# ROARRunlimited — architecture, version 1.1

**Evidence:** `ROARRunlimited.lua` and `ROARRunlimited.toc` on 2026-10-26. Static analysis only.

## Data flow

```text
Player presses an action-bar button
    |
Wrapped global UseAction(slot, checkCursor, onSelf)
    |-- ensureLoaded(): bind account-wide ROEDDB.slots
    |-- WATCH_MODE? -> report physical action slot
    |-- for each configuration instance in WATCH_SLOTS:
    |      if cfg.slot matches pressed slot:
    |         doBattleEmoteForSlot(cfg)
    |           |-- ENABLED?
    |           |-- GetTime() - cfg.last >= cfg.cd ?
    |           |-- cfg.last = now   <-- before chance roll
    |           |-- random <= cfg.chance ?
    |           '-- DoEmote(random token) or fallback EMOTE text
    '-- forward original arguments to _Orig_UseAction
```

The ordinary action is delegated regardless of whether any emote is fired. The trigger checks the **button press**, not combat state or cast success.

## Configurations are numbered instances

```text
ROEDDB
  enabled = true / false
  slots = {
    [1] = { slot = 13, chance = 40, cd = 6, last = ... },
    [2] = { slot = 24, chance = 80, cd = 12, last = ... },
    ...
  }
```

`slot1 13` means “instance 1 watches physical slot 13”, not “watch physical slot 1”. `chance1` and `timer1` edit instance 1's settings. Slots and numbered instances are different concepts.

- New instance: default `chance = 100`, `cd = 6`, `last = 0`.
- `slotX` resets the instance's `last` timestamp to zero even when retargeting an existing instance; chance/cooldown remain otherwise unchanged.
- Loaded saved entries with nil fields are normalized by `ensureLoaded`.
- `/roed reset` clears every configuration instance. There is no per-instance delete command.
- `/roed on/off` toggles one global enabled flag, not per-instance switches.
- The code imposes no small fixed instance count. It scans **all instances on every action press**, so resource cost rises with the number of entries.

Two instances may watch one physical slot, so a single press can independently evaluate both (and potentially emit multiple emotes).

## Emote output

The source contains **four** `DoEmote` tokens: `ROAR`, `CHARGE`, `CHEER` and `FLEX`. The earlier BORED token was removed in January 2026. If `DoEmote` is unavailable, the fallback is `SendChatMessage("makes a battle cry!", "EMOTE")`. Exact animation/chat behavior depends on client support and has not been tested here.

## Persistence and lifecycle

The TOC declares account-wide `SavedVariables: ROEDDB`. `ensureLoaded()` only runs from the `UseAction` wrapper and `/roed` command handler. `PLAYER_LOGIN` seeds the global Lua random generator; `PLAYER_LOGOUT` writes `ROEDDB.slots` and `ROEDDB.enabled`.

**Risk A, session-relative clocks:** `cfg.last` is updated in a configuration table that is persisted. `GetTime()` reports client uptime, which changes across game sessions. Restoring a large previous `last` after a fresh start could make `now - cfg.last < cfg.cd` true for an unexpectedly long time. The source does not reset all loaded timestamps at login.

**Risk B, uninitialized logout:** logout writes local `WATCH_SLOTS = {}` and `ENABLED = true` if no slash command or `UseAction` call triggered `ensureLoaded`. This may overwrite previously saved settings. Both risks are source-derived, **not reproduced in a game client**.

**Risk C, global hook:** capturing and replacing `UseAction` can interact with other addon wrappers according to load order.

## Packaging and Lua compatibility

- Repository file: **`ROARRunlimited.lua`** (capitalized).
- TOC script reference: **`roarrunlimited.lua`** (lowercase).
- Case-sensitive environments may fail to load the Lua; resolve/verify before claiming successful deployment.
- Version 1.1, interface `11200`; slash command `/roed`.
- Command patterns use Lua 5.0-era `string.find` rather than the original v1.0 `string.match`.
- Numeric inputs are parsed with `tonumber`, without enforcing physical action-slot bounds or validating small integer-only indices.

No Lua, TOC, license, sound/media, GUI, or network-layer changes were made in the documentation pass.

# ROARRunlimited — interaction and expressive design

**Creative author:** Babuni.dev.

## The action bar as a rhythmic instrument

The creator's original tagline—**“ROARRunlimited turns your action bar into a war drum.”**—nicely captures the interaction. Instead of one special button making the character roar, different actions can carry their own intermittent gestures. An intense ability might roar frequently; another might occasionally cheer or flex.

This is not audio sequencer functionality: the “war drum” is a metaphor for expressive timing. The output is a built-in WoW emote chosen from four tokens.

## A number means two different things

The key UX distinction is between a **configuration instance** and a **physical action slot**:

| Setting | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| `/roed slot1 13` | Numbered instance **1** watches physical action-bar slot **13** |
| `/roed chance1 40` | Instance **1** gets a 40% chance |
| `/roed timer1 6` | Instance **1** gets a six-second cooldown |
| `/roed slot2 24` | Independent instance **2** watches physical slot **24** |

The suffix is a label chosen by the player, not a limit or the action slot itself. The code accepts many instance numbers; there is no “slot3 button” prerequisite.

`/roed watch` prints pressed slot IDs, making the system learnable without a visual UI. `/roed info` prints configured instance settings. `/roed reset` removes all instances at once; no current command deletes one particular numbered instance.

## Timing and duplication

Each instance runs its own elapsed-time gate. **The timestamp is advanced before the probability roll**, so an unsuccessful roll uses the cooldown too. The selected token is random after a successful chance roll. Two configurations targeting the same physical action slot may produce more than one emote from one press; no deduplication is implemented.

The addon can be globally silenced with `/roed off` without losing its configurations, but no in-game category controls or per-instance on/off flags are provided.

## Practical usability checks

- Does debug mode report understandable numeric slots across custom bar layouts?
- Are `slotX` / `chanceX` / `timerX` commands easy to remember?
- Does the global reset feel too destructive compared with a single-instance removal option?
- How does the addon behave if many instances are configured or one slot is registered multiple times?
- Are repeated in-world emotes appropriate for group play and accessible to players using localized game clients?

These are design verification questions, **not approved redesign requirements**.

# ROARSounds — let Azeroth roar again

**Creative author:** Babuni.dev  
**GitHub repository:** `babunidev/ROARSounds`  
**In-game addon folder / title:** `ROAR`  
**Declared interface:** `30300` (WoW 3.3-era, **not** the Vanilla 1.12 interface number)  
**Source of truth:** [`ROAR/ROAR.lua`](ROAR/ROAR.lua) and [`ROAR/ROAR.toc`](ROAR/ROAR.toc)  
**Verification:** Git/source inspection on 2026-10-26. In-game playback and client compatibility were not tested in this documentation pass.

ROARSounds restores a missing bit of character presence to the `/roar` emote by calling **existing World of Warcraft client sound files**. When the addon receives a recognized text-emote event, it can play the appropriate built-in roar for the player's own character or another identifiable character. The sound depends on the resolved character's race and sex.

There are **no bundled WAV replacements**. The addon maps 16 race/sex combinations to existing paths under `Sound\\Character\\PlayerRoars\\`; the game client must actually contain those files.

## What the addon can identify

The code recognizes the local player and attempts to resolve the text-emote sender using these unit contexts, in order:

1. Your own character.
2. Your current target.
3. Mouseover.
4. Focus.
5. Up to 40 raid unit references **if in a raid**, otherwise up to four party unit references **if in a party**.

If an emote sender cannot be resolved to one of those units, or there is no sound mapping, the source does **not** play a roar for them. Seeing a message in nearby emote chat does not by itself provide the race/sex information needed to choose a file. This is not a nearby-player scanning system and does not estimate distance.

The event is `CHAT_MSG_TEXT_EMOTE`, not a direct hook into the emote command. The recognizer searches English text for `" roars"` or `" roar"` (case-insensitive). That matching rule is broad, not language-independent, and should be tested for false positives and localized clients.

## Installation

The repository contains a ready-made folder `ROAR/` and a separate `ROAR.zip` download artifact.

To install from the **current repository files**, copy the `ROAR` folder so that these two files appear together:

```text
World of Warcraft/
└── Interface/
    └── AddOns/
        └── ROAR/
            ├── ROAR.toc
            └── ROAR.lua
```

Restart or reload the game, enable the addon where supported, and test the built-in `/roar` emote.

**Compatibility caution:** The TOC declares `## Interface: 30300` rather than `11200`. On a different era/build, the client may flag it as outdated or fail to support its event/API behavior. Do not change the interface number without testing the Lua code and sound paths on that client. The `ROAR.zip` archive exists in Git, but its contents were **not independently compared** with the working source during this review; inspect it before distributing it as the authoritative build.

## Supported sound mapping

The source maps both male and female variants of these eight race tokens: **Dwarf, Gnome, Human, NightElf, Orc, Tauren, Troll, and Undead**. `Scourge` returned by `UnitRace` is normalized to `Undead`.

There are no mappings for Blood Elf, Draenei or other races beyond those eight. For a race not in the table, the addon silently has no matching built-in path. The map is source-declared; successful playback of every asset has **not** been verified.

## Behavior and limitations

- Plays through `PlaySoundFile(path)` using game-supplied sound files.
- Initializes the local player's name/race/sex on `PLAYER_LOGIN`; refreshes the local mapping on a player `UNIT_MODEL_CHANGED` event.
- Suppresses candidate roar events from the **same normalized sender name** within **0.3 seconds** of one another.
- The timestamp is recorded *before* checking whether a nonlocal sender can be identified. An unresolved event may therefore consume that sender's brief cooldown without making a sound.
- The code strips realm suffixes from sender names; this may confuse different people sharing the same name across realms.
- Current source has **no slash commands, configuration panel, persistent saved variables, chat messages sent by the addon, or addon-to-addon communication**.

# ROARSounds — concept and creative purpose

**Creative author:** Babuni.dev  
**Addon as installed:** ROAR  
**Document status:** Source-based reconstruction, not a transcript of initial brainstorming.

## Giving a familiar emote its voice

The project began with a small game-world observation: the player may see the text of a character's `/roar` emote without hearing the race-specific roar that helps the gesture feel alive. ROARSounds makes that expressive moment audible again by selecting a **built-in game sound** rather than inventing or replacing the sound palette.

The project's subject is presence and immersion, not statistics, combat advantage, UI ornament or voice chat. It is an auditory companion to a deliberate roleplay gesture. The sound should make a textual action feel more physical and characterful.

## Expanding who can be heard

The earliest committed code responded to the local player's own roar. Later April commits attempted to let other addon users hear roaring over explicit addon communication. That approach was subsequently removed in favor of recognizing nearby `CHAT_MSG_TEXT_EMOTE` messages and identifying sender race/sex from an accessible game unit: target, mouseover, focus, group or raid roster.

This shift is a **documented implementation iteration**. It reduces protocol coordination but introduces limits: a text speaker must correspond to an identifiable unit, and the message text must match the addon's English substring rules. The exact original reasoning for abandoning addon messages was not recorded in the available Git messages; do not invent an approval conversation.

## A deliberately small footprint

The current code contains one Lua file and one TOC file. There are no config menus, custom sound downloads, character statistics, accounts, backend servers, emote macros or scheduled timers. A short, sender-specific gate prevents rapid duplicate playback. The user still chooses when to use `/roar`; this addon observes and reacts.

Eight races with male/female sound variants are declared; the addon uses client assets and cannot create audio for an unsupported race. Its TOC targets `30300`, so WoW versions other than that era need explicit compatibility tests.

## Related work, separate history

`ROARSounds` is **not** the same addon as the action-slot-controlled `roar`, `roarr`, `ROARRunlimited`, `RoarGuild`, or later `RoarForever`. A common creative taste for expressive game characters can be discussed in Babuni.dev's portfolio, but code lineage, approved integration plans and release compatibility must be established rather than assumed.

Babuni.dev remains the original creative director. Technical and documentation assistance from AI must be attributed separately and only when supported by records.

## April 19, 2026 — letting the roar be heard

ROARSounds began with a narrow act of game-world restoration. The original `ROAR.lua` committed on **April 19, 2026** (`5d54503`) watched for an emote message from the player's own character. When text indicated a roar, it selected the corresponding built-in game audio using the character's race and sex. It did not create a new sound pack or require the user to configure an ability rotation; it simply made a familiar roleplay gesture audible.

This is the core creative idea associated with Babuni.dev. It is expressed by the repository's purpose and first implementation. The available commits do not preserve a conversation where the author explains the exact moment of inspiration, so this journal treats the connection between sound and character immersion as a **source-grounded interpretation**, not a verbatim personal recollection.

The earliest code listed race-specific sound variants in a nested table keyed by race and sex, including an alias for the Undead/Scourge naming. It subscribed to `PLAYER_LOGIN`, `UNIT_MODEL_CHANGED`, and `CHAT_MSG_TEXT_EMOTE` and used `PlaySoundFile`. At first it cared only about the speaker who installed the addon.

## April 20 — experimenting with communication

The first visible expansion (`0d1fafb`, **April 20**) flattened the race+sex map into combined identifiers and attempted to share roar IDs using addon messages. In that snapshot, a local roar could trigger `SendAddonMessage` toward a raid, party or guild, and other addon users could play the corresponding file after receiving `CHAT_MSG_ADDON`.

This matters because it documents an approach that did **not** remain in the finished version. It shows the authorial project exploring a larger experience: not just one's own roar, but sound from fellow players. It also introduced communication dependencies that a simple text-emote listener would not need.

On **April 22**, `ff9f8bf` developed the concept further with normalized names, unit-token lookup, and a range check for received addon messages. This stage tried to reconcile sender identity with the game-world position of the player rather than simply accepting every packet.

Git establishes the code path; it does not establish who suggested the addon-message strategy or how anyone assessed its success.

## April 22 — another direction, fewer moving parts

A subsequent April 22 change (`fcc2be8`) removed the outgoing/received addon-message protocol and moved toward resolving players from the text-emote event itself. The rewritten `FindUnitBySender` checks the player's own unit, then target, mouseover, focus, raid or party references. When it can identify a sender, `GetRoarIDForUnit` combines the race and sex into one of the mapping keys.

This change is the strongest technical **pivot** in the record. The desired experience—audible roars with a character-specific voice—stayed recognizable, but the implementation abandoned network coordination. It became reactive to chat messages the client was already receiving. The tradeoff is that somebody whose name appears in emote text may still be unknowable as a unit: the addon cannot pick their sound unless target/roster information is available.

A little later that same day, `42023c0` introduced a **0.3-second cooldown keyed by normalized sender name**. It is a pragmatic anti-duplication measure rather than a roleplay mechanic. The timing is recorded before the code verifies the sender's sound, so an unresolved event can briefly suppress a later one. The implementation is consistent with suppressing noise, but the original reasoning cannot be recovered from source alone.

# ROARSounds — code architecture

**Source examined:** `ROAR/ROAR.lua` and `ROAR/ROAR.toc`, 2026-10-26. Source inspection, **not** executed client tests.

## Runtime flow

```text
PLAYER_LOGIN
  -> NormalizeName(UnitName("player"))
  -> GetRoarIDForUnit("player")
       -> UnitRace + UnitSex -> raceMale/raceFemale
       -> alias Scourge -> Undead
  -> cache player's matching built-in sound path

UNIT_MODEL_CHANGED for "player"
  -> refresh player sound mapping

CHAT_MSG_TEXT_EMOTE(text=arg1, sender=arg2)
  -> IsRoarText(text) checks English substrings " roars", " roar"
  -> NormalizeName(sender) strips "-realm" suffix
  -> per-normalized-sender GetTime() gate (0.3 seconds)
  -> if sender equals player:
       PlaySoundFile(cached player path), if mapped
     else:
       FindUnitBySender:
         target -> mouseover -> focus -> raid1..40 OR party1..4
       GetRoarIDForUnit(matched token)
       PlaySoundFile(path) if in 16-key mapping
```

No current `CHAT_MSG_ADDON`, `SendAddonMessage`, `COMBAT_LOG` detection, repeating timer, saved variables, or slash-command interface.

## Identity and supported assets

Sound map: 16 fixed combinations of eight race tokens (**Dwarf, Gnome, Human, NightElf, Orc, Tauren, Troll, Undead**) and two sex flags (2→Male, 3→Female). `Scourge` is normalized to Undead. Paths have the form:

```text
Sound\\Character\\PlayerRoars\\CharacterRoars<Race><Male|Female>.wav
```

There are no physical WAV files committed to the repo. All sound files are expected to exist inside the **game client** and must be tested against the exact client version. Unmapped races yield no playback.

`FindUnitBySender` only sees unit-token data exposed by the game. It does **not** enumerate every nearby player, and `focus` support or other API behavior may vary by client.

## Deduplication and edge cases

`lastRoarTimeBySender` maps **normalized sender name** to last qualifying text-emote event time. If the same name triggers another matching text emote within **0.3s**, it returns before playback. The state is session-local.

Crucially, it records that timestamp **before** verifying the other player's unit token or sound map. An unmatched/silent roar can therefore suppress a later resolvable event within that interval. Normalizing different name–realm pairs to the same bare name can conflate two speakers, including local and remote characters.

The English substring check may match a phrase where the word roar appears but a full `/roar` action was not performed, and it may miss translated emote messages. These are **testable source-level limitations**, not confirmed player-facing bug reports.

- Manifest title `ROAR`, author Babuni.dev, `Interface: 30300`; no explicit `Version` or `SavedVariables`.

The working audio path selection uses `PlaySoundFile`; sound output volume, availability, client UI settings and error handling have not been exercised in this audit.

# ROARSounds — auditory interaction and experience design

**Creator:** Babuni.dev.

## A roleplay gesture you can hear

The surface is intentionally invisible: type `/roar` (or hear another player's roar) and let the world answer with the character's own **client-provided** roar sound. The addon introduces no HUD, overlay, menu or animation of its own. It treats a text-emote event as the cue for a small sonic moment that can make player characters feel less mute.

This choice differs from ROARRunlimited/RoarGuild, which use action-slot presses to generate emotes. ROARSounds does not generate emotes: it **listens** to a text-emote event and chooses a sound. The projects can share an expressive interest without sharing an implementation history.

## Audience and visibility

The local player can be identified directly after login. Other voices are attempted through visible game unit identities—target, mouseover, focus, party, raid. An unknown stranger's chat message need not translate to an audible voice, even if the text is seen. That limitation comes from the information the game API makes available, not a creator-authored distance model.

Different playable-race styles matter in the fantasy fiction: the addon does not play a generic roar for everyone, but maps eight race families with male/female variants. For unsupported races it currently chooses silence rather than a fabricated mapping.

## Timing and unobtrusiveness

A **0.3-second** sender-specific gate limits closely repeated detection. It is not a global mute, long cooldown, or animation queue. The source does not track how often a player roars, collect social data, save emote history, or broadcast messages to others.

At present, a sender can consume the cooldown even when sound resolution fails; this is a technical side effect worth considering if the experience is made more reliable.

## Open interaction questions

- Should players be able to choose local-only, party-only or all resolvable voices?
- Is silence better than a neutral fallback for unsupported races?
- What emote formats/languages should trigger sound?
- What player cues should appear, if any, when a sound file is absent?
- Should sound overlap, stacking or repeated roars be moderated differently?

These are **proposals**, not approved feature requirements. No actual playtesting, usability study or verified target audio was conducted during the documentation review.

# Social Forever

**Author:** Babuni.dev

**Social Forever remembers the people you meet while playing World of Warcraft: Forever.**

While you quest, the same players often cross your path again and again. Social Forever keeps a small list of those people above your chat so they are easier to recognize, target, invite, and remember the next time you meet.

Over time, strangers can become familiar names.

Built by **Babunigaming** for **World of Warcraft: Forever** (Interface 16001).  
Current version: **0.4.6-beta**

## What it does

Social Forever keeps track of players you encounter and gives you a simple social history for them.

You can:

- See recently encountered players in a small movable window.
- Click a name to target that player.
- Invite them directly from the list.
- See how often you have encountered them before.
- See where you have met them in the past.
- Mark players as **Green**, **Yellow**, or **Red** based on your experience with them.
- Add flags such as **Really friendly**, **Generous**, **Weird**, or **Bad behavior**.
- Create your own custom flags.
- Mark someone as **Kill on sight**.
- Rate party members after a group ends.
- Exchange marks with nearby players who also use Social Forever.
- Quietly notice familiar faces again (blue or purple names) with a soft chat thought.
- Reset one remembered player, or all of them, from Settings → Memory.

Your social memory is stored account-wide in `SocialForeverDB`.

## The player list

The window is split into two kinds of players.

### Nearby

Players the addon has recently detected around you appear at the top.

A nearby player can stay up to **3 minutes** after the last sighting, but Social Forever also checks presence every few seconds. If the client can prove they are more than 50 yards away, they leave the list right away. If they simply stop showing up on any unit token, they leave after a short grace period (about 15–30 seconds). Seeing them again clears that and keeps them.

Out in the world, moving into another subzone removes players from the previous subzone immediately. Capital cities are treated as one larger place, so walking between areas of Ironforge or Stormwind does not clear everyone from the list.

Party and raid members remain while they are still in your group.

### In this zone

**In this zone** lists people who are on your **General** channel roster (you must be joined to General — you do not need to speak). People who speak in General, and people who yell, are added the same way.

They remain there for **10 minutes** after speaking, or while they stay on the roster.

You do not need to say anything yourself. Roster-only and yell names do not raise familiarity. A real encounter (mouseover, buff, nameplate, and so on) still can.

A player who is already in the Nearby section is not shown twice.

When you change to another main zone, players left over from the previous zone are cleared after about **30 seconds**.

## How players are ordered

The list tries to keep the most relevant people near the top.

It prioritizes:

1. Players in your current zone and area.
2. Players marked **Kill on sight** within their section.
3. People you have encountered more often.
4. Players seen more recently.

The order refreshes every few seconds rather than constantly jumping around.

New names fade in, departing names fade out, and names that change position briefly fade before moving.

## Targeting and inviting

Click a nearby player's name to try to target them.

If the target does not resolve to that player, Social Forever removes them from the nearby list rather than pretending they are still there.

Your current target is highlighted with a gold frame.

The button beside a player can show:

| Button | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Invite** | Ready to invite them. |
| **Invited** | An invitation has been sent. |
| **Declined** | They declined. You can click again to invite them once more. |

The invite button disappears while that player is already in your group and returns after they leave.

If the other player is still in combat, their invite popup waits until they leave combat — that can look like a long delay even when your click already went through.

## Familiar faces

Social Forever remembers how often you encounter each player.

A “Been nearby” count rises when someone enters Nearby in a **new** place (subzone, or whole city in a capital). If they leave the list and return in the **same** place — including after a reload — that does not add another count.

Names gradually change color based on how familiar that person is compared with the player you have encountered most often:

| Color | Familiarity |
| --- | --- |
| **White** | First encounter, or up to 30% of your highest count |
| **Blue** | 31% to 80% |
| **Purple** | 81% to 100% |

Players of the other faction use a dusty war-red instead of the familiarity colors, so they read as hostile without looking like a Red mark.

A Green, Yellow, Red, or Kill on Sight mark overrides familiarity and faction color.

### Recognition

When a **blue** or **purple** familiar appears on Nearby (not only on the zone tab), or when you target them, Social Forever may print a quiet gray thought in chat, such as:

I've seen this Human Paladin before.

It waits a few seconds after they join Nearby so the list can settle first. Each person has a 20-minute cooldown that survives reload and logout. Party or raid members do not trigger it. There is no sound and no popup.

Hover over a player to see more of their history, including:

- Last seen: the place.
- Seen before: other zones or dungeons where you have met them.
- How many times they have been nearby.
- How many times you have grouped together.
- How many times they declined your invite (in red, when it has happened).
- Your mark and the shared mark, when set.
- Flags, when you have attached any.

Their level appears to the right of the name once WoW has reported it through your target, mouseover, or group. It uses that player's class color. Between the name and the level is a small icon for their race and class together (including Skyborne). A chat message by itself does not reveal a player's level.

## Marks, flags, and Kill on Sight

Right-click a player to add your own impression of them.

### Marks

- **Green** — someone you would happily group with again.
- **Yellow** — neutral.
- **Red** — someone you had a bad experience with.

### Flags

Flags are your private reminders. They stay on your machine and are never shared with other Social Forever users.

The built-in flags are:

- Really friendly
- Generous
- Weird
- Bad behavior

You can also create your own custom flags.

### Kill on Sight

**Kill on sight** is personal. It is never shared with other Social Forever users.

## Rating a group

When a party ends, or when someone leaves your party, Social Forever can ask:

**How was this group?**

Each player can be rated:

- **Again**
- **Okay**
- **Bad**

These become Green, Yellow, and Red marks.

Converting the group into a raid does not open the rating window.

## Shared marks

If another nearby player is also using Social Forever, the two addons can quietly exchange **marks only** (Green, Yellow, Red) through WoW's addon-message system.

Nothing is printed in normal chat.

Shared marks use a simple score:

- Green = +1
- Yellow = 0
- Red = -1

Your own mark is included in the result. The tooltip shows how many good, okay, and bad marks contributed to the shared impression.

Some information always stays personal and is never shared:

- Flags (including custom ones).
- How often you have seen someone.
- Kill on sight.
- How many times you have grouped with someone.
- How many times they declined your invite.

Two-word character names are not contacted through the hidden addon whisper because this client can incorrectly report those players as offline even while they are standing nearby.

## How "nearby" works

Social Forever does **not** scan every player within a fixed radius. WoW does not give addons a simple list of everyone standing around you.

Instead, Social Forever builds the nearby list from players the game has already exposed through things such as:

- Your target, mouseover, focus, or soft target.
- Friendly nameplates, if you have turned them on yourself (Shift+V). Social Forever never changes that setting.
- Someone who buffs you, when Forever still exposes the caster.
- A resurrection cast on you.
- Other players from the **current** damage meter after a fight ends, only while they are still online and present to the client.
- Party and raid members who are online and actually within range. Offline group members are not kept on the list.
- Say, emotes, craft lines, duel, and trade.

**In this zone** is broader and weaker. It includes people who speak in General, people currently on the General channel roster, and yell. Being on that roster alone does not count as an encounter or raise familiarity.

Because of that, a silent player standing beside you may not appear immediately if the game has not exposed them to the addon yet.

Social Forever does not enable nameplates or use `/who` to build the list. The combat log event stream is not used.

## Window and settings

The window normally sits above the chat frame.

- The close **x** sits in the top-left corner, away from the gear button.
- Hover the **x** for a reminder that `/sf` or `/socialforever` brings the window back.
- Drag the title bar to move it.
- Drag the `..` grip in the bottom-right corner to resize it.
- Use the gear button to change grouping options, name size, background opacity, and Memory reset (one player or all remembered players).
- Use the mouse wheel to scroll longer lists.
- Press Escape to close the right-click menu or group-rating window. The main Social Forever window stays open.

Use:

```text
/sf
```

or

```text
/socialforever
```

to show or hide the window. The addon-compartment button does the same.

## Installation

Copy the `SocialForever` folder into:

```text
Interface/AddOns/SocialForever
```

Then reload the game:

```text
/reload
```

The Great Iceflow Relay

Hi yall,

This is a little relay ball game add-on for World of Warcraft 1.12, played on Iceflow Lake in Dun Morogh.
It’s a simple but fun RP activity where you and your friends run through checkpoints, pass the ball around, and try to score the most Iceflow Shards while avoiding penalties.

I made this addon because I love throwing the ball in WoW, but just passing it back and forth got a little stale. So I thought, why not turn it into a proper mini-game? I’m new to addon development and not much of a coder, so I used AI help to put this together. It’s pretty simple, mostly chat commands, but I think it adds a cute bit of gameplay for anyone who enjoys RP events and silly fun with the ball.

🏁 How the game works

There are 6 checkpoints: one Start, four in between, and one Finish.

The race begins at the landing stage in Brewnall Village.

To prepare, you can:

Type /iceflow checkpoints → see coordinates of all checkpoints.

Move to a spot and type /iceflow check → see if you are standing inside a checkpoint.

🎮 Commands

/iceflow ready → Arms the addon and signals the group that you’re ready.

Enter the Start checkpoint → Relay begins and everyone gets a group message.

/iceflow end → Disarms the addon.

/iceflow pos → Prints your current coordinates.

/iceflow ballcheck → Tells you if you have a leather ball in your bags.

💎 Scoring

Players earn Iceflow Shards when:

Catching the ball.

Entering a checkpoint.

Players get penalties for:

Holding the ball too long.

Standing too close to another player (must stay at least 28 yards apart).

At the Finish checkpoint, the addon posts a summary to the group chat:

Total Shards earned.

Total Penalty collected.

Net Shards (your final score).

👥 Group Play

Designed mainly for pairs, but works fine with more players too.

Example: three players can run in a triangle, passing two or even three balls around at once.

Works in both party and raid groups.

🗺️ Route

The checkpoints can be tricky to find, so here’s a marked map of the course:
https://imgur.com/a/eQcNdPX


✨ Closing words

This addon is meant as a light RP mini-game for World of Warcraft 1.12. It’s not super polished, but it’s fun if you like silly challenges with friends.

Wishing yall lots of joy and many Iceflow Shards in Azeroth!

## Current source snapshot (v0.72)

**Scope:** The source targets a World of Warcraft 1.12 / Lua 5.0-style client. The source has **not** been retested in game for this documentation review. The rules below describe implementation, which sometimes differs from the event's idealized group-play description above.

1. Every participant who installs and arms the addon tracks their **own** run. The code does not send a synchronized scoreboard, coordinate other players' state, or enforce that every player visits the same stops.
2. Four intermediate checkpoints can each award **one shard once per run**. The current code accepts them in any order and allows the player to finish without visiting all four.
3. Receiving an item matching the **Heavy Leather Ball** icon through `ITEM_PUSH` can award **one shard**, subject to a 0.1-second duplicate-event guard.
4. If a Heavy Leather Ball is found in bags while a run is active, the current polling implementation adds **one penalty per two-second check**. It does **not** measure elapsed holding seconds precisely or provide a grace period.
5. The ~28-yard proximity test uses `CheckInteractDistance` on **your current target**, whether or not that unit is a teammate. A nearby untargeted player is not checked.
6. The finish message reports net shards, total earned shards, and accumulated penalties to party/raid chat (or locally when solo). There is no built-in ranking of multiple finishers.

### Installation and setup

Install `TheGreatIceflowRelay.lua` and `TheGreatIceflowRelay.toc` directly inside `Interface/AddOns/TheGreatIceflowRelay/`, restart your game and enable the addon. The addon's manifest declares interface `11200` and version `0.72`.

Use `/iceflow rules` to read the in-game rules and `/iceflow checkpoints` to print every checkpoint rectangle. Use `/iceflow ready` to arm the run and enter the start area. The addon then polls for checkpoints, bag contents, and proximity. `/iceflow end` stops it; `/iceflow pos`, `check`, and `ballcheck` provide diagnostics.

# The Great Iceflow Relay — creative concept

**Creative author:** Babuni.dev  
**Format:** cooperative/competitive in-world roleplay event supported by a small World of Warcraft 1.12 addon.

## Where the idea began

The creator explains the motivation in their own words in [README.md](README.md): they enjoyed **throwing a ball around in WoW**, but simply passing it back and forth began to feel stale. Instead of replacing the social activity with a separate video game, they imagined rules for playing with that existing object in the game world.

That creative leap—to turn an informal player ritual into a structured relay with an actual course, points and consequences—belongs to Babuni.dev. The original README also openly acknowledges AI assistance with **coding**. This is one of the clearest first-person records of the project's creative authorship, so preserve its voice.

## The experience the project aims for

Friends gather at **Iceflow Lake in Dun Morogh**, near Brewnall Village, and pass a **Heavy Leather Ball** while navigating a six-stop course. The activity balances two impulses: collect **Iceflow Shards** through catches and intermediate stops; avoid penalties by passing quickly and spreading out. A finish message turns the improvised chase into a memorable group moment.

The original description proposes pairs or small groups, including three people passing multiple balls in a triangle. That is an **event concept**: the addon is currently per-player, and participants still organize the shared physical game themselves.

## Design pillars

- **In-world play:** use the actual lake, the actual game item, game emotes and social proximity.
- **Lightweight invitation:** chat commands and printed coordinates, no custom arena or complex UI.
- **Roleplay before competitive rigor:** the joy of the activity matters more than a perfectly synchronized esport rules engine.
- **Visible consequences:** catches and checkpoint entries build shards; holding and closeness lead to penalties.
- **Player ownership:** the creator's course and rules define the activity; AI-assisted technical execution is a separate contribution.

## Boundaries and accuracy

This is not a stand-alone game or automated group tournament. Current code uses local state on each client and does not authenticate ball transfers between players, enforce the checkpoint order or identify every nearby teammate. Those gaps do not erase the original concept; they are part of the development story. See [architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) and [design decisions](docs/DECISIONS.md).

The repository records a 0.72 addon. No in-game multiplayer validation occurred during the 2026-10-26 documentation reconstruction.

# The Great Iceflow Relay — development journal

**Creative creator:** Babuni.dev  
**Reconstruction date:** 2026-10-26. Evidence comes from the creator's README, GitHub history and committed Lua/TOC. Where original chat discussions are absent, this entry is explicitly **retrospective**, not a transcript.

## Before the addon: a ball and an idea

The most important piece of source material is not a formula. It is the author's own README introduction. Babuni.dev describes enjoying throwing a ball around in World of Warcraft with friends, until repeatedly passing it back and forth felt a little stale. The author wondered why that playful existing mechanic could not become a proper mini-game.

What followed was a design for an outing at Iceflow Lake: a starting point near Brewnall Village, named checkpoints around the lake, shards earned by moving and catching, penalties for lingering with the ball or getting too close, and the delight of sharing an ending with a group. The README gives the idea a clearly social purpose. It describes pairs and, for example, three people running a triangle while multiple balls circulate. Those are the creator's ideas, not features invented during this documentation pass.

The author also says, plainly, they were new to addon coding and used **AI help to put it together**. That admission is an important part of the project history: human imagination and direction shaped the play, while AI support made it practical to prototype in Lua. The old README is preserved unedited above the new technical notes; readers can encounter that voice directly.

## 11 September 2025: shape of the game emerges

GitHub shows the addon manifest committed as `5ffa935` and the first Lua as `5c86d98` on **2025-09-11**. That first Lua used five **triangular** geographic areas and geometric point-in-triangle detection. Later revisions on the same day moved to **axis-aligned rectangular** zones, introduced separate start and finish checkpoints, managed unique visited locations and incremented a shard count. This is a concrete technical transition, not a claim that the author had a formal design meeting about geometry.

The unusually long sequence of “Update TheGreatIceflowRelay.lua” commits throughout the afternoon and evening tells its own story: there was a great deal of short-cycle iteration. The commit names by themselves do not say which ideas were proposed or rejected, nor whether each change worked on the first try. The few individually inspected diffs do, however, show the game growing from location detection into a stateful relay.

By a later 11 September revision (`55cc340`), the source distinguishes a **ready/armed** state from an **active run**, adds an explicit `/iceflow ready` action and uses the first start-zone entry to begin. Other changes brought inventory scanning for a **Heavy Leather Ball** and periodic position checks. The result remained intentionally humble: a single small addon with chat output rather than an invented physical ball mechanic.

## 12–13 September 2025: catching, costs and group presentation

A revised Lua snapshot (`957f4a1`) shows the next layer: an `ITEM_PUSH` hook awarding an immediate shard on a matching ball-icon event, with a short duplicate-event guard. This was distinct from the recurring bag scan used to detect whether the player was holding a ball.

As the penalty system developed, a subtle discrepancy appeared between explanatory language and actual time accounting. The present `CHECK_INTERVAL = 2` runs a polling pass roughly every two seconds; each detected ball-holding pass increments `totalBallTime` and `totalPenalty` by exactly one. The source comment calls these seconds, but the counter behaves like **poll ticks**. The target-distance check likewise tests the **currently targeted unit**, not a continuously measured distance from every teammate. These are observations from code, not a retroactive accusation that any player misunderstood the rules.

The 13 September commits include a visible refactoring of penalty reset/finish arithmetic (`39a85fd`), followed by changes to final-score phrasing (`ab474ad`). Another change (`6b69b48`) made announcements work in raids as well as parties, keeping solo fallback in local chat. The game was becoming more legible to an audience watching the event happen, even though each character's counters stayed local.

## 16–17 September 2025: explanation becomes part of the project

The TOC received help wording and declared version **0.72**. On **2025-09-17**, the creator-facing README appeared (`3e04880`) and was edited further (`03b275d`) to include the marked course-map link. Its tone matters. Rather than presenting the addon as a polished platform, the author called it a simple, cute RP activity and openly acknowledged both the coding learning curve and the AI assistance. That is a valuable design artifact and source of authorship context, not marketing copy to overwrite.

## 2026: preservation and review

On **2026-09-18**, descriptions were adjusted to refer to compatible WoW 1.12 clients without tying the project to one provider (`8c91d36`). On **2026-10-26**, earlier documentation passes standardized **Babuni.dev** author credit and generated a small initial scaffold. That skeleton did not adequately preserve the project's iteration or explain the gap between social rules and current scoring.

The present review read the source and historical commits, retained the creator's own explanation, and developed dedicated architecture, design, content, decision and collaboration files. **No runtime code was changed**, and no game client, real ball transfer, multiplayer session, checkpoint path or addon compatibility test was executed.

## What remains open

The biggest unanswered question is not “how do we make the code more sophisticated?” It is how much mechanical enforcement Babuni.dev actually wants. An informal RP relay may benefit from human refereeing and flexibility; a strict tournament would need verified distances, robust catch detection, route-order rules and shared results. The current documentation leaves that choice with the creator and marks all proposed changes as proposals.

**Attribution and evidence discipline:** Babuni.dev supplied the human concept, world choice and authorial voice. The repository acknowledges earlier AI coding assistance without a complete contribution ledger. In this 2026 review, AI inspected and reconstructed documentation from public code and Git; no original design decision is newly credited to AI and no test outcome is invented.

# The Great Iceflow Relay — architecture (v0.72)

**Evidence:** `TheGreatIceflowRelay.lua`, `TheGreatIceflowRelay.toc`; source inspected 2026-10-26. **No game-client execution in this review.**

## Runtime layout

A single Lua script creates `TheGreatIceflowRelayFrame`, registers the `ITEM_PUSH` event, installs `OnEvent` and `OnUpdate` handlers, and registers the `/iceflow` command. The frame starts hidden. `/iceflow ready` resets local state, sets `armed = true`, and shows the frame. Entering the starting rectangle while armed switches to `runActive = true`.

The frame's update handler checks elapsed `GetTime()` against `CHECK_INTERVAL = 2` and calls three functions while armed or active:

1. **`CheckCheckpoint`:** `SetMapZoom(0)` and `SetMapToCurrentZone()` precede `GetPlayerMapPosition("player")`; normalized coordinates are multiplied by 100. Automatic checkpoint handling also checks `GetZoneText() == "Dun Morogh"`. Intermediate areas award +1 only on first visit in a run. Finish computes `playerShards - totalPenalty`, sends summary, and disables active run.
2. **`CheckBallInInventory(true)`:** scans bag links for the literal substring `Heavy Leather Ball`. During a run, every poll where a ball is present adds **1 to `totalBallTime` and 1 to `totalPenalty`**. Despite its name and comments, `totalBallTime` is a tick count, not measured seconds; a two-second poll makes any UI “sec” wording approximate/inaccurate.
3. **`CheckTargetDistance`:** checks current `target` with the client interaction-distance API indices 1–4, then adds 1 penalty on a positive result; if out of range, it prints “Distance ok!”. It does **not** iterate party/raid members or assert target membership.

`ITEM_PUSH` separately calls `OnItemPush`, which looks for `INV_Misc_ThrowingBall_01` in the second event argument and adds one shard when active and outside a 0.1-second duplicate-event window. This is an event/icon check; not proof that the player actually received the specific named ball under every client/localization scenario.

## State and lifecycle

- **Run:** `armed`, `runActive`, `startTriggered`, `finishTriggered`.
- **Score:** `playerShards`, `totalPenalty`, per-run table `visitedCheckpoints`.
- **Item/clock:** `hasBall`, `totalBallTime`, `lastCheck`, `lastBallCatch`.
- **Persistence:** no saved-variable declaration, network protocol or shared scoreboard is implemented. Reloading resets run state.
- **End:** `/iceflow end` hides frame/disarms; finishing sets `runActive = false`, while the frame may remain visible and `armed` still true.

## Chat and multiplayer boundary

`RelayGroupMessage` uses `RAID` if in a raid, else `PARTY`, else local chat. `RelayLocalMessage` always prints locally. All score computations happen **on the local player’s machine**. Party/raid chat displays results; it is not synchronization.

## Behavior discrepancies to test or decide

- No requirement for visiting all intermediate checkpoints or visiting them in order before finish.
- A player can re-enter the start after a finished run while still armed, potentially starting again.
- Proximity is tested only against the current target, which may be a nonplayer.
- `/iceflow check` tests coordinates without the automatic Dun Morogh zone check.
- Area boundaries use small, axis-aligned rectangles, not world-space yard radii.
- Polling may skip brief boundary crossings or ball possession between two checks.
- The interface number is **11200**; modern addon API behavior is not implied.

These are code observations and possible effects, not measured game-client failures.

# The Great Iceflow Relay — gameplay and experience design

**Creative direction:** Babuni.dev.

## The physical play space

The lake is not decoration: its banks, obstacles and travel distances provide the playground. The start/finish at Brewnall Village make the route legible as an outing, while intermediate landmarks—The Tree, Carcass Island, Wet Log and Behind the Branch—give players places to shout, meet, pass and improvise.

The player's ball is an existing WoW item. Movement and real conversation remain in the normal game client. The addon offers lightweight structure through chat rather than taking over the interface with custom screens.

## Player journey

1. Gather friends, distribute one or more Heavy Leather Balls, and decide how to referee fair passing.
2. Find the course using `/iceflow checkpoints`, `/iceflow pos` and the [creator-linked marked map](https://imgur.com/a/eQcNdPX).
3. Arm individual copies with `/iceflow ready`; enter the starting rectangle.
4. Move between landmarks, throw and receive balls. Each newly reached middle checkpoint awards one shard; eligible `ITEM_PUSH` events award catches.
5. Avoid the recurring ball-hold and **target** proximity penalties as implemented.
6. Enter the finish rectangle and share your final tally.

This sequence describes a suggested social event flow. **The source does not mechanically require the landmark order, nor a full traversal before the finish.**

## Scoring rhythm in current source

The reward side is simple and discrete: **one shard per unique middle checkpoint** and **one per qualified ball item event**. The cost side is recurrent: **one penalty every approximately two seconds of detected bag possession** and **one per poll when the currently targeted unit is within any checked interaction range**. The net result is `earned - penalties` and can be negative.

The source description frames the spacing rule as staying 28 yards from other players, but the code only examines a single selected target. Avoid describing the current implementation as comprehensive teammate-distance validation.

## What makes it a roleplay toy

The invitation to run in pairs or make a triangle with three players is a creator-authored social invention; it gives others room to develop their own event etiquette. The “Good Game, Well Played!” finish message acknowledges shared activity even when the technical score is individual.

## Accessibility and usability considerations (unverified)

The addon relies heavily on text feedback, English item/zone names and manually entered chat commands. Route coordinates are precise but not represented by in-game waypoints. The large amount of penalty/status chat can be distracting; it should be observed during an actual event before proposing output throttling.

# Totem Timers

**Creator / creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Release:** 1.3.7 · **WoW client target:** Vanilla 1.12 / interface 11200 · **Author in TOC:** Babuni.dev  
**Historical name:** Octo Totem Timers (renamed September 18, 2026)  
**Current source:** [TotemTimers.lua](TotemTimers.lua) and [TotemTimers.toc](TotemTimers.toc)  
**Audit basis:** code, Git history, metadata and migration helper inspected October 27, 2026; no in-game tests run in this audit.

Totem Timers is a compact, movable **Shaman-specific** status panel for four elemental totem slots, shield charges, and weapon imbues. Its style takes cues from Blizzard's own frames rather than asking the player to maintain a separate settings-heavy interface. During combat it can draw a red **!** over an empty totem element.

It tracks **what the client reports or what the player attempted to cast**. On an older 1.12 client without a native totem-status API, its totem countdowns are predictions: a failed cast may still create a timer, and destroying or removing a totem early may not be detected. It does **not** grant faster casting, remove the global cooldown, cast spells for you, or independently verify the server has spawned a totem.

## Install and run

```text
World of Warcraft/
└── Interface/
    └── AddOns/
        └── TotemTimers/
            ├── TotemTimers.toc
            └── TotemTimers.lua
```

The [published v1.3.7 release](https://github.com/babunidev/TotemTimers/releases/tag/v1.3.7) contains a [TotemTimers.zip](https://github.com/babunidev/TotemTimers/releases/download/v1.3.7/TotemTimers.zip) and a checksum file. Extract the **TotemTimers** folder into Interface/AddOns or copy the two files above from this repo. Restart the client or use `/reload`. The manifest loads **one Lua source** and uses no external addon dependency.

The code checks `UnitClass("player")` when entering the world. If the player is **not a Shaman**, it unregisters addon events and does not create the display. That does not mean every slash command is gated by class; commands are registered outside the class check and should not be used on unsupported classes without testing.

## What the panel displays

| Location | Content | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Earth** | A current Earth totem / blank placeholder | 34px icon, remaining time or `--`, red exclamation while in combat and empty |
| **Water** | Water totem | Same, with water-specific placeholder color |
| **Fire** | Fire totem | Same; replaces a previous Fire timer when another Fire totem is attempted |
| **Air** | Air totem | Same |
| **Upper-left smaller icon** | Lightning Shield, Water Shield or Earth Shield | Reads player buff texture, tooltip and available charge information |
| **Upper-right smaller icon** | Weapon enchant | Rockbiter, Flametongue, Frostbrand or Windfury, recognized by a weapon tooltip |

**Display order is Earth → Water → Fire → Air**, even though the code's internal element indices and native API order are **Fire → Earth → Water → Air**. The panel deliberately maps the two orders.

A shield slot displays a gray Lightning Shield placeholder and red exclamation when no recognized shield is found. For an active shield, charge text is green at the observed maximum, gold with more than one charge but fewer than maximum, or red at one/zero. Recognized default maxima: Lightning Shield **3**, Water Shield **3**, Earth Shield **6**; higher observed counts can raise those maxima within the session.

Weapon enchant display checks for enchant presence, scans the equipped weapon tooltip for the four named imbues, and displays that item's tooltip on hover. It checks **main hand first**, then off hand only if no main-hand enchant is present. It does not maintain separate main/off-hand enchant timers or a precise enchant duration.

The fallback table recognizes **23 named totems**: 5 Fire, 5 Earth, 6 Water and 7 Air. These are documented individually in [content inventory](docs/CONTENT.md). A spell/action tooltip duration is preferred; the named fallback durations are used when a tooltip cannot supply one. Tooltip parsing expects English phrases such as “Lasts 30 sec”; localization/custom spell text may affect timing.

## Commands

| Slash command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `/totemtimers unlock` | Allow left-button dragging |
| `/totemtimers lock` | Prevent dragging |
| `/totemtimers show` | Show the full panel, even with empty elemental slots |
| `/totemtimers hide` | Hide the panel completely |
| `/totemtimers reset` | Restore the original center-relative position |
| `/ttimers ...` | Short alias for the same command set |
| `/totemtimers` | Print command help |

The addon stores `locked`, `hidden`, `alwaysShow`, and placement (`point`, `relativePoint`, `x`, `y`) in account-wide `TotemTimersDB`. **alwaysShow defaults to true**, so all four empty elemental slots are visible; `hide` overrides everything. The only implemented `show` mode sets both hidden=false and alwaysShow=true; there is **no current slash toggle** to make `alwaysShow` false.

**Totemic Recall:** attempts under the names `Totemic Recall`, `Totemic Call` and `Recall Totems` clear all four predicted slots. If native `GetTotemInfo` is available, the next refresh replaces predictions with that API's state. A normal totem cast replaces the estimate for its elemental slot.

## How timing works

There are two paths, with important different reliability:

1. **Native API path:** if the particular client supplies `GetTotemInfo`, the addon queries four slots on refresh and uses the reported name, start, duration and icon; empty slots are cleared.
2. **Legacy prediction path:** it wraps global `CastSpell`, `CastSpellByName` and `UseAction` to detect a recognized spell **before** delegating to the game's original function. It reads a tooltip or falls back to its duration table, and starts a local `GetTime()` deadline. The hooks are rechecked roughly every **0.10 seconds** so other addon wrappers can be noticed.

In legacy prediction mode a pressed ability may be resisted, fail for mana/range, or never place a totem. The code registers failure/interruption events but does **not** reconcile those events against its predicted slot state. Totem destruction and range/expiration differences also need in-game verification. “Supports rapid no-GCD totem casting” in the historic README means the code can notice multiple quick attempts; **this addon does not remove GCD restrictions**.

Shield state is read through `UnitBuff` and tooltips; weapon enchant presence through `GetWeaponEnchantInfo` and inventory tooltips. These are observations, not perfect verification across custom servers or all languages.

## Upgrade from Octo Totem Timers

If you played under the older **OctoTotemTimers** folder and **OctoTotemTimersDB** variable, you need to migrate SavedVariables when moving to **TotemTimers / TotemTimersDB**. Merely renaming the addon folder does not load older settings.

With WoW **closed**, retain the old installed folder and run the supplied helper from the new addon directory:

```powershell
.\Upgrade-SavedData.ps1 -ClientPath "C:\Games\World of Warcraft" -PreviousAddonName "OctoTotemTimers"
```

The script reads the old and new TOC, backs up originals under `AddonUpgradeBackups`, creates renamed files without overwriting existing ones, and replaces top-level SavedVariables declarations without running the Lua contents. It keeps original saved files. This source behavior was inspected; **the helper was not executed during this audit**. Its test fixture is [tests/test_upgrade.ps1](tests/test_upgrade.ps1). Test with backups before using real settings.

If using Linux, manually copy a **backup** of `WTF/Account/.../SavedVariables/OctoTotemTimers.lua` to the new file name and rewrite **only the top-level** variable assignment to `TotemTimersDB`, with WoW closed. Preserve the old file until successful verification.

## Current limitations and testing

- **Predictive cast detection** is not a guarantee a totem spawned. Failed casts, destroys and nonstandard totem effects can drift in old clients.
- Native `GetTotemInfo` is **optional** and cannot be assumed on an ordinary original 1.12 client.
- Tooltip parsing uses some **English phrases** and Shaman spell names; full multilingual support hasn't been tested here.
- Global wrappers can interact with other addons wrapping the same functions. Rapid 0.1s rewrapping deserves compatibility/performance tests.
- The shield scan only inspects the first **32** player buffs; charge data can be missing or interpreted differently on custom clients.
- The weapon effect display prioritizes the main-hand enchant and only scans known names; unusual enchants use a generic label.
- There is **no LICENSE** in this repository; public source does not automatically grant reuse rights.
- The release notes report historical syntax/migration checks, but the release ZIP and checksum were **not** independently downloaded/verified in this documentation session, and **no game tests were run**.

# Totem Timers — creative concept

**Creator / creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Platform:** WoW 1.12, Shaman class, original 1.12 API constraints.

## Make four invisible commitments understandable

A Shaman can maintain several short-lived elemental tools at once. The game makes these abilities powerful and characterful, but the player must remember which Earth, Water, Fire and Air totem is still in the world and how soon each will vanish. Totem Timers condenses that attention problem into a **small, movable quartet of icons with countdowns**.

The visual intention is modest and specific: a **Blizzard-style frame**, not an alien productivity overlay. A brown/gold-bordered dark backing and familiar spell icons make it seem close to the game's existing interface. Empty elemental slots remain visible by default, so the player can see the complete four-part structure rather than merely remembering what's active. In combat, an absent element gets a red **!**.

This design does not insist that four totems always be active. A missing marker is a visual cue, **not a gameplay recommendation** to spend resources or drop a strategically unnecessary totem. The player remains in charge.

## Extend the same glance to adjacent Shaman states

Two smaller icons above the elemental row answer related questions: Is a Lightning/Water/Earth Shield active, and with how many charges? Is the weapon imbued with Rockbiter, Flametongue, Frostbrand or Windfury?

These are the sorts of details a Shaman can otherwise track across buff icons, inventory tooltips and memory. Bringing them into a compact arrangement offers a more legible combat instrument without automating spells or modifying the game world.

## Respect the old client, and its uncertainty

Original 1.12 does not necessarily expose a modern native totem-status API. The project handles this by observing which spell or action was *attempted*, reading its tooltip for a duration and tracking a local expiration estimate. When `GetTotemInfo` exists on a compatible variant, the code uses that stronger source.

This tradeoff is central to the concept: **help the player read the fight** despite limited data, while not asserting that a timer predicted from an attempted cast is proof that a totem actually spawned. Failures, recalls, destruction, spell renames and custom-client behavior complicate certainty.

## A small, authored interface

The code's presentation order is **Earth, Water, Fire, Air**, mapping an internal Fire/Earth/Water/Air model to the intended human-readable layout. The panel can be dragged, locked, hidden or restored; its position and choices persist account-wide. A 0.1-second display refresh keeps timers smooth without introducing a complex settings surface.

The original purpose, interaction goals and creative authority belong to **Babuni.dev**. This concept is an interpretation of the September 2026 source and documentation; the exact first ideation conversation was not recovered. No future changes have been approved simply by recording them as options.

# Totem Timers — creative and technical development journal

**Creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev  
**Retrospective prepared:** October 27, 2026, from the current Git tree, TOC, full 600-line Lua implementation, September commit diffs, published release metadata and README. The original human/AI planning dialogues were not recovered; this journal does **not** invent them.

## The Shaman's four-part attention problem

The idea behind Totem Timers is one of those interface improvements that appears small because it responds to a very specific gameplay experience. A Shaman can place totems tied to four elements, each with its own duration and purpose. In combat, remembering every placement, its remaining lifetime and the state of nearby personal enhancements means looking at several different places in the client or mentally counting time.

Babuni.dev's project brings that information into a **Blizzard-looking, draggable instrument**. Four familiar icons organize Earth, Water, Fire and Air into one compact row. Above them, two smaller status icons track shield charges and temporary weapon enchants. Empty elements don't disappear by default: the frame's silhouette stays complete. During combat, an empty elemental position gets a red exclamation, giving an at-a-glance sign that no totem is currently known in that category.

The point isn't to play the class for the player. The source doesn't select totems, automatically cast spells or change the global cooldown. It tries to make existing Shaman state legible. Whether every empty element should prompt a warning remains a gameplay/UX question, not a demonstrated rule that all four must be used.
