## Reading an old client's limited information

The central technical challenge is discovering which totem exists in the world. Modern-compatible clients may expose `GetTotemInfo`, allowing actual four-slot duration/state reads. The source checks for this API and prefers it when present.

But the classic 1.12 surface is more limited. The implementation therefore wraps **CastSpell**, **CastSpellByName** and **UseAction**. When the player *tries* to use a recognized totem, the addon first records the attempt with a start time and duration (from the tooltip if possible, otherwise a fallback list). The original game function is then invoked.

This solution supports rapid back-to-back actions without waiting for a fixed cooldown tick. The original README described “rapid no-GCD totem casting”; the code itself **does not remove or bypass the global cooldown**. It observes eligible attempts made by the player.

There is a price. The addon **predicts** a totem instead of confirming one was placed. A failed cast can create a convincing countdown in legacy mode, and the registered failure/interrupted events don't actually roll that countdown back. A totem destroyed early can likewise appear until local expiry. If the native API exists it replaces the predicted status at refresh, but availability and slot semantics depend on the client. The documentation treats this as a verification need, not as proof of a live defect on the creator's client.

The spelling of names and fallback seconds mattered. The code has **23** recognized totem spells, divided among Fire, Earth, Water and Air. For spellbook/action buttons it attempts to read duration phrases from a hidden tooltip. For `CastSpellByName` it uses its known table. Recognizing a new same-element totem replaces the old local slot; known recall variants clear all four estimates.

The code further checks a player's first **32 buff slots** for Lightning, Water or Earth Shield and extracts observed charge counts. It scans temporary weapon enchants through equipped-item tooltips, prioritizing main hand. Those represent a desire for one readable Shaman status widget rather than unrelated addon popups. Charge text uses simple green, yellow and red states to help the player notice depletion.

## Visual logic rather than a full interface replacement

The panel uses built-in WoW tooltip borders and backgrounds, 34-pixel totem icons and 26-pixel secondary status icons. Internal indices follow Fire/Earth/Water/Air, but display order is **Earth/Water/Fire/Air**. This deliberate mapping brings the elements into the visual order found in the original source rather than blindly exposing the game's internal enumeration.

The countdown changes format as expiry approaches: **minutes:seconds** above a minute, whole seconds down to ten, then tenths. The panel can be dragged and locked and remembers placement and visibility in account-wide **TotemTimersDB**. The saved `alwaysShow` preference defaults to true, preserving empty positions; `hidden` can hide everything.

This is the kind of work for which the development itself belongs in a portfolio. The result may simply look like four icons, but the code balances old-client API limits, tooltip-derived metadata, time predictions, auxiliary buff identification, and interoperability with independently written addons.

The hook management is one unresolved concern. Roughly every **0.10 seconds**, the addon checks whether another addon changed its hooked global functions, and if so it wraps them again while delegating. That preserves the attempt to keep receiving casts, but can create complex nested hook chains when multiple addons use similar strategies. No recursion or frame-rate issue has been demonstrated in this audit; it deserves actual joint-addon testing.

# Totem Timers — architecture and state accuracy

**Audited:** `TotemTimers.lua` (600 lines), `TotemTimers.toc`, migration script/test, September Git diffs, October 27, 2026. This is **static inspection**, not gameplay verification.

## Installed package and state

```text
TotemTimers.toc (Interface 11200 / Version 1.3.7)
    SavedVariables: TotemTimersDB
    TotemTimers.lua
      ├── static spell/element duration and texture tables
      ├── cast/action hooks and native totem state option
      ├── UnitBuff shield and inventory-tooltip enchant lookups
      ├── 4-element visual row + shield/weapon icons
      └── events and repeating ~0.10s refresh
```

The native-totem query is `GetTotemInfo` if defined. It is **not guaranteed in original Vanilla 1.12**. No external library, network communication, image asset directory or server interaction is bundled.

## Class gating and event lifecycle

The frame subscribes to `VARIABLES_LOADED`, `PLAYER_ENTERING_WORLD`, spellcast stop/fail/interrupted, player totem changes, combat state, aura/inventory and spellbook changes. On world entry `InitializeAddon` checks the second return of `UnitClass("player")` for **SHAMAN**. Non-Shamans unregister addon events; Shamans create one display, scan tooltip, initialize global cast wrappers, then refresh on event or **0.10-second OnUpdate**.

The code registers both slash aliases **/totemtimers** and **/ttimers** globally even when initialization doesn't create the panel. This asymmetry could affect command use on non-Shamans; test before asserting full class-gated command behavior.

## Four-element state

The totem table stores a **slot index** and fallback duration for 23 recognized English spell names. Internally the order is:
- **1 Fire**
- **2 Earth**
- **3 Water**
- **4 Air**

The displayed `DISPLAY_ORDER={2,3,1,4}` produces **Earth, Water, Fire, Air**. Default empty textures and earth/water/fire/air-color hints are associated with internal indices, not visible column numbering.

`QueueTotem(name,duration,texture)` normalizes a trailing “(Rank X)” and, for a recognized totem, stores a new entry in its elemental slot with `GetTime()`-based `startTime` and `expires`. Casting a new same-element totem **overwrites its previous estimate**. The names `Totemic Recall`, `Totemic Call` and `Recall Totems` clear all four estimates.

`ScanSpell` asks a hidden GameTooltip for `SetSpell` title and duration. `ScanAction` uses `SetAction`. `CastSpellByName` passes the incoming name to the same queue without scanning a tooltip, so it always uses the fallback duration for a known named totem. If the tooltip gives no duration or is an unsupported locale, built-in seconds are used.

### Native versus predicted status

```text
OnUpdate or status-relevant event
   -> EnsureCastingHooks()
   -> UpdateDisplay()
         -> if hidden: hide and return
         -> if GetTotemInfo exists:
              for 1..4 native slots:
                  copy server/client-provided name/start/duration/texture
                  or clear
         -> else:
              use predictions from CastSpell / CastSpellByName / UseAction
         -> check shield UnitBuff and enchant tooltip
         -> update four countdowns and empty warnings
```

**Potential correctness problem:** all three wrappers call `QueueTotem` **before** delegating to the original spell/action API. A missed/failed cast can therefore begin a local timer. `SPELLCAST_FAILED` and `SPELLCAST_INTERRUPTED` are listened to but only cause a display refresh, **not rollback of the predicted slot**. Similarly, if a totem is destroyed early or expires unpredictably and native info isn't available, the estimate can remain until its deadline.

The native status path `UpdateFromNativeAPI` overwrites all four slots on each visible refresh. That is more authoritative *when actually supported by the client*, but does not prove server-specific versions/slot indexes are compatible in every variant.

## Global wrappers and interop

`EnsureCastingHooks` checks whether the globals `CastSpell`, `CastSpellByName` and `UseAction` still equal this addon's wrapper. If not, it captures their current function and sets a new wrapper that looks up a totem first then delegates. This check runs about ten times per second after initialization.

Because different addons can wrap these same globals, chains can be composed more than once if a second addon repeatedly rewraps a global; the source does not have an explicit chain-depth cap. This is a **potential interoperability/performance risk**, not a demonstrated infinite recursion from a real client.

## Shield observations and limitations

The addon inspects the first **32 UnitBuff("player", index)** slots. For each it uses texture matching against dynamically refreshed spellbook textures, or a cleaned tooltip title, to recognize **Lightning, Water and Earth Shield**. It reads a charge count from UnitBuff applications or the tooltip's “N charges” text, defaulting to zero if unavailable.

Max-charge defaults are **3 / 3 / 6** but increase if a higher observed count appears. The UI paints current charges green when at/above max, yellow with 2..max-1, red at 0 or 1; absent shield becomes a dim placeholder plus a warning. No exact shield uptime timer is displayed.

## Weapon enchant observations

`GetWeaponEnchantInfo` checks a temporary main-hand enchant, else an off-hand enchant. It scans inventory slot **16** or **17** tooltip lines for one of **Rockbiter, Flametongue, Frostbrand, Windfury**. Matching names select a spellbook icon when present, falling back to a known game icon. An unrecognized temporary enchant can display as “Weapon Enchant” using its equipped item texture; no two-hand list, enchant count or remaining-duration clock exists.

## Layout and persistence

The backing panel uses WoW's tooltip backgrounds/borders, four **34px** elemental buttons and two **26px** auxiliary shield/weapon buttons. The frame is draggable when `TotemTimersDB.locked` isn't set. Position saves `point`, `relativePoint`, `x`, `y`; `hidden` overrides all drawing, while `alwaysShow` defaults true and leaves empty element placeholders visible.

`UpdateDisplay` clears an expired estimated slot, formats time as `m:ss`, seconds or tenths below ten seconds, and shows missing-element red **!** only in combat when empty slots are enabled.

## Migration and tests

On September 18 the project switched from **OctoTotemTimersDB** to **TotemTimersDB** and added `Upgrade-SavedData.ps1`. It reads TOC declarations, backs up discovered saved files, rewrites root assignments in copies and refuses overwrite. `tests/test_upgrade.ps1` creates temporary synthetic account/per-character fixtures with Unicode and checks backups/overwrite/path refusals. The historic v1.3.7 release notes report tests passed; **they were not rerun in this audit**, and no live client was used.

# Totem Timers — visual and interaction design

**Creative direction:** Babuni.dev.  
**Source:** current UI-building Lua and original README; no screenshot assets included in this repository.

## A Blizzard-looking instrument

The addon deliberately uses **native-feeling tooltip frame styling**: a black translucent backing, muted earthy border, familiar spell icons, restrained gold countdown numbers and compact type. It sits as a movable four-column instrument rather than a conventional configuration window.

The code creates a panel sized for **four 34px elemental icons**, spaced 5px apart, with two **26px supporting icons** above it. Its visible order is **Earth, Water, Fire, Air**, distinct from the internal game/native index order. This is a genuine interaction choice, not just a technical accident.

No custom icon textures or fonts are bundled. All imagery is referenced from the game client's existing UI/spellbook, making the interface feel at home within old WoW.

## Empty state has a purpose

**alwaysShow** defaults to true, so even before the player has placed a totem the four elemental compartments show a dim familiar icon and **--** for remaining time. During combat a red exclamation appears over each missing element; outside combat the exclamation is hidden.

This is not evidence of a gameplay rule saying four totems should always be cast. It is a visual status cue. Its usefulness, annoyance or interpretation needs genuine player testing. A player can hide the whole panel with **/totemtimers hide**, then bring it back with **show**.

The auxiliary shield slot stays visible even when shield buffs are absent, with a dim Lightning Shield icon and red **!**; the weapon enchant icon hides when no temporary enchant is detected. These asymmetries match current code and should be explained in screenshots if the portfolio later adds them.

## Shields and enchants at a glance

An active shield displays a charge number in green, gold or red, inviting the player to notice a low-charge state without scanning another buff bar. A weapon imbue shows a small icon, with the item tooltip on hover.

The current implementation does not measure enchant duration or show main and off hands independently. A visual redesign should not claim these are present.

## Movement and frame ownership

Use **/totemtimers unlock** to drag with the left mouse button, **lock** to finish, and **reset** to return to the default center-relative position. The setting and anchor survive reload via account-wide SavedVariables. The **/ttimers** alias offers the same commands. There is no standalone settings screen or keybinding UI.

## Design questions for future testing

- Are time fonts readable at common UI scales and color-vision settings?
- Does a red **!** for each empty element encourage unnecessary totem casting?
- Would users want a neutral no-warning mode or only warnings for previously active elements?
- Does the shield corner show enough context when tooltip charge reads zero or Earth Shield has more than six charges?
- Is a high-frequency 0.1-second refresh necessary for every tooltip-backed auxiliary state?
- Do the side icons and tooltip hover work reliably next to other addons?

These are unapproved questions, not new features or tested accessibility conclusions.

## Engineering problems to resolve with the creator

**Attempt versus confirmed totem:** Wrapping functions is low-friction but can show failed casts as real countdowns. Native API availability determines whether that estimate is corrected. A server/client-tested repair might reconcile failures and destruction, but the creator has not approved one.

**Fast detection versus safe hooks:** Polling and wrapping globals every 0.1s can coexist with some addons yet also risks accumulating wrapper chains in an arms race with another hook manager. Test before claiming this is an observed failure.

**Missing reminders versus player choice:** A combat exclamation for every empty element might support awareness but could create unhelpful pressure; a future opt-out isn't approved yet.

**Localization and custom clients:** Some shield/enchant names and tooltip duration patterns are English literals; compatibility is not universal by declaration alone.

**Account-wide versus personal placement:** Keeping one setting across all characters is efficient, but per-character layouts are a possible alternative only if chosen.

**Names are literal English keys** (with trailing Rank suffix removed), not class-independent IDs. Durations in the table are used when the addon can't derive duration from a spell/action tooltip. Client-specific totem changes and rank-specific durations require verification.

| Element | Named totem | Fallback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire | Searing Totem | 30s |
| Fire | Fire Nova Totem | 5s |
| Fire | Magma Totem | 20s |

# Warrior Start Attack

**A small Warrior quality-of-life addon for World of Warcraft Vanilla 1.12.1**

**Project creator:** Babuni.dev  
**Addon version:** 1.0.0  
**Declared interface:** `11200`  
**Implementation:** [`WarriorStartAttack.lua`](WarriorStartAttack.lua) and [`WarriorStartAttack.toc`](WarriorStartAttack.toc)  
**Documentation audit:** October 26, 2026 — source and Git history examined; **not tested in a game client**.

**Warrior Start Attack** starts regular melee auto-attacks when a Warrior attempts one of 20 configured offensive abilities and has a **living, attackable target**. It does so *before* the original action is processed, so pressing Heroic Strike with insufficient rage can still start white-weapon swings. Repeated watched presses are designed **not** to toggle off an attack that is already running.

**Intimidating Shout is the intentional exception:** its recognized icon tries to stop auto-attacking. This is an action-trigger convenience tool, not a spell-success detector, a combat rotation system, or a replacement for the player's control.

## Installing it

```text
World of Warcraft/
└── Interface/
    └── AddOns/
        └── WarriorStartAttack/
            ├── WarriorStartAttack.toc
            └── WarriorStartAttack.lua
```

Copy both files into that folder, restart WoW or reload the UI, and enable **Warrior Start Attack** in the addon list. The source prints `Warrior Start Attack loaded.` in chat when the file executes.

The addon has **no slash commands, options panel, SavedVariables, or other configuration UI**. You configure it by editing the icon tables near the start of the Lua file. The repository also has **no committed LICENSE file**; do not assume an open-source license from the presence of public code.

## How it behaves

1. The addon notices an action through **`UseAction`**, **`CastSpell`**, or **`CastSpellByName`**. It wraps each global function, checks the ability's icon, and then calls the original function.
2. If the icon is in the offensive whitelist, the player is a **Warrior**, and the target exists, is alive and is hostile/attackable, it checks whether melee auto-attack is already active.
3. If the attack appears inactive, the code calls the Vanilla API **`AttackTarget()`** once. This matters because **`AttackTarget()` toggles attack** and would switch it off if called blindly.
4. If the icon matches **Intimidating Shout**, the code instead attempts to switch off an active attack. This stop branch is not currently guarded by `IsWarrior()`; see [architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) and the [roadmap](ROADMAP.md).
5. The original action function still runs afterwards. The addon doesn't check mana/rage, success/failure, attack range or whether a cast was completed before attempting its extra attack-state change.

The auto-attack-state check scans action-bar slots **1–120** for an active **Attack** action (`IsAttackAction` and `IsCurrentAction`). If it cannot find one, it relies on a locally tracked flag updated by `PLAYER_ENTER_COMBAT`, `PLAYER_LEAVE_COMBAT`, and the addon's own attack toggles. This is a useful fallback, **not necessarily perfect evidence of active melee swings** on every client or combat situation.

## Built-in offensive whitelist

The initial and current code contains **20** icon mappings:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bloodthirst | Cleave | Demoralizing Shout |
| Disarm | Execute | Hamstring |
| Heroic Strike | Intercept | Mortal Strike |
| Mocking Blow | Overpower | Pummel |
| Rend | Revenge | Shield Bash |
| Slam | Sunder Armor | Taunt |
| Thunder Clap | Whirlwind | |

**Stop-attack mapping:** Intimidating Shout (`Ability_GolemThunderClap` icon).

Some of these are shouts, tactical actions or taunts rather than damaging hits; the whitelist expresses the creator's selection of **combat-initiating attempts**, not a claim that every item deals physical damage.

### Change the whitelist

Open `WarriorStartAttack.lua` and edit `offensiveIcons` or `stopAttackIcons`. Keys are the game client's internal icon texture paths, such as:

```lua
["Interface\\Icons\\Ability_Rogue_Ambush"] = true, -- Heroic Strike
```

The same icon is used across ranks of a spell, and the code avoids using translated spell names as the whitelist. For `CastSpellByName`, it uses the incoming **localized name only to find a spellbook entry**, then compares that spell's icon to the whitelist.

**Limit:** icons are **not guaranteed unique spell IDs**. Other abilities or macros sharing a recognized texture may cause an unintended match. Conversely, icon-path changes on a particular game client can prevent a match. Test changes on the actual client.

## Intended safeguards and limitations

- **Starts only for Warriors:** `StartAttackIfPossible` checks `UnitClass("player")` for `WARRIOR`.
- **Target checks:** requires `UnitExists("target")`, a living target, and `UnitCanAttack("player", "target")`.
- **Repeated triggers:** aims to avoid `AttackTarget()` when an attack is already active; whether detection works without an Attack button present is a test item.
- **Stop behavior:** triggered by Intimidating Shout icon; its current function lacks the class guard used for starting attacks.
- **No player configuration persistence:** icons are code-defined, not SavedVariables.
- **Client version:** TOC specifies interface 11200 and Lua comments specify **1.12.1 / Lua 5.0**. Function behavior on custom Vanilla servers or other eras remains unverified.
- **Compatibility with other addons:** replacing the global casting/action functions can interact with other hooks according to installation/load order.

The claim of **client-language independence** is an implementation intention supported by icon matching; it was **not** verified by testing localized clients during this review.

## Troubleshooting checklist

If the addon doesn't load, confirm the folder and filenames and look for the startup chat line. If a configured action fails to start auto-attack, check that you are playing a Warrior, have a living hostile target, and that the actual spell's icon matches a table key. If repeated presses stop combat unexpectedly, test whether a normal **Attack** action is on a bar and whether the state fallback is getting out of sync; capture actual steps and client version before proposing a fix.

# WarriorStartAttack — creative concept

**Creative author:** Babuni.dev  
**Scope:** World of Warcraft 1.12.1 Warrior melee quality-of-life enhancement.

## Combat intent without repetitive busywork

In Vanilla WoW, an attempted Warrior ability is not always a completed attack. Rage can be insufficient; an ability can be unusable or fail. The creative premise of **Warrior Start Attack** is that choosing an aggressive move should nevertheless let the character begin **ordinary melee swings** against a living hostile target. This lets the player focus on actions and character rather than on keeping the auto-attack toggle in the correct state.

The source's example is especially clear: pressing **Heroic Strike with too little rage** should still begin regular attacks. That makes the feature fundamentally **input-driven**, not the result of parsing combat events or choosing abilities automatically.

It also avoids a common trap with the old API: `AttackTarget()` is a toggle. Calling it each time a button is pressed could undo the player's attack. The addon therefore tries to learn whether auto-attack is active before touching it. Defensive/non-offensive abilities are not indiscriminately added; a whitelist expresses which abilities have the desired meaning.

## The revealing exception

**Intimidating Shout** has a different emotional/combat function. The implementation puts its icon on a **stop-attack list**, separating “begin attacking” from “disengage swinging” behavior. This explicit exception makes the addon more than a generic auto-attack macro applied to every button.

A future portfolio entry should preserve this relationship between player intent and the two opposite behaviors. The code's current stop branch can run for any class if an icon matches; whether that is a bug or a harmless consequence requires client testing and a creator decision about expected scope.

## The 1.12 technical constraint

Vanilla's `CastSpell` API receives a **spellbook slot**, and the current code doesn't rely on server spell IDs. The solution is to resolve **language-independent icon texture paths**, including when a translated spell name is supplied through `CastSpellByName`. This is a creative technical adaptation to the older game's capabilities.

Using icons means spell ranks share recognition and translated spell labels need no whitelist entries. It also introduces a tradeoff: icon graphics are not unique identifiers. The project should not be described as guaranteed perfect across every localized or modified client without tests.

## What the project is not

There is no GUI, networking, saved preferences, automation of rotations, target selection, automatic spell casting or performance optimization model. It is a **minimal gameplay usability idea**, implemented through legacy UI functions.

The Git history supplies one initial August 2026 implementation and October documentation changes. It does **not** preserve the original brainstorming transcript or a comparative test of alternatives, so no private intentions or AI authorship claims have been invented here.

**Creator and creative director:** Babuni.dev

## A practical frustration becomes a small interface idea

The project rests on a very particular experience of playing a Warrior in old World of Warcraft: the player presses an offensive ability to begin engaging an enemy, but that ability may not execute yet. The most concrete case preserved in the original README is **Heroic Strike with insufficient rage**. The player already decided to attack; nevertheless, the character may need a separate auto-attack activation before normal swings begin.

WarriorStartAttack attempts to remove that extra repetitive step. It makes the player's ordinary offensive input serve a second, tightly scoped function: start white-weapon auto-attacking a living, hostile target, even if the chosen ability doesn't fire. This is an interaction and convenience idea by **Babuni.dev**. The assistant documenting it later did not invent that goal.

The source makes clear that the addon is not a rotation engine. It doesn't pick the next spell, decide whom to target, or simulate combat. It reacts to an action the player initiated and then lets the original game function process the action as normal. That narrowness is part of what makes it distinctive as a usable, minimal addon rather than a large UI project.

## The August 10, 2026 first upload

The repository was created on **August 10, 2026** and received the commit **`b1f1ea1`** (“Add files via upload”). That commit already contained its core **160-line Lua file**, a version **1.0.0** manifest, and a practical short README. There is **only one visible functional upload** in the inspected history, so we cannot tell whether earlier local prototypes, experiments or debugging conversations preceded it.

The initial Lua selected **20** offensive abilities by their internal client icons, including Heroic Strike, Bloodthirst, Sunder Armor, Rend, Pummel, Taunt and Whirlwind. It also specified a special stop-action icon for **Intimidating Shout**. The author did not ask the addon to start attacking on every interaction; the whitelist establishes boundaries around which inputs imply engagement.

That choice matters more in the old client than it would appear at first. As the source comments explain, Vanilla's `CastSpell` receives a spellbook slot, not a modern spell ID for addon lookup. The code therefore intercepts three places where a spell action may be attempted—`UseAction`, `CastSpell`, `CastSpellByName`—and turns each into a texture lookup. For a `/cast` macro it uses the localized spell name to locate the spellbook entry and **then** uses its internal icon for inclusion in the table.

The benefit is that individual spell ranks and localized client spell labels need not each be stored in a handcrafted language whitelist. The price is that icon textures are not unique spell identities: the program may match two abilities sharing artwork. That is a source-supported technical limitation, not an observed player bug.

## Making a toggle act like a one-way start action

The second problem is subtler. The 1.12 API `AttackTarget()` is a **toggle**, not a guaranteed one-way “start.” The simple solution of calling it on every Heroic Strike press would sometimes undo exactly what the player wanted: if melee auto-attack was already active, pressing an offensive button could stop it.

To avoid that, the addon first scans action-bar slots **1 through 120** for a visible Attack action that the client marks both an attack action and current. If it finds one, it assumes auto-attacking already exists and doesn't toggle. If it doesn't find one, it uses a local `attackActive` flag. That flag changes when this addon toggles the attack and in response to `PLAYER_ENTER_COMBAT` and `PLAYER_LEAVE_COMBAT`.

The difference between being **in combat** and **actively swinging a weapon** deserves attention. The source uses combat events as a fallback, but they don't independently prove that an auto-attack is running. If the player has no Attack action on a bar, or if another addon changes attack state, the local flag could become inaccurate. Because the addon is working with a toggle, wrong state detection could produce unwanted behavior. No actual in-game failure was reported or reproduced in this audit.

## The meaningful stop-action exception

Intimidating Shout is on a different list, `stopAttackIcons`. When a recognized shout input is attempted, the addon checks attack state and may call `AttackTarget()` to **stop** the swing. That is an explicit part of the source's intended player experience, not an accidental omitted offensive skill.

A technical nuance surfaced during this documentation review: the **start** function checks that the player is a Warrior, but the **stop** function does not. The hooked action functions are global; on a non-Warrior using a matching icon, the stop logic could also run. The creator hasn't approved changing this behavior in this session. The prudent next step is an actual target-client test, followed by a decision, rather than silently broadening the work from documentation to code modification.

# WarriorStartAttack — architecture and API behavior

**Version observed:** 1.0.0, interface 11200.  
**Code source:** `WarriorStartAttack.lua` on 2026-10-26. **Static analysis only.**

## Event and hook flow

```text
WoW player input
  |-- Action-bar button: UseAction(slot, checkCursor, onSelf)
  |      -> GetActionTexture(slot)
  |-- Spellbook action: CastSpell(spellSlot, bookType)
  |      -> GetSpellTexture(slot, bookType)
  '-- Macro / /cast / API: CastSpellByName(localizedName, onSelf)
         -> strip trailing "(...)" suffix
         -> iterate GetSpellName / GetSpellTexture across spellbook
         -> match icon for same localized spell name
               |
               v
       known stop icon? -> StopAttackIfActive()
       known offensive icon? -> StartAttackIfPossible()
       neither? -> no extra action
               |
               v
       call original WoW action/casting function
```

These wrappers are assigned **globally** at file load, so unrelated addons may interact according to load order. The code does not intercept every conceivable ability call: only these three functions and the textures/names they expose.

## Offensive gating

`StartAttackIfPossible()` calls `AttackTarget()` only if all of these source checks pass:

1. `UnitClass("player")` returns class token **WARRIOR**.
2. `UnitExists("target")` is true.
3. `UnitIsDead("target")` is false.
4. `UnitCanAttack("player", "target")` is true.
5. `IsAutoAttacking()` is false.

After calling the toggle, it immediately sets `attackActive = true`. It does **not** test range, rage, cast outcome or the presence of an ongoing swing timer. This intentional **pre-action** timing makes insufficient-rage Heroic Strike a useful example.

## Stop behavior

`StopAttackIfActive()` checks `IsAutoAttacking()` and calls the same **toggle** to stop, then sets `attackActive = false`. The sole stop icon is `Interface\\Icons\\Ability_GolemThunderClap`, annotated as **Intimidating Shout**.

Unlike starting, the stop function is **not** conditional on `IsWarrior()`. All three globally installed wrappers can therefore activate the stop path if an icon happens to match on another class. This is a source-level risk requiring actual client tests and a creator decision, **not a proven in-game bug**.

## Detecting current attacks

```text
IsAutoAttacking():
  for actionSlot = 1..120:
      if IsAttackAction(actionSlot)
         and IsCurrentAction(actionSlot):
           return true
  return attackActive
```

The boolean `attackActive` is updated by the addon when it toggles attacks, as well as through registered `PLAYER_ENTER_COMBAT` and `PLAYER_LEAVE_COMBAT` events using Vanilla's global `event` variable. That event fallback is **not the same as a guaranteed server-confirmed melee auto-attack status**. Without a visible Attack action and with other external state changes, it may be stale or too broad.

Because `AttackTarget()` is a **toggle**, the correctness of starting/stopping depends on correctly detecting the live attack state. The README describes intended behavior; a reliable client test must confirm it.

## Icon matching and localization

There are **20 true entries** in the `offensiveIcons` table, each referencing a literal internal texture path. They are used for all spell ranks with that texture. The stop table contains one icon.

`CastSpellByName` is special: it receives a possibly translated spell name. `SpellNameHasIcon` removes a parenthesized suffix, walks the spellbook using `GetSpellName`, selects entries whose name equals the supplied localized name, and only then checks their `GetSpellTexture` against the icon table. **Whitelist membership remains icon-based**, though spellbook lookup still depends on same-language name equality.

This reduces translation maintenance but can be fooled by shared/mismatched icons and should be tested with localized clients and rank syntax.

## Packaging and persistence

The TOC declares `Interface 11200`, title **Warrior Start Attack**, author **Babuni.dev**, and version **1.0.0**, loading one Lua file. There is **no SavedVariables directive**, addon frame UI, slash command, chat transmission, timer, database or external network interaction. Startup prints one status message in the default chat frame.

The game client is not present in this audit. Source analysis does not establish verified behavior on specific 1.12 custom clients or other client generations.

# WarriorStartAttack — player interaction and ergonomics

**Creative author:** Babuni.dev.

## Invisible until needed

WarriorStartAttack has no panel. Its design is a behavior change at the moment a player presses a familiar ability. Instead of adding another visible button or requiring the player to remember `/startattack` before each move, it uses the underlying game action to infer when normal melee swings should begin.

The hero example is a **Heroic Strike press without enough rage**. A player has shown intent to attack, even when the special ability cannot fire yet. The addon attempts to start normal swings, allowing the encounter to begin without a separate toggle. This is not a guarantee that the Heroic Strike itself will cast.

## Keep the gesture reversible

Unlike a macro that always executes `AttackTarget()`, which could turn active auto-attack off, the addon first checks for a running attack. The same recognition system has a **stop** list: Intimidating Shout asks the addon to stop auto-attacking.

This pair of interactions makes the addon feel responsive to different combat intentions. The player still chooses the ability; the addon only manages basic auto-swing state. The stated intent is that repeated uses of offensive buttons do not interrupt attack.

## The whitelist is part of the design

Twenty combat actions are recognized. The list includes not just direct blows but utility or threat-related actions (Taunt, Disarm, Demoralizing Shout and others). Their presence represents a broad “actively engaging an enemy” interpretation, while defensive buttons remain outside the table unless the user edits source.

Customization currently requires changing icon paths in Lua and reloading. That is minimal, but not an accessible configuration method for everyone. A settings menu is a possible future choice, **not a currently approved requirement**.

## Limitations of invisible feedback

If auto-attack state is misread or the player lacks a recognized Attack action on a bar, there is no UI warning; the user discovers it through combat behavior. A startup chat line confirms the Lua loaded, not that every hook was exercised.

The global stop branch currently lacks a class gate, which also matters to usability if non-Warriors install the addon. Both issues should be evaluated in the game before any design correction is declared necessary.

## Proposed usability checks, not test claims

Does the addon feel seamless at low rage? Does it avoid accidental disengagement on repeated presses? Does Intimidating Shout reliably stop and allow resumption? Is source-level icon editing sufficient for Babuni.dev's preferred audience? Preserve the creator's decision authority when evaluating alternatives.

# WorkThatGodBod

**Creator and author:** Babuni.dev  
**Target:** World of Warcraft 1.12.1 / Interface `11200`  
**Current declared version:** **1.1**  
**Status:** Source inspected on 2026-10-26; **not tested in-game** during this documentation review.

**WorkThatGodBod** is a tiny roleplay-flavored prompt generator for real-life microbreaks during World of Warcraft. Pressing one of the action-bar slots you have chosen can occasionally produce a short, randomized prompt about **movement, posture, breathing, screen breaks, or drinking water**. The content blends everyday actions with fantasy imagery—stretching like a banner in the wind, refilling mana, or loosening adventurer joints.

It does **not** monitor your health, count completed exercises, or force a break. It integrates with action-button presses rather than interrupting you on a periodic background timer. The current source contains **99 unique prompts**.

## Important: some prompts are posted to other players

**The addon is not strictly private.** After a reminder qualifies, `outputExercise` randomly routes it to local chat **86%** of the time or attempts to send it to group/public-facing channels **14%** of the time:

| Output target | Share of qualifying reminders |
| --- | ---: |
| Local chat frame (only you) | 86% |
| Guild chat | 4% |
| Say | 2% |
| Yell | 2% |
| Party | 6% |

These are exact branches of the present source—not a verified distribution of **successfully delivered** messages. A send may fail when the player is not in the required group. The historical README presented the tool as quiet chat-only nudges but did not explain these transmissions. The addon **does not have a local-only toggle** in v1.1; `/godbod off` disables all prompts.

**This documentation corrects the description only.** It does not alter which messages are transmitted. The creator has not yet selected whether future behavior should be local-only or explicitly opt-in to sharing.

## Installation

Place `WorkThatGodBod.lua` and `WorkThatGodBod.toc` inside:

```text
Interface/
└── AddOns/
    └── WorkThatGodBod/
        ├── WorkThatGodBod.toc
        └── WorkThatGodBod.lua
```

Restart the game, enable the addon, and verify that it loads on your chosen 1.12-compatible client. This review did not perform that installation.

## Commands and setup

The current version supports **multiple watched action slots**. This differs from the original one-slot design and from the older README description.

| Command | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `/godbod watch` | Toggle showing action-bar slot numbers when buttons are pressed |
| `/godbod slot <number>` | **Add** an action slot to the watched set |
| `/godbod unslot <number>` | Remove one watched slot |
| `/godbod clear` | Remove **all** watched slots |
| `/godbod timer <seconds>` | Set minimum seconds between eligible prompt attempts (default **60**) |
| `/godbod chance <0-100>` | Set chance of producing a prompt on an eligible attempt (default **100%**) |
| `/godbod on`, `/godbod off` | Enable or disable reminders |
| `/godbod info` | Display watched-slot count, chance, timer, and enabled state |

For example, use `/godbod watch`, press an ability button, and note its slot. Use `/godbod slot 3` (adjust the number), then `/godbod watch` to stop printing slot numbers. Add further slots as wanted. To stop reminders altogether, use `/godbod off`.

There is **no** `/godbod cd` command in the current source. The current interval command is **`timer`**. The parser accepts command words case-insensitively.

## How the implementation behaves

The Lua wraps WoW's global `UseAction`. On each watched-slot press it checks enabled state, the interval since the previous eligible attempt, and a random percentage. The original action is then called with its arguments; WorkThatGodBod does not cast abilities for you.

The cooldown timestamp is updated **before** testing the random chance. A failed chance roll therefore still consumes the configured interval. There is no autonomous recurring timer or tracking of elapsed gaming-session duration; `GetTime()` is used as a gate when watched actions are pressed.

The TOC declares an **account-wide** `WorkThatGodBodDB` table, but the Lua stores each character's settings separately under `chars["name-realm"]`. Slot preferences, chance, interval, and enabled state are character-specific in that schema. There is no health-history or completed-activity log.

## A small wellbeing nudge, not medical guidance

Prompts are playful suggestions, not personalized exercises or instructions from a healthcare professional. Some propose balance, neck movement, squats or other movements that will not suit every player or environment. Skip anything uncomfortable or unsafe. The creator's original intention is a **gentle interruption of static play**, not a measure of physical performance.

## Development history and licensing

The repository began on **2025-12-14** as a simpler `v0.1` with one watched slot and local chat output. During **January 2026**, Git revisions expanded the prompt pool, added multiple slots, experimented with shared chat destinations, and reorganized preferences into per-character records. The significant **v1.1** rewrite on **2026-01-24** turned the prompts into Azeroth-themed writing and removed earlier `/world` and `/general` routes while retaining limited guild, say, yell, and party sends.

The project is released under its existing **MIT license**, which credits **Babuni.dev**. No runtime Lua, TOC or license file was changed for this documentation update.

# WorkThatGodBod — concept

**Creative author:** Babuni.dev  
**Format:** lightweight World of Warcraft addon for voluntary real-world microbreak prompts.

## A moment of movement inside the game

The idea is modest and appealing: instead of asking a player to run a fitness app alongside an evening of World of Warcraft, attach occasional suggestions to an action they already perform. A button press sometimes produces a small invitation to move, shift posture, rest eyes, take a few breaths, or drink water.

The original project README sets the tone: **“No timers, no UI, no nagging—just small nudges when you’re already in motion.”** Its meaning is that the addon does not continuously interrupt with scheduled alarms. The current implementation **does** use a configurable elapsed-time threshold to space out eligible prompts. Those are compatible distinctions as long as documentation says “no background alarm,” rather than literally “no timing.”

## Fantasy gives ordinary care a playful voice

The current text pool narrates mundane gestures in familiar Azeroth language. Water becomes a mana refill. Rolling shoulders becomes loosening worn armor. Looking away from a screen resembles watching the horizon for gryphons. That framing connects the player to their game world while inviting a short, voluntary real-world action.

The repository's January 24, 2026 source rewrite demonstrates the transition from mostly plain exercise instructions to **fantasy-themed micro-prompts**. That is evidence of a change to the creative expression. The original discussion and who proposed every individual metaphor are not recorded, so they are not invented here.

## Design principles supported by the source

- **Voluntary:** `/godbod off` disables the nudge; no compliance reporting exists.
- **Action-associated:** checks occur when the user presses configured action slots, not on a repeating background alarm.
- **Occasional:** a configurable interval and chance control frequency; chance failure still consumes an interval.
- **Minimal UI:** feedback uses text chat; there is no overlay, exercise log or progress bar.
- **Game-world flavor:** 99 unique written prompts mix hydration, posture, breath, balance and movement with fantasy references.
- **Character-specific preferences:** the account-wide saved table is organized by character name and realm.

## Important tension with the original quiet intent

Although the README describes private-feeling “small nudges,” source v1.1 intentionally routes a minority of emitted messages to PARTY, GUILD, SAY or YELL. **14% of qualifying reminders are sent to one of those nonlocal destinations, not merely shown privately.** The reasons for this design choice are not established by the available conversations. Public delivery, possible spam and player consent are unresolved creative decisions, not silently endorsed features.

## Boundaries

This is **not** medical advice, health tracking, an inactivity detector, an automatic workout planner, or a competitive fitness product. It does not verify that the prompted action was completed. The document is a source-grounded concept reconstruction; only explicit future creator decisions should change its scope.

## The creative premise: make a tiny break feel like play

WorkThatGodBod begins with a problem familiar to people who spend long stretches in a game: a person can become so involved in the world on the screen that small acts like moving, drinking water or changing posture fade into the background. The original README presents a very specific tone for the solution: **“No timers, no UI, no nagging—just small nudges when you’re already in motion.”**

The concept belongs to Babuni.dev. Rather than putting a monitoring dashboard beside WoW, the project makes the existing action bar a low-friction trigger. The player chooses actions that happen naturally; every so often the addon selects a short, voluntary suggestion. A reminder does not compel or even track whether a movement was done. Its success is conceived as a small pause without turning recreation into another job.

This is an interpretation consistent with the original description and implementation. The repository does not preserve a prompt-by-prompt authoring record, so the exact first conversation and AI role in conceiving individual mechanics cannot be reconstructed.

GitHub shows the addon manifest and initial Lua committed on **2025-12-14** (`1c10ea1`, `8631405`). The code header called itself **v0.1**. It used a single watched action slot, a 60-second interval, configurable probability, and short practical prompts. Its output went to the local chat frame, not to other players' channels. A separate same-day change (`8bd285b`) altered the color presentation of the GodBod prefix. Such tiny revisions matter in aggregate: the tool was being shaped not only as a mechanism but as something comfortable to glance at while playing.

# WorkThatGodBod — technical architecture v1.1

**Source:** `WorkThatGodBod.lua` and `.toc` on 2026-10-26. **Static source inspection only**, no WoW execution.

## Control flow

```text
Player presses an action bar slot
  -> replaced global UseAction(slot, checkCursor, onSelf)
     -> GOD_LoadOnce() binds the character's saved config
     -> if watchMode, print the slot locally
     -> if slot exists in GOD.slots:
          -> GOD_Trigger(GetTime())
             -> enabled?
             -> enough seconds since GOD.last?
             -> set GOD.last = now
             -> math.random(1,100) <= GOD.chance?
                -> pick one of 99 EXERCISES
                -> outputExercise(text)
                   -> 86% local
                   ->  4% GUILD
                   ->  2% SAY
                   ->  2% YELL
                   ->  6% PARTY
     -> call captured _Orig_UseAction(slot, checkCursor, onSelf)
```

The original button is delegated after the attempt. No check of spell success, combat state or whether the suggested movement was performed. The addon has no repeating update loop, so its named `timer` value is an interval between eligible **action-driven attempts**, not a continuously ringing alarm.

## Source structure

- **`EXERCISES`:** a flat table of **99 different prompt strings**. `U.pick` selects uniformly using `math.random(1, n)`.
- **`U` helpers:** `trim`, `upper`, `split_cmd` using `string.find`, and `pick`.
- **`charKey()`:** joins `UnitName("player")` with `GetRealmName()` (fallbacks if absent).
- **`GOD` table:** bound character configuration (`db`, `slots`, `timer`, `chance`, `enabled`), unsaved `watchMode`, unsaved `last` (initially `0`), plus `_loaded`.
- **`outputExercise()`:** chooses a chat destination; it does not verify eligibility for guild/party messaging or fall back locally after a failed send.
- **Slash handler:** `/godbod` with nine case-insensitive commands: `slot`, `unslot`, `clear`, `watch`, `chance`, `timer`, `on`, `off`, `info`.

## Configuration/persistence

The TOC has `## SavedVariables: WorkThatGodBodDB` (account-wide). Lua uses:

```text
WorkThatGodBodDB
└── chars
    └── "<character-name>-<realm-name>"
        ├── slots       -- table: slot ID => true
        ├── timer       -- default 60 seconds
        ├── chance      -- default 100
        └── enabled     -- default true
```

`GOD_LoadOnce` is called on a `UseAction` press or slash command, creating the current character record when needed. `PLAYER_LOGIN` seeds `math.random`. `PLAYER_LOGOUT` writes values back **if `GOD.db` has already been bound**, avoiding a write from an uninitialized per-character record.

Because settings reside inside an account-level table under distinct character keys, “per-character” refers to **application-level separation**, not the TOC's `SavedVariablesPerCharacter` mechanism.

## Output distribution — read the condition, not the comment

| `math.random(1,100)` outcomes | Path | Calculated share |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| 1–86 | `godChat` local | 86% |
| 87–90 | `SendChatMessage(..., "GUILD")` | 4% |
| 91–92 | `... "SAY"` | 2% |
| 93–94 | `... "YELL"` | 2% |
| **95–100** | `... "PARTY"` | **6%** |

The nearby comment says “95-96 /party”; that comment is **inaccurate** because the actual code compares `roll >= 95`. These percentages are conditional on an emote/prompt actually being produced. Invalid group/party state can affect delivery. No code-level route to general/world channels remains in v1.1.

## Remaining source-level edge cases

- `GOD.last` begins at zero; a first press shortly after entering the game could be suppressed if `GetTime()` is below the configured `timer`.
- Timestamp is advanced **before** the probability roll; a missed roll still consumes the interval.
- `/godbod slot` checks `n >= 1` but does not require an integer or validate legal action IDs; `unslot` accepts any numeric value.
- Wrapper chaining with other add-ons depends on load order and delegation.
- `outputExercise` attempts social sends without explicit player opt-in or destination-failure fallback.
- `math.randomseed` resets the global Lua PRNG state on login.
- Some characters' settings may become inaccessible after renaming or changing realms because they are keyed by name-realm.

These are **source-supported possibilities**, not verified game-client defects.

# WorkThatGodBod — interaction and experience design

**Creator:** Babuni.dev.

## A tiny interruption that belongs to the world

WorkThatGodBod takes the practical advice to look away from a screen or move briefly, and wraps it in a miniature adventure. Its current prose is gently theatrical: a player's shoulders may feel like armor, hydration like restoring mana, and a stretch like raising a banner. The aim visible in the README is a low-friction invitation rather than a fitness regimen or nagging scheduler.

The interface is intentionally small. There is no window to keep open: the player chooses action slots and receives a reminder only when a watched button is pressed and the current time/probability gates allow it.

## The player journey

1. Run `/godbod watch` to learn action slot numbers.
2. Use `/godbod slot <n>` to add one or several actions; turn watch mode off afterward.
3. Choose a comfortable minimum interval with `/godbod timer` and an occasional response rate with `chance`.
4. Play normally. A qualifying press may select a new prompt from the 99-line pool.
5. Ignore, adapt, or follow it as personally appropriate; `/godbod off` disables reminders.
6. Use `unslot`, `clear` or `info` to adjust the tool.

The only automatically tracked state is the short-term time gate and configured preferences. There is no compliance or personal wellness history.

## An important tension: quiet nudges versus shared messages

The original README describes **“no UI, no nagging”** and implies a gentle interruption. The code in v1.1, however, may broadcast a prompt to nearby players or a social channel. Of qualifying messages, **14%** are routed to GUILD, SAY, YELL, or PARTY. Players not expecting that could see it as embarrassing or disruptive, and other participants did not request a reminder.

This tension is a real design question, not a historical motive we can assign from the source. The previous v0.2 output routing even included general/world channels; v1.1 explicitly removed those routes but kept limited sharing. **No local-only preference is implemented in v1.1.**

## Tone and accessibility

Prompts are imaginative and usually concise. They cover sitting and standing, arm/leg movement, eye breaks, breathing and hydration. Some mention balance with eyes closed, neck motion or higher-effort exercises. The addon cannot judge someone's needs or safety. Readers should understand these as optional suggestions, never obligations or health advice.

Potential future design improvements—user choice of local-only output, a “skip movements” filter, shorter chat copy, and clearer notification of public sending—belong in the roadmap as **proposals**, not unapproved changes.

## No category selector

Although the writing falls into recognizable themes, the source uses one flat `EXERCISES` list and selects uniformly across it. “Hydration,” “movement,” and “posture” are editorial content tags, not implemented filtering options.

**Creative authority:** Babuni.dev.

This register distinguishes direct source observations from assumptions and from decisions Babuni.dev still needs to make.

## Current implementation evidence

| Topic | Code / history | Status and qualification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Optional movement/hydration cues during play | Original README, `EXERCISES` | Stated project purpose and implemented text |
| No background alarm loop | `UseAction` wrapper; no OnUpdate timer | Implemented; a time **threshold** still exists |

| Fantasy-themed prose | January 24 rewrite `9b67d16` | Visible content change; authoring dialogue unavailable |
| Social message routing | `outputExercise` and January historical diffs | Source includes 14% nonlocal routes; reason/approval not recovered |

## Evolution, not invented deliberations

The first v0.1 source used one watched slot and local chat, with relatively plain prompts. A 2026-01-05 revision introduced random chat destination routing, including world/general channel codes. Subsequent commits added multi-slot support. On 2026-01-24, the code was refactored into a standalone 1.1 structure, introduced character-keyed saved settings and rewrote the prompt pool in fantasy language. The rewrite removed world/general sending, **but** retained party/say/yell and added guild sends.

The Git diffs prove these changes happened; they do **not** prove what discussions, safety evaluations, user approvals or rejection rationales led to them.

## Material discrepancy between README and source

The old README called the addon “zero UI, chat-only” and “no nagging,” without disclosing the 14% chance to route a produced prompt to other players. It also described one chosen slot, although the source supports many. The expanded README corrects these facts rather than silently modifying runtime behavior.

A separate source comment describes party messages as `95–96` only; actual `roll >= 95` selects `95–100` (**6%**). This is an implementation/comment discrepancy, not a tested statistical result.

## Open creator decisions

1. **Visibility and consent:** should reminders be strictly private by default? Should public routes require explicit opt-in?
2. **Time semantics:** should the cooldown restart on every eligible attempt, or only when a reminder is actually delivered?
3. **Intensity:** should some prompts be excluded/modified for accessibility or user preference?
4. **Character configuration:** should per-character settings remain nested in the account-wide DB, or use TOC-level character saved variables?
5. **Portfolio narrative:** how does the creator personally explain the move from straightforward reminders to Azeroth-themed writing?

This pass answered none of those questions on Babuni.dev's behalf. Only documentation changed.

# WorkThatGodBod — prompt writing and content inventory

**Author:** Babuni.dev  
**Canonical text:** `EXERCISES` table in `WorkThatGodBod.lua`.

## Current corpus

The current v1.1 source contains **99 unique English-language prompt strings** in a single Lua table. Each selection is uniform across the same pool; there is no in-code category tag, preferred ordering, intensity scoring, or localization layer.

Representative wording:

> “Drink water as if refilling mana. Inhale deep. Exhale slow.”

> “Stand proud like an NPC with a backstory.”

> “Move joints gently. No force. Longevity matters.”

These examples demonstrate the desired relationship: a mundane real-world action is reframed as something a character might recognize in Azeroth. The text remains an *invitation*, not a measurement or requirement.

## Editorial motifs (not runtime categories)

| Editorial theme | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Hydration | Water as mana replenishment or a helpful buff |
| Posture | Shoulder alignment, neutral stance, jaw relaxation |
| Movement | Walking, marching, squats, stretches and joint motion |
| Eyes and screen breaks | Looking at the horizon, resting the eyes and blinking |
| Breath and calm | Gentle breathing, release of tension and quiet pauses |
| Humor and roleplay | Armor, dragons, taverns, NPCs, gryphons and warhorses |

No categories are selected in the code; one randomly chosen line can span multiple themes.

## Proven textual evolution

- Initial **v0.1** source on **2025-12-14** had a shorter, predominantly plain-language movement pool.
- A **2026-01-05** revision added many suggestions, then a **2026-01-06** change corrected a missing comma between list entries.
- The **2026-01-24** rewrite (`9b67d16`) replaced much of the plain phrasing with an expanded, consistent fantasy style. This is the strongest source evidence for the current content direction.

Git confirms changes to text; it does not establish which individual words Babuni.dev versus an AI assistant first drafted or why every metaphor was changed. Do not fabricate an authoring dialogue.

## Safety and content stewardship

The prompts are not medical recommendations. Particular movements will be inappropriate for some people, situations, or physical limitations, and the addon never observes whether one was done. Preserve the playful, optional character voice and include a clear ability to ignore prompts. A future filter or lower-intensity pool would require author approval.

Some prompts can be **shared in chat**. This affects both the player and recipients; content curation must consider context, consent and chat etiquette as well as style.

To edit the corpus, revise the canonical Lua table rather than maintaining a duplicated 99-line list here. Document why the creator chose the new tone, what actually changed and whether the client was tested.

## Local Wi-Fi serving (2026-10-26 source addition)

`main.cjs` now includes a Node HTTP server that binds to all IPv4 network interfaces on port 4173 only when requested from the desktop menu. It allows only enumerated game assets and supports GET/HEAD; it stops when disabled or the app exits. `preload.cjs` exposes three IPC actions to the trusted Electron main frame. `game/wifi.js` and menu controls show hosting status and LAN URLs only when the preload API exists. Browser visitors have no host controls or Node access.

The previously noted OGG routing gap was addressed in source, not yet verified in a packaged build.

The earlier imported-source finding that the custom Electron protocol did not allow OGG files is **historical**: the 2026-10-26 Wi-Fi source change expanded the relevant allowlist. Its successful operation in a packaged build has not been independently demonstrated. The LAN HTTP host is separate from the `raketenspiel://` local Electron protocol: the former serves a fixed allowlist over `http://<LAN IPv4>:4173/` on explicit request, while the latter loads the desktop window itself. `preload.cjs` exposes only `status`, `start`, and `stop`; `game/wifi.js` does not reveal host controls unless that Electron bridge is present.
